subject: synth
title: Audio Engineering
summary: What happens to your synth's signal after it leaves the jack: acoustics and hearing, microphones, loudspeaker drivers and enclosures, crossovers, power amplifiers, live and studio sound systems, and the room you listen in.

lessons.title: Pressure waves, speed and wavelength
lessons.summary: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally.
lessons.body:
Everything in this module happens in air. Your synth makes a voltage; a loudspeaker turns it into moving air; a room bounces it about; an ear or a microphone turns it back into something useful. Before looking at any of those devices, you need a working model of what sound in air actually is and how it behaves with distance.

Module 1 covered decibels as ratios and dBFS, and module 5 covered dBu and dBV for signal voltages. This lesson adds the decibel scale for *sound in air*: dB SPL.

## Sound is a pressure wave

A loudspeaker cone moving forward squashes the air in front of it slightly (a **acoustic compression**); moving back, it leaves the air slightly thinner (a **rarefaction**). Each layer of air pushes on the next, so the disturbance travels outward. The air molecules themselves only jiggle back and forth around where they started. What travels is the *pattern* of pressure.

```diagram
 cone   compression   rarefaction
  |  ||||||||    |   |   |   |||||||
  |  ||||||||    |   |   |   |||||||
  ---------> direction of travel
```

Two consequences matter for audio engineering:

- Sound is **longitudinal**: the air moves along the direction of travel, not across it.
- The pressure changes are **tiny**. Atmospheric pressure is about 101,325 Pa. A 120 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 20 Pa; a 60 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 0.02 Pa. These are pressure examples, not hearing-safety thresholds.

## Speed of sound and wavelength

In dry air the speed of sound depends mainly on temperature: warmer air molecules move faster, so they pass the disturbance on faster. For ideal dry air at fixed temperature, static pressure cancels from the sound-speed relation. Humidity also changes the speed, so precise outdoor alignment needs the actual conditions. A standard ideal-gas approximation, good for everyday air temperatures, is:

```formula
c = 331.3 √(1 + T / 273.15)
where
c: the speed of sound in dry air, in metres per second (m/s)
T: the air temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); everyday values are about 0–35 °C
331.3: the speed of sound in dry air at 0 °C, in m/s
273.15: the number you add to a Celsius temperature to get kelvin (absolute temperature), so 1 + T / 273.15 is the absolute temperature divided by that of 0 °C
√: square root: the number that, multiplied by itself, gives what is inside the brackets
In words: the speed of sound grows with the square root of the absolute temperature, which works out at roughly 0.6 m/s faster for every 1 °C warmer near room temperature.
```

Worked example at a room temperature of 20 °C:

```formula
c = 331.3 √(1 + 20 / 273.15)
c = 331.3 √(1.0732)
c = 331.3 × 1.0359
c ≈ 343.2 m/s
where
c: the speed of sound in dry air, in metres per second (m/s)
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
m: metres
s: seconds
In words: at 20 °C sound travels about 343 metres every second.
```

The approximation assumes dry air behaving as an ideal gas. Humidity generally raises the speed; its effect depends on temperature and water-vapour content. The dry-air calculation is an approximation, not a measured outdoor value. The same calculation as a short program:

```python
import math

def c_air(t_c):
    # Dry-air model; return metres/second.
    return 331.3 * math.sqrt(
        1 + t_c / 273.15)

for t in (0, 20, 30):
    print(f"{t:>2} C: {c_air(t):.1f} m/s")
```

```output
 0 C: 331.3 m/s
20 C: 343.2 m/s
30 C: 349.0 m/s
```

The usual working figure is **343 m/s at 20 °C**, which is about 1 metre every 2.9 ms. That number turns up everywhere: speaker delay times, room modes, crossover alignment.

**Wavelength** is how far the wave travels in one cycle. In one second the wave travels about 343 metres and completes as many cycles as its frequency, so each cycle covers the speed divided by the frequency:

```formula
λ = c / f
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength: the distance the wave travels during one cycle, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
f: the frequency of the sound, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, the unit of frequency: one cycle per second
In words: the wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency, so doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.
```

Worked example for a 1 kHz tone (1000 Hz):

```formula
λ = (343 m/s) / (1000 Hz)
λ = 0.343 m
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength, in metres (m)
m/s: metres per second, the unit of speed
m: metres
s: seconds
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: a 1 kHz tone has a wavelength of about 34 cm.
```

The same division gives the table below. It applies to any wave, as long as you use the speed for the medium the wave is in (sound in water travels about four times faster, so its wavelengths are four times longer).

| Frequency | Wavelength (at 343 m/s) |
|---|---|
| 20 Hz | 17.15 m |
| 100 Hz | 3.43 m |
| 1 kHz | 34.3 cm |
| 10 kHz | 3.43 cm |
| 20 kHz | 1.7 cm |

Audible wavelengths span a factor of 1,000, from longer than a house to shorter than your thumb. Relative size strongly affects diffraction and scattering. Reflection and absorption also depend on material impedance, construction, mounting and incidence angle.

## Key takeaways
- Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally.
- Temperature changes sound speed and therefore travel time.
- At a fixed sound speed, doubling frequency halves wavelength.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Taking the speed of sound as 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of a 343 Hz tone in air?

options.explanation: Correct. Sound covers 343 m in a second and completes 343 cycles in that time, so each cycle is 1 m long.
That is the distance sound travels in a whole second, not in one cycle. Divide by the frequency.
Off by a factor of 100. 1 cm wavelengths are around 34 kHz, above hearing.
That is the wavelength of 1 kHz (343 / 1000), not 343 Hz.

questions.workedExample:
Wavelength is the distance the wave travels during one cycle, so divide the speed by the number of cycles per second:

```formula
λ = c / f
λ = (343 m/s) / (343 Hz)
λ = 1 m
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in air, here 343 metres per second (m/s)
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
m: metres
s: seconds
In words: a 343 Hz tone has a wavelength of exactly 1 m when sound travels at 343 m/s.
```

A handy anchor: 343 Hz ↔ 1 m, so 3.43 kHz ↔ 10 cm and 34.3 Hz ↔ 10 m.

questions.prompt: You set a delay on a speaker 50 m from the stage assuming sound travels at 343 m/s, but the outdoor gig is at 0 °C, where it travels at about 331.3 m/s. About how far out is your delay setting?

options.explanation: Too small. The speed difference is about 3.5%, and 3.5% of roughly 146 ms is about 5 ms.
Correct. Sound takes about 150.9 ms to cover 50 m at 0 °C, but you set 145.8 ms, so the true arrival is about 5.1 ms later than you set.
That would mean the speed of sound had changed by about a third.

options.text: No difference: the speed of sound is constant
options.explanation: It varies with air temperature, by about 0.6 m/s per °C near room temperature.

questions.workedExample:
Travel time is distance divided by speed:

```formula
t = d / c
t_set = 50 m / (343 m/s) ≈ 145.8 ms
t_true = 50 m / (331.3 m/s) ≈ 150.9 ms
Δt = 150.9 ms − 145.8 ms ≈ 5.1 ms
where
t: the time sound takes to travel, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
d: the distance, here 50 metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, in metres per second (m/s)
t_set: the delay you set, using 343 m/s
t_true: the real travel time at 0 °C
Δt: the error; Δ (delta) means "change in"
m: metres
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: cold air slows the sound by about 3.5 %, so the real arrival is about 5 ms later than the delay you set.
```

At 50 m, a few milliseconds matters for the time alignment between main and delay speakers, so set delays by measurement on the day.

lessons.title: Read sound pressure in dB SPL
lessons.summary: The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS.
lessons.body:
## Sound pressure level: dB SPL

Sound pressure is the changing pressure around the ambient value, measured in pascals (Pa). For a level measurement, we use its RMS value: an average size over a specified time interval. Because the range is so huge, we use decibels relative to a reference of **20 µPa** (20 millionths of a pascal), roughly the quietest 1 kHz tone a young, healthy listener can detect. The sound pressure level is:

```formula
L_p = 20 log_10(p / p_0)
p_0 = 20 µPa = 0.00002 Pa
where
L_p: the sound pressure level, in decibels relative to 20 µPa (dB SPL)
p: the RMS sound pressure you measure, in pascals (Pa)
p_0: the reference pressure, 20 µPa, which is defined to be 0 dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you must raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(1000) = 3
µ: micro, meaning one millionth (0.000001)
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure: one newton of force per square metre
In words: count how many times bigger than 20 µPa the pressure is, take the base-10 logarithm and multiply by 20; every tenfold increase in pressure adds 20 dB.
```

The multiplier is 20, not 10, because pressure is a field quantity, like voltage: for a progressive wave in the same medium, sound intensity is proportional to pressure squared, and squaring a ratio doubles its logarithm (module 1 explains why). Worked example for a pressure of 1 Pa:

```formula
L_p = 20 log_10(1 Pa / 0.00002 Pa)
L_p = 20 log_10(50000)
L_p = 20 × 4.699
L_p ≈ 93.98 dB SPL
where
L_p: the sound pressure level, in dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure
dB: decibel, a tenth of a bel: a logarithmic way of expressing a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning the decibel figure is relative to 20 µPa
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a sound pressure of 1 pascal is about 94 dB SPL.
```

As a program, for a few pressures:

```python
import math

def spl(p_pa):
    # Compare RMS pressure to 20
    # micropascals.
    return 20 * math.log10(p_pa / 20e-6)

for p in (20e-6, 0.02, 1.0, 20.0):
    print(f"{p:>8} Pa = "
          f"{spl(p):6.2f} dB SPL")
```

```output
   2e-05 Pa =   0.00 dB SPL
    0.02 Pa =  60.00 dB SPL
     1.0 Pa =  93.98 dB SPL
    20.0 Pa = 120.00 dB SPL
```

Remember **1 Pa ≈ 94 dB SPL**. Microphone sensitivities are quoted at 1 Pa (the microphone units) and calibrators often produce 94 dB SPL for exactly this reason.

## Key takeaways
- The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS.
- One pascal RMS is approximately 94 dB SPL.
- Pressure ratios use twenty times the base-ten logarithm.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: A sound level meter shows an RMS pressure of 2 Pa. What is the sound pressure level?

options.explanation: This uses a multiplier of 10, the formula for power ratios. Pressure is a field quantity, so the multiplier is 20.
94 dB SPL is 1 Pa. Doubling the pressure adds 6 dB, giving 100.
Correct. 2 Pa is 100,000 times the 20 µPa reference, and a pressure ratio of 100,000 is 100 dB.
The decibel scale is relative to 20 µPa, not to 1 Pa.

questions.workedExample:
Sound pressure level compares the measured pressure with the 20 µPa reference:

```formula
L_p = 20 log_10(p / p_0)
L_p = 20 log_10(2 Pa / 0.00002 Pa)
L_p = 20 log_10(100000)
L_p = 20 × 5
L_p = 100 dB SPL
where
L_p: the sound pressure level, in dB SPL
p: the measured RMS pressure, here 2 pascals (Pa)
p_0: the reference pressure, 20 µPa = 0.00002 Pa
µ: micro, one millionth
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure (one newton per square metre)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning decibels relative to 20 µPa
In words: 2 Pa is 100,000 times the reference; the logarithm of that is 5, and 20 × 5 gives 100 dB SPL.
```

Cross-check: 1 Pa ≈ 94 dB SPL, and doubling pressure adds 6 dB, so 2 Pa ≈ 100 dB SPL.

lessons.title: Predict free-field distance loss
lessons.summary: Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field.
lessons.body:
## The inverse square law

A small source in open space (a **free field**, with no reflections) spreads its power over the surface of a growing sphere. The area of a sphere grows with the square of its radius, so the same power is shared over more and more air:

```formula
I = P_ac / (4πr^2)
p ∝ 1 / r
where
I: the sound intensity: the acoustic power passing through each square metre, in watts per square metre (W/m²)
P_ac: the acoustic power the source radiates, in watts (W); this is sound power, not the amplifier's electrical power
π: pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159
r: the distance from the source, in metres (m)
p: the RMS sound pressure at distance r, in pascals (Pa)
∝: "is proportional to": when one side is multiplied by some factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor
In words: 4 × π × r² is the area of a sphere of radius r, so intensity falls with the square of distance. Intensity is proportional to pressure squared, so pressure falls in proportion to 1/r: double the distance and the intensity quarters while the pressure halves.
```

This is the **inverse square law**. Turning the pressure ratio into decibels (20 × log, because pressure is a field quantity) gives the working form, which predicts the level at one distance from a level measured at another:

```formula
L_2 = L_1 − 20 log_10(r_2 / r_1)
where
L_1: the measured level at distance r_1, in dB SPL
L_2: the predicted level at distance r_2, in dB SPL
r_1: the distance where you know the level, in metres (m)
r_2: the distance you want the level at, in metres (m)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
In words: the level falls by 20 times the logarithm of the distance ratio, so it depends only on how many times further away you are, not on the distance in metres.
```

Each **doubling of distance** therefore loses the same amount:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(2)
ΔL = 20 × 0.30103
ΔL ≈ 6.02 dB
where
ΔL: the drop in level for a doubling of distance, in decibels (dB); Δ (delta) means "change in"
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: in a free field, every doubling of distance costs about 6 dB, usually rounded to 6 dB.
```

```python
import math

# The 1 m reference must be in the far
# field.
L1 = 100.0  # dB SPL at 1 m
for r in (1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 25):
    L = L1 - 20 * math.log10(r / 1)
    print(f"{r:>2} m: {L:6.2f} dB SPL")
```

```output
 1 m: 100.00 dB SPL
 2 m:  93.98 dB SPL
 4 m:  87.96 dB SPL
 8 m:  81.94 dB SPL
10 m:  80.00 dB SPL
25 m:  72.04 dB SPL
```

Worked example: a speaker gives 100 dB SPL at 1 m. What does a listener at 25 m get?

```formula
L_2 = 100 − 20 log_10(25 m / 1 m)
L_2 = 100 − 20 × 1.398
L_2 = 100 − 27.96
L_2 ≈ 72 dB SPL
where
L_2: the level at 25 m, in dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
m: metres
dB: decibels
SPL: sound pressure level (relative to 20 µPa)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 25 times further away loses about 28 dB, leaving about 72 dB SPL. Ten times the distance would cost exactly 20 dB.
```

> [!warning] Where the law doesn't hold
> - **Indoors**, reflections build a *reverberant field*. Beyond a certain distance (the critical distance) the level stops falling at 6 dB per doubling and levels off. The room-acoustics units cover rooms.
> - **Close to a source**, particularly a large one or a line of speakers, the level doesn't fall in neat inverse-square steps (see the later boundaries and fields unit).
> - **Acoustic line sources** (long columns of speakers) fall closer to 3 dB per doubling over part of their range, because the energy spreads over a cylinder rather than a sphere.

## Key takeaways
- Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field.
- Each distance doubling reduces pressure level by about six decibels.
- Reflections, line-source geometry and near-field behaviour need different models.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Outdoors, away from reflecting surfaces, a small speaker gives 94 dB SPL at 2 m. Roughly what will you measure at 4 m?

options.explanation: Doubling distance doesn't halve the decibel value. It subtracts about 6 dB.
−3 dB per doubling applies to a line source over part of its range, not a small point-like source.
Sound does lose level with distance in a free field as it spreads over a larger sphere.
Correct. Doubling the distance from a point source halves the pressure, which loses about 6 dB.

questions.workedExample:
In a free field the intensity falls with the square of distance, so the pressure falls in proportion to distance. In decibels:

```formula
L_2 = L_1 − 20 log_10(r_2 / r_1)
L_2 = 94 − 20 log_10(4 m / 2 m)
L_2 = 94 − 20 × 0.301
L_2 = 94 − 6.02
L_2 ≈ 88 dB SPL
where
L_1: the known level, 94 dB SPL
L_2: the level at the new distance, in dB SPL
r_1: the distance of the known level, 2 metres (m)
r_2: the new distance, 4 metres (m)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
m: metres
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning decibels relative to 20 µPa
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: twice as far away, the level is about 6 dB lower: 88 dB SPL.
```

questions.prompt: A PA speaker produces 100 dB SPL at 1 m. Assuming far-field spreading along the same direction, negligible air absorption and free-field conditions, what level reaches a listener 16 m away?

options.explanation: This subtracts 16 dB, as if it were 1 dB per metre. The law is logarithmic in distance.
Correct. 16 m is four doublings of 1 m; 4 × 6.02 ≈ 24 dB, giving about 75.9 dB.
That is two doublings (4 m). 16 m is four doublings.
That is only one doubling (2 m).

questions.workedExample:
Use the inverse square law in decibel form:

```formula
L_2 = L_1 − 20 log_10(r_2 / r_1)
L_2 = 100 − 20 log_10(16 m / 1 m)
L_2 = 100 − 20 × 1.204
L_2 = 100 − 24.08
L_2 ≈ 75.9 dB SPL
where
L_1: the level at 1 m, 100 dB SPL
L_2: the level at 16 m, in dB SPL
r_1: the reference distance, 1 metre (m)
r_2: the listener distance, 16 metres (m)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
m: metres
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning decibels relative to 20 µPa
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 16 times further away loses about 24 dB, leaving about 76 dB SPL.
```

Or count doublings: 1→2→4→8→16 m is four doublings, each about 6 dB, so about 24 dB lost.

questions.prompt: A speaker produces 110 dB SPL at 1 m. A neighbour's boundary is the point where the level must be no more than 85 dB SPL. In a free field, how far away must it be?

options.explanation: Correct. A 25 dB drop needs a distance ratio of about 17.8 (10 raised to 25 divided by 20).
That treats it as 1 dB per metre. The drop depends on the logarithm of the distance ratio.
That distance only gives a 10 dB drop (a ratio of about 3.16).
That divides the 25 dB by 10 instead of 20, as if it were a power ratio. Pressure falls in proportion to distance, so divide by 20.

questions.workedExample:
Find the required drop, then solve the inverse square law for the distance:

```formula
ΔL = 110 dB − 85 dB = 25 dB
20 log_10(r / r_1) = 25 dB
log_10(r / r_1) = 25 / 20 = 1.25
r / r_1 = 10^1.25 ≈ 17.8
r ≈ 17.8 × 1 m = 17.8 m
where
ΔL: the drop in level needed, in decibels (dB); Δ (delta) means "change in"
r: the distance to the boundary, in metres (m)
r_1: the reference distance, 1 m
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; undoing it means raising 10 to that power
10^1.25: 10 raised to the power 1.25, about 17.8
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
m: metres
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: losing 25 dB needs about 17.8 times the distance, so about 17.8 m.
```

In reality the ground, buildings and weather change this, so treat it as a first estimate.

lessons.title: Combine unrelated and coherent sources
lessons.summary: Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources.
lessons.body:
## Adding sources

Independent sound sources (for example unrelated noise sources) can be treated as **incoherent sources** over the averaging interval: their waveforms are unrelated, so their mean-square pressures add, with the correlation cross-term averaging to zero. To add levels, turn each one back into a relative mean-square pressure, add those values, and turn the total back into decibels:

```formula
L_total = 10 log_10(Σ 10^{L_i / 10})
where
L_total: the combined level at the listening position, in dB SPL
L_i: the level of source number i on its own, at the same position, in dB SPL
i: a counter that runs over the sources: 1, 2, 3 and so on
10^{L_i / 10}: the relative power of source i (10 raised to the power of its level divided by 10)
Σ: sigma, "sum of": add up the term for every source
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
In words: convert each level to a power, add the powers, and convert back to decibels with 10 × log because these are powers, not pressures.
```

Worked example, two equal 90 dB SPL sources, then a 90 and an 80:

```formula
L_total = 10 log_10(10^9 + 10^9)
L_total = 10 log_10(2 × 10^9)
L_total = 10 × 9.301 ≈ 93.01 dB SPL
L_mix = 10 log_10(10^9 + 10^8)
L_mix = 10 log_10(1.1 × 10^9)
L_mix = 10 × 9.0414 ≈ 90.41 dB SPL
where
L_total: the combined level of two 90 dB SPL sources, in dB SPL
L_mix: the combined level of a 90 dB SPL and an 80 dB SPL source, in dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
10^9: the relative power of a 90 dB source (10 to the power 90 / 10)
10^8: the relative power of an 80 dB source
dB: decibels
SPL: sound pressure level
≈: approximately equal to
In words: two equal unrelated sources give 3 dB more than one; adding a source 10 dB quieter raises the total by only about 0.4 dB.
```

This assumes the sources really are unrelated and you average over a long enough time. The same sum as a program:

```python
import math

def lsum(*levels):
    # Sum uncorrelated mean-square
    # pressures.
    return 10 * math.log10(
        sum(10 ** (l / 10) for l in levels))

print(round(lsum(90, 90), 2))
print(round(lsum(90, 80), 2))
print(round(lsum(90, 90, 90, 90), 2))
```

```output
93.01
90.41
96.02
```

- Two equal incoherent sources: **+3 dB**.
- A source 10 dB quieter adds only about 0.4 dB. The loud one dominates.
- Four equal sources: +6 dB.

**Coherent sources** are different. Two speakers playing the *same* signal at the same distance add in pressure, so they can give up to **+6 dB** where they arrive in phase, and deep cancellation where they arrive out of phase. Compare doubling the pressure with doubling the power:

```formula
ΔL_coh = 20 log_10(2) ≈ +6.02 dB
ΔL_inc = 10 log_10(2) ≈ +3.01 dB
where
ΔL_coh: the gain from adding a second, identical, in-phase copy (pressure doubles), in decibels (dB)
ΔL_inc: the gain from adding a second, equal but unrelated source (power doubles), in decibels (dB)
Δ: delta, "change in"
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibels
In words: two identical in-phase copies double the pressure (+6 dB); two equal unrelated sources double the power (+3 dB).
```
 For delayed broadband copies, the repeating frequency peaks and notches are **comb filtering**; a single tone instead shows spatial interference, and it is why the microphone units’ 3:1 rule and the crossover units’ driver alignment exist.

## Key takeaways
- Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources.
- Identical in-phase copies double pressure, giving about six decibels.
- Delayed broadband copies can create comb filtering.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)

questions.prompt: Two unrelated noise sources (say, two air-conditioning units) each produce 85 dB SPL at your position. What is the combined level?

options.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic; you can't add them arithmetically.
+6 dB applies to two *coherent* copies of the same signal arriving in phase, not unrelated sources.
Correct. Incoherent sources add in power, and doubling the power adds about 3 dB.
Adding a second source does add energy.

questions.workedExample:
Convert each level to a relative power, add, and convert back:

```formula
L_total = 10 log_10(10^8.5 + 10^8.5)
L_total = 10 log_10(2 × 10^8.5)
L_total = 85 + 10 log_10(2)
L_total = 85 + 3.01
L_total ≈ 88 dB SPL
where
L_total: the combined level, in dB SPL
10^8.5: the relative power of one 85 dB source (10 to the power 85 / 10)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning decibels relative to 20 µPa
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: two equal unrelated sources carry twice the power of one, which is 3 dB more: 88 dB SPL.
```

Unrelated sources have random relative phase, so on average their powers, not their pressures, add.

questions.prompt: A synth in a room produces 90 dB SPL at the mix position, and the room's background noise there is 80 dB SPL. What is the total level?

options.explanation: +3 dB happens only when the two sources are equal.
Averaging decibel values isn't how levels combine.
Decibels don't add arithmetically.
Correct. Converting both to powers, adding and converting back gives about 90.4 dB.

questions.workedExample:
Unrelated sources add in power:

```formula
W_1 = 10^{90/10} = 10^9
W_2 = 10^{80/10} = 10^8
L = 10 log_10(W_1 + W_2)
L = 10 log_10(1.1 × 10^9)
L ≈ 90.41 dB SPL
where
W_1: the relative power of the 90 dB SPL synth (no unit)
W_2: the relative power of the 80 dB SPL background noise (no unit)
L: the combined level, in dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
SPL: sound pressure level, meaning decibels relative to 20 µPa
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the noise carries a tenth of the synth's power, which raises the total by only about 0.4 dB.
```

A source 10 dB below another adds only about 0.4 dB. This does not prove the quieter source is inaudible: masking depends on frequency content, timing and the listener.

questions.prompt: Which statements about combining two sources at a listener's position are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two singers each at 80 dB SPL give about 83 dB SPL together
options.explanation: Correct. Independent sources are incoherent, so their powers add: +3 dB.

options.text: Two speakers playing the same signal always add +6 dB everywhere in the room
options.explanation: Equal coherent copies can cancel at positions where their path difference is half a wavelength. For delayed broadband copies this produces comb filtering across frequency; a single tone instead shows spatial interference.

options.text: Coherent sources can partly cancel at some frequencies and positions
options.explanation: Correct. When arrivals are out of phase, pressures subtract.

options.text: Two identical subwoofers fed the same signal, equidistant from you, can give up to +6 dB at low frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. Coherent, in-phase signals add in pressure, and doubling the pressure adds about 6 dB.

questions.workedExample:
Coherent copies add in pressure; unrelated sources add in power:

```formula
ΔL_coh = 20 log_10(2) ≈ +6.0 dB
ΔL_inc = 10 log_10(2) ≈ +3.0 dB
where
ΔL_coh: the gain from two identical in-phase copies (pressure doubles), in decibels (dB)
ΔL_inc: the gain from two equal unrelated sources (power doubles), in decibels (dB)
Δ: delta, "change in"
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(100) = 2
dB: decibels, a logarithmic measure of a ratio
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: doubling the pressure gives +6 dB; doubling the power gives +3 dB.
```

Out of phase, coherent copies cancel deeply instead. Which case you are in depends on whether the signals are copies of each other and on their path lengths compared with the wavelength.

lessons.title: Relating wavelength to boundaries and fields
lessons.summary: Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows.
lessons.body:
## Reflection, absorption and diffraction

At a boundary, sound can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed; diffraction describes spreading around edges and openings. Wavelength, impedance and construction all matter.

**Sound reflection.** A hard, large, flat surface (a wall, a desk, a window) reflects sound like a mirror reflects light: angle in equals angle out. This only works well when the surface is large compared with the wavelength. A stiff 30 cm panel can give a directional reflection at 10 kHz (wavelength 3.4 cm). At 100 Hz (wavelength 3.4 m), diffraction around it is important; its actual reflection and transmission still depend on material and mounting.

**Sound absorption.** Porous materials (mineral wool, thick fabric) turn some of the sound's energy into heat. Each material has an **absorption coefficient**, the fraction of incident energy not returned as reflected sound in the room-acoustics convention; it may include transmitted energy:

```formula
α = 1 − E_ref / E_inc
where
α: alpha, the absorption coefficient of the surface; it has no unit and lies between 0 and 1
E_ref: the sound energy reflected back from the surface
E_inc: the sound energy arriving at (incident on) the surface
In words: the absorption coefficient is the share of the sound that does not come back. 0 means a perfect reflector, 1 means nothing returns (as from an open window).
```

For example, a panel that reflects 30 % of the arriving energy has an absorption coefficient of 0.7. The coefficient varies with frequency, so it is quoted per octave band. Thin foam absorbs high frequencies well and does almost nothing to bass, because bass wavelengths are far longer than the foam is thick.

**Diffraction.** Waves bend around obstacles and spread out through openings. When an obstacle is small compared with the wavelength, sound diffracts around it with hardly a shadow. When it's large, it casts an acoustic shadow. This is why you can hear the bass, but not the cymbals, from a band round the corner; why your head shadows high frequencies but not low ones (the hearing units); and why a loudspeaker radiates almost equally in all directions at low frequencies but beams forward at high frequencies (the loudspeaker-driver units).

| Size vs wavelength | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Object much smaller | Sound diffracts round it |
| Comparable | Partial, frequency-dependent |
| Object much larger | Reflection and shadowing |

## Near field and far field

Very close to a source, the sound field is complicated: different parts of the source (the cone, the edges of the cabinet, several drivers) are at noticeably different distances from you, and their contributions interfere. Level can change sharply as you move a few centimetres, and it doesn't follow the inverse square law.

Further away, in the **far field**, the source behaves like a point: level falls 6 dB per doubling, and the balance between drivers settles down. The distance needed depends on source geometry, frequency and the measurement criterion. Several source dimensions alone is not a universal far-field test for a large array; follow the manufacturer's measurement method and verify that distance-scaled responses converge. Datasheet figures are quoted "at 1 m", but large speakers are often measured further away and the result scaled back to 1 m with the inverse square law.

> [!tip] "Near-field monitor" means something else
> Studio "near-field monitors" are small speakers listened to from about 1–2 m, so that you hear more direct sound than room reflections. They aren't about the acoustic near field of the speaker itself. The room-acoustics units cover them.

## Key takeaways
- Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows.
- Absorption also depends on material, mounting and incidence angle.
- A reverberant room and an acoustic near field do not follow a simple distance law.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Which of these behaviours depend mainly on the size of an object compared with the wavelength? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thin acoustic foam absorbs high frequencies but barely touches bass
options.explanation: Correct. Porous absorbers need a thickness that's a meaningful fraction of the wavelength to work.

options.text: Sound in air travels faster when it's warm
options.explanation: That depends on temperature, not on object size or wavelength.

options.text: A stiff 30 cm panel can give a directional reflection at 10 kHz, while diffraction around it matters at 100 Hz
options.explanation: Correct as a size comparison. The wavelengths are about 3.4 cm and 3.4 m respectively. Material impedance, thickness, mounting and incidence also determine reflection and transmission.

options.text: You hear the bass but not the cymbals of a band playing round a corner
options.explanation: Correct. Long bass wavelengths diffract round the building; short high-frequency wavelengths are shadowed.

questions.workedExample:
Work out the wavelengths to compare with object sizes:

```formula
λ = c / f
λ = (343 m/s) / (100 Hz) = 3.43 m
λ = (343 m/s) / (1000 Hz) = 0.343 m
λ = (343 m/s) / (10000 Hz) = 0.0343 m
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
m: metres
s: seconds
In words: 100 Hz is about 3.4 m long, 1 kHz about 34 cm and 10 kHz about 3.4 cm.
```

- Object much larger than the wavelength: reflects and shadows.
- Object much smaller than the wavelength: sound diffracts round it.
- Thin porous layer directly on a rigid wall: usually little low-frequency absorption; resonant absorbers and air gaps require separate analysis.

The speed of sound depends on air temperature (≈ 331 m/s at 0 °C, 343 m/s at 20 °C), which is a separate effect.

questions.prompt: Indoors, you measure a speaker at 1, 2, 4 and 8 m: 90, 85, 82 and 81 dB SPL. Why doesn't it lose 6 dB per doubling?

options.text: Reflections build a reverberant field whose level is roughly constant across the room, so beyond some distance it dominates the direct sound
options.explanation: Correct. Close in, the direct sound dominates and falls with distance; further out the reverberant level takes over and the total levels off.

options.text: The meter is faulty; the inverse square law always holds
options.explanation: The law assumes a free field with no reflections. Rooms aren't free fields.

options.text: The speaker is too quiet for the law to apply
options.explanation: The inverse square law doesn't depend on level.
The speed of sound depends on air temperature, not on being indoors, and wouldn't change level anyway.

questions.workedExample:
1. Direct sound alone: 90, 84, 78, 72 dB (−6 dB per doubling).
2. Measured: 90, 85, 82, 81 dB, levelling off.
3. The extra is reflected sound. In a room, the reverberant field is roughly uniform, so as the direct sound falls the total approaches the reverberant level.
4. The distance where direct and reverberant levels are equal is called the **critical distance**. The room-acoustics units cover reverberation.

lessons.title: Why equal SPL is not equal loudness
lessons.summary: Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level.
lessons.body:
A sound level meter measures pressure. You hear something else: loudness, pitch, direction and timbre, all built by your ear and brain from that pressure. **Psychoacoustics** studies the gap between the two. For anyone mixing, designing speakers or building instruments it explains why a bass line vanishes at low volume, why a quiet pad disappears under a loud lead, and why a delay speaker can be louder than the stage without pulling the image towards it.

It also explains how hearing gets damaged. That part is not optional reading.

## The range of hearing

The commonly quoted range is **20 Hz to 20 kHz**. Treat both ends as soft:

- The top end falls with age and noise exposure. Many adults hear little above 15–16 kHz. Your synth's 18 kHz content may be inaudible to you and obvious to a teenager (or to your dog).
- At the bottom, below about 20 Hz, very loud sound is felt more than heard.
- Hearing is most sensitive roughly between **2 and 5 kHz**, partly because the ear canal resonates in that region.

In level, hearing spans from the threshold near 0 dB SPL at mid frequencies to very high levels that can cause pain and damage. Pain thresholds vary, and harmful exposure can occur far below pain; a 120 dB level difference represents a millionfold pressure ratio.

## Equal-loudness contours

Play a 100 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone at the same dB SPL and the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter. An **equal-loudness contour** joins up the levels at which pure tones of different frequencies sound equally loud. Each contour is labelled in **phons**: for example, the forty-phon contour passes through 40 dB SPL at one kilohertz. The standard specifies young, otologically normal listeners, frontal free-field pure tones and binaural listening; it is not a calibration of every listener or broadband music.

The first such curves were Fletcher and Munson's (1933). The current international standard is **ISO 226**. Its 2003 edition replaced older curves that had been shown to be inaccurate, and it was revised again in **2023** with small changes.

```diagram
 dB SPL
 120 |\                        /
     | \___  80 phon     ___/
  80 |     \___________/
     |\
  40 | \___  20 phon     __/
     |     \___________/
   0 +-----+-----+-----+-----+
     20   100    1k    5k   20k Hz
```

(A sketch of the shape only: read real values and listening conditions from the applicable ISO 226 edition.)

Three things to take from the curves:

- **Bass needs much more SPL** than mid frequencies to sound equally loud, especially at low listening levels.
- **The curves flatten as level rises.** The difference between bass and mids is smaller at 80 phon than at 20 phon.
- So **a mix sounds different at different volumes.** Turn it down and the bass and extreme treble seem to fade first. Mix at one consistent, moderate level, and check at quiet and loud levels.

## Key takeaways
- Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level.
- Equal-loudness contours describe pure tones under specified conditions.
- A mix’s perceived balance changes with listening level.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)
- [ISO 226:2023 scope and history — Estonian standards body](https://www.evs.ee/en/iso-226-2023)

questions.prompt: You play a 60 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone, both at 50 dB SPL. How do they compare in loudness?

options.text: The 60 Hz tone sounds much quieter
options.explanation: Correct. The equal-loudness contours show low frequencies need considerably more SPL to sound as loud as 1 kHz at moderate levels.

options.text: They sound equally loud because the SPL is the same
options.explanation: Equal SPL doesn't mean equal loudness. Hearing is much less sensitive at low frequencies, especially at low levels.

options.text: The 60 Hz tone sounds much louder
options.explanation: It's the reverse: hearing is least sensitive at the low end.

options.text: You can't hear 60 Hz at all
options.explanation: 60 Hz is inside the audible range, just at reduced sensitivity.

questions.workedExample:
1. Equal-loudness contours (ISO 226) show the SPL needed at each frequency to match the loudness of a 1 kHz tone.
2. At low phon levels the contours rise steeply below a few hundred hertz.
3. So at 50 dB SPL, the 60 Hz tone is well below the loudness of the 1 kHz tone.
4. Practical consequence: turning a mix down makes the bass seem to disappear first.

questions.prompt: Your monitoring sounds balanced at 85 dB SPL. When you turn it down to 60 dB SPL to rest your ears, the mix seems to lose bass. What's happening?

options.text: The speakers' bass driver switches off at low power
options.explanation: Loudspeakers are broadly linear; their frequency response doesn't change that much with level.
Upward spread of masking actually grows with level, not the other way round.

options.text: A-weighting is applied by the speakers
options.explanation: A-weighting is a measurement filter in a meter, not something speakers do.

options.text: The equal-loudness contours are steeper at low levels, so bass seems quieter relative to mids
options.explanation: Correct. The ear's bass sensitivity falls faster than its middle-frequency sensitivity as level drops.

questions.workedExample:
1. Higher-level equal-loudness contours are relatively flatter; a broadband mix at 85 dB SPL is not automatically 85 phon.
2. At lower loudness levels the contours rise more steeply at low frequencies.
3. So the same mix sounds bass-light when quieter.
4. Mix at a consistent moderate level and check at several volumes, rather than adding bass to compensate for quiet monitoring.

lessons.title: Understand A, C and Z weighting
lessons.summary: A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading.
lessons.body:
## A and C weighting

Sound level meters apply a **frequency weighting** to make a single number track human response better. The two that matter, both defined for sound level meters in **IEC 61672-1**:

- **A-weighting** (dB(A) or dBA) strongly reduces low frequencies (about −19 dB at 100 Hz, −30 dB at 50 Hz) and slightly boosts 2–4 kHz. It was based on the 40-phon Fletcher–Munson curve. It is the standard weighting for noise exposure and for many noise-floor specifications.
- **C-weighting** (dB(C)) is nearly flat from about 31.5 Hz to 8 kHz (−3 dB points). It is used for **peak level** measurements, and for loud, bass-heavy sound where A-weighting would hide the low end.
- **Z-weighting** is flat ("zero").

The A-weighting curve is defined by a formula in IEC 61672-1. It describes a set of simple filters: two that cut below about 20 Hz, one each near 108 Hz and 738 Hz that shape the low-mid roll-off, and two that cut above about 12.2 kHz. You don't need to memorise it, but it shows that "dB(A)" is a precisely defined filter, not a vague idea:

```formula
R_A = 12194^2 f^4 / D
D = (f^2 + 20.6^2)(f^2 + 12194^2)
  √((f^2 + 107.7^2)(f^2 + 737.9^2))
A = 20 log_10(R_A) + 2.00
where
R_A: the A-weighting response at frequency f, as a plain gain ratio (no unit)
f: the frequency being weighted, in hertz (Hz)
D: the denominator, written on its own lines only to keep them short
20.6, 107.7, 737.9, 12194: the corner frequencies of the weighting's filter stages, in hertz (Hz)
√: square root
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number
2.00: a rounded correction in decibels that makes the weighting approximately 0 dB at 1 kHz
A: the A-weighting at frequency f, in decibels (dB); negative means the meter reduces that frequency
In words: a fixed filter shape, turned into decibels and nudged so that 1 kHz is unchanged; it cuts deep bass and extreme treble and slightly lifts 2–4 kHz.
```

Worked example at 100 Hz:

```formula
R_A = (1.487 × 10^16) / (1.696 × 10^17)
R_A ≈ 0.0877
A = 20 log_10(0.0877) + 2.00
A = 20 × (−1.057) + 2.00
A ≈ −19.1 dB
where
R_A: the A-weighting gain ratio at 100 Hz (no unit)
A: the A-weighting at 100 Hz, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: an A-weighted meter reads a 100 Hz tone about 19 dB lower than its true sound pressure level.
```

The same formula as a program, evaluated at several frequencies:

```python
import math

def a_weight(f):
    # f is in Hz; the gain is dimensionless.
    f2 = f * f
    ra = (12194**2 * f2**2) / (
        (f2 + 20.6**2)
        * math.sqrt((f2 + 107.7**2)
                    * (f2 + 737.9**2))
        * (f2 + 12194**2))
    return 20 * math.log10(ra) + 2.00

for f in (50, 100, 1000, 4000, 10000):
    a = a_weight(f)
    print(f"{f:>5} Hz: {a:6.1f} dB")
```

```output
   50 Hz:  -30.3 dB
  100 Hz:  -19.1 dB
 1000 Hz:    0.0 dB
 4000 Hz:    1.0 dB
10000 Hz:   -2.5 dB
```

> [!note] Why live engineers watch dB(C) as well as dB(A)
> A kick drum and sub-bass can carry enormous energy at 40–60 Hz while barely moving a dB(A) meter. Venues often monitor both.

## Key takeaways
- A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading.
- Great Britain workplace exposure uses A-weighting for dose and C-weighting for peaks.
- Weightings are measurement filters, not a loudspeaker behaviour.

## Further reading
- [A-weighting measurement implementation — Son, Kyung and Cho (2019)](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/sensors/sensors-19-03633/article_deploy/sensors-19-03633.pdf)
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

questions.prompt: Which weighting is normally used for Great Britain occupational noise exposure in dB, and which for peak sound pressure?

options.text: C for exposure, A for peaks
options.explanation: It's the other way round.
Exposure regulations use A-weighting for the daily dose and C-weighting for peaks.
A-weighting would understate the low-frequency content of impulsive peaks; C-weighting is used for those.

options.text: A for exposure, C for peaks
options.explanation: Correct. For example, UK action values are in dB(A) for LEP,d and dB(C) for LCpeak.

questions.workedExample:
- **A-weighting** follows hearing's low sensitivity to bass at moderate levels; it's used for the daily/weekly dose (LEP,d).

The HSE action values show both: 80/85 dB(A) and 135/137 dB(C).

lessons.title: Masking and auditory filter bandwidth
lessons.summary: Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level.
lessons.body:
## Masking

A loud sound can make a quieter one inaudible. This is **masking**, and it's the reason a mix "gets muddy": parts that each sound fine alone hide each other when played together.

- **Simultaneous masking** is strongest when the two sounds are **close in frequency**.
- It **spreads upwards**: a loud low sound masks higher frequencies much more effectively than a loud high sound masks lower ones. The effect grows with level. That's why a heavy bass part can dull a whole mix.
- **Temporal masking** also happens: a loud sound can hide quieter sounds just after it (and, briefly, just before it).

Lossy codecs such as MP3 and AAC exploit masking: they spend fewer bits on what masking will hide anyway.

## Critical bands, intuitively

The cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters. Critical-band measurements and auditory-filter bandwidths both describe frequency selectivity, but their numerical widths depend on how they are measured. ERB is the width of an ideal rectangular filter with the same peak gain and integrated response as the actual filter. Two tones inside one band interact strongly: they mask each other, beat or sound rough. Tones in well-separated bands are heard more independently.

The bands are narrow at low frequencies and wider at high frequencies. One standard model, Glasberg and Moore's **equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB)**, gives the width of the auditory filter centred on a given frequency. It was fitted to listening-test data from young, normally hearing listeners at moderate levels:

```formula
ERB = 24.7 (4.37f / 1000 + 1)
where
ERB: the equivalent rectangular bandwidth of the auditory filter, in hertz (Hz)
f: the centre frequency of the filter, in hertz (Hz)
24.7: the bandwidth in hertz the formula gives at very low frequencies
4.37: how fast the bandwidth grows with frequency, per kilohertz of centre frequency
1000: converts f from hertz to kilohertz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: the auditory filter is about 25 Hz wide at the bottom of the range and gets wider in proportion to frequency, approaching about 11 % of the centre frequency at high frequencies.
```

Worked example at a centre frequency of 1 kHz (1000 Hz):

```formula
ERB = 24.7 (4.37 × 1000 / 1000 + 1)
ERB = 24.7 × 5.37
ERB ≈ 133 Hz
where
ERB: the equivalent rectangular bandwidth, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: around 1 kHz, a 133 Hz-wide equivalent rectangular band describes the auditory filter; whether two tones interact depends on their spacing and the overlapping responses.
```

The formula is an average fit, not a sharp boundary: real filters overlap, and their widths change with level and between listeners.

| Centre | ERB |
|---|---|
| 100 Hz | ≈ 35.5 Hz |
| 1 kHz | ≈ 133 Hz |
| 4 kHz | ≈ 456.5 Hz |

In practice: two bass parts a few tens of hertz apart are fighting inside the same band, so EQ-ing space between parts (or choosing different octaves) does more for clarity than turning one up.

## Key takeaways
- Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level.
- Auditory filters overlap and generally widen as centre frequency rises.
- ERB summarizes a filter response; it is not a sharp separation boundary.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

questions.prompt: A loud bass synth makes a quiet hi-hat part hard to hear, but a loud hi-hat barely affects the bass line. Which psychoacoustic effect explains the asymmetry?

options.explanation: That concerns localisation of first-arriving sounds, not one sound hiding another in frequency.
That's a localisation cue, not a masking effect.
Correct. Masking spreads more towards frequencies above the masker, and the spread grows with level.
A weighting is a meter filter, not a perceptual effect.

questions.workedExample:
1. Masking is strongest within a critical band around the masker.
2. The masking pattern is asymmetric: it extends much further upward than downward, especially at high levels.
3. So a loud low sound can mask higher sounds, but a loud high sound does little to lower ones.
4. Fix in a mix: reduce the bass level or carve its upper harmonics with EQ.

questions.prompt:
Glasberg and Moore's equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB) formula is:

```formula
ERB = 24.7 (4.37f / 1000 + 1)
where
ERB: the auditory filter bandwidth, in hertz (Hz)
f: the centre frequency, in hertz (Hz)
24.7: the bandwidth in Hz at very low frequencies
4.37: how fast the bandwidth grows per kilohertz
1000: converts f from hertz to kilohertz
In words: the auditory filter is about 25 Hz wide at low frequencies and widens in proportion to frequency.
```

At a 1 kHz centre frequency, roughly what auditory filter bandwidth does it give?

options.explanation: That is just the constant 24.7, missing the frequency term.
Far too wide. Auditory filters at 1 kHz are a little over a tenth of the centre frequency.
That's the ERB at 4 kHz.

questions.workedExample:
Use a centre frequency of one kilohertz in the supplied formula:

```formula
ERB = 24.7 (4.37 × 1000 / 1000 + 1)
ERB = 24.7 (4.37 + 1)
ERB = 24.7 × 5.37
ERB ≈ 132.6 Hz
where
ERB: the equivalent rectangular bandwidth, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: around 1 kHz the auditory filter is about 133 Hz wide.
```

The ERB summarizes an overlapping filter response, not a sharp boundary. Interaction between tones also depends on separation, level, timing and the listener.

lessons.title: Locate sound and understand precedence
lessons.summary: Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies.
lessons.body:
## Localisation: ITD and ILD

You locate a sound left or right mainly from two cues:

- **Interaural time difference (ITD).** A sound from the side reaches the near ear first. Maximum adult ITDs are of order 0.6–0.7 ms and vary with head size, frequency and source direction; simply dividing ear spacing by sound speed neglects diffraction around the head. ITD (as phase differences) is the main cue at **low frequencies**, below about 1 kHz.
- **Interaural level difference (ILD).** The head casts an acoustic shadow, but only for wavelengths small compared with the head (the acoustics units’ diffraction rule). So ILD is the main cue at **high frequencies**, above about 1.5 kHz.

Between roughly 1 and 1.5 kHz both cues contribute. This "duplex theory" goes back to Lord Rayleigh (1907). Neither cue separates front from back or up from down; for those the brain uses the filtering of the **outer ear (pinna)** and small head movements.

> [!tip] Why one subwoofer is usually enough
> At very low frequencies the head casts almost no shadow (so ILD vanishes), the interaural time difference becomes a tiny fraction of a cycle, and in a room the modes and reflections swamp what cues remain. So localisation of deep bass is poor, which is why a single subwoofer can usually be placed off-centre without the bass seeming to come from it. An 80 Hz crossover is a common system choice, not a hard hearing boundary; it only works if the crossover is low and the sub's distortion and port noise don't add higher-frequency content you *can* locate.

## The precedence (Haas) effect

In a room, you hear the direct sound plus many reflections from other directions, yet you perceive one sound coming from the source. The **precedence effect** is the reason: the auditory system localises a sound by the **first-arriving wavefront** and suppresses the direction of early reflections.

Precedence depends on signal, level, delay, direction and listening conditions. Fusion (hearing one event), localization dominance (hearing it toward the first source), and suppression of information about the reflection are related but distinct; one can persist after another breaks down. There is no universal delay/level boundary guaranteeing all three. Exact Haas-derived limits are absent here because their original experimental conditions were not reliably established in this review.

This has a direct engineering use (the sound-system units): a **delay speaker** is aligned using the difference between stage-to-listener and fill-to-listener travel times, plus any deliberately chosen precedence offset:

```formula
t_delay = (d_main − d_fill) / c + t_off
where
t_delay: the electronic delay applied to the delay speaker, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
d_main: the distance from the main stage speakers to the listener, in metres (m)
d_fill: the distance from the delay speaker to the listener, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
t_off: an extra delay, expressed in the same time unit as the path-time term, chosen so the stage sound arrives first; an example to evaluate by listening, not a fixed rule
In words: hold back the delay speaker by the extra time the stage sound needs to reach the listener, plus a little more so the stage wins the race.
```

For example, if the stage path is 34.3 m longer, the travel-time difference is 34.3 m divided by 343 m/s, which is 100 ms; with a chosen 10 ms offset the starting setting is 110 ms. The formula ignores electronic latency and temperature changes. Account for electronic latency, then measure and listen across the coverage area. A large offset can cause audible echoes or comb filtering rather than guarantee stage localization.

## Key takeaways
- Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies.
- Outer-ear filtering and head movements provide additional direction cues.
- Delay alignment uses path and electronic-latency differences; an extra offset is a design choice to evaluate.

## Further reading
- [Auditory pathways and localisation — David Heeger, NYU](https://www.cns.nyu.edu/~david/courses/perception/lecturenotes/localization/localization.html)
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

questions.prompt: Which statements about left–right localisation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: ILD is large at 100 Hz because the head blocks the sound
options.explanation: At 100 Hz the wavelength (3.4 m) is far larger than the head, so sound diffracts round it and ILD is tiny.

options.text: Maximum adult ITDs are of order 0.6–0.7 ms
options.explanation: Correct as an approximate scale; head geometry, diffraction and frequency affect the value.

options.text: ITD is the main cue at low frequencies, below about 1 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. Long wavelengths make phase differences between the ears unambiguous.

options.text: ILD is the main cue at high frequencies, above about 1.5 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. The head only shadows wavelengths that are small compared with it.

questions.workedExample:
- ITD: time (phase) difference. Max is of order 0.6–0.7 ms; ear-spacing divided by sound speed is only a crude illustration. Unambiguous when the half-wavelength is larger than the head, i.e. at low frequencies.
- ILD: level difference from head shadowing. Needs wavelengths comparable with or smaller than the head, i.e. high frequencies.
- Between about 1 and 1.5 kHz both contribute (Rayleigh's duplex theory).

questions.prompt: At the chosen audience position, the stage path is 34.3 m longer than the delay-speaker path. Taking the speed of sound as 343 m/s, and with a deliberately chosen 10–20 ms precedence offset, what electronic delay gives the calculated starting setting, ignoring other latency?

options.explanation: That is only the extra offset. Without the 100 ms acoustic travel time, the delay speaker's sound arrives first.
Correct as the calculation: 34.3 m at 343 m/s takes 100 ms, plus the chosen 10–20 ms offset. Verify by measurement and listening; localization is not guaranteed.
With no delay, the nearby speaker's sound arrives about 100 ms before the stage sound, pulling the image and producing a late echo from the stage.
Far too long. It would be heard as a separate echo.

questions.workedExample:
Delay the speaker by the extra travel time of the stage sound, plus the chosen offset:

```formula
t_path = Δd / c
t_path = 34.3 m / (343 m/s)
t_path = 0.100 s = 100 ms
t_delay = t_path + t_off
t_delay = 100 ms + (10–20 ms)
t_delay ≈ 110–120 ms
where
t_path: the extra time the stage sound needs to reach the listener, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
Δd: the path difference, 34.3 metres (m); Δ (delta) means "difference in"
c: the speed of sound, 343 metres per second (m/s)
t_off: the chosen precedence offset, 10–20 ms
t_delay: the electronic delay to set, in ms
m: metres
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the stage sound needs 100 ms more to arrive, so delay the speaker by that plus the 10–20 ms offset, about 110–120 ms.
```

The offset lets the stage wavefront arrive first. Check localization, intelligibility and echoes across the audience area. The assumed offset is an example to evaluate, not a universal rule.

lessons.title: Great Britain workplace noise duties
lessons.summary: Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time.
lessons.body:
## Hearing damage and safe exposure

Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent. It depends on **level and time together**: the dose. Tinnitus (ringing) after a loud session is a warning sign.

**Great Britain workplaces: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005** (HSE). These apply to music and entertainment work too.

| Threshold | Daily LEP,d / weekly LEP,w | Peak (LCpeak) |
|---|---|---|
| Lower action value | 80 dB(A) | 135 dB(C) |
| Upper action value | 85 dB(A) | 137 dB(C) |
| Exposure limit | 87 dB(A) | 140 dB(C) |

At the lower action value the employer must assess the risk, provide information and training, and make hearing protection available to anyone who asks for it; at the upper one, hearing protection and hearing protection zones become mandatory. The exposure limit values take account of the reduction given by hearing protection and must not be exceeded; the action values do not (regulation 4(5)), so they're judged on unprotected exposure.

## Key takeaways
- Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time.
- Action values use unprotected exposure.
- The exposure limit takes hearing protection into account; peak exposure also needs assessment.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

questions.prompt: Under the Great Britain Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, at what daily or weekly exposure must an employer provide hearing protection and hearing protection zones?

options.explanation: This is the lower action value: noise risk assessment, information/training and hearing protection made available on request. The upper value triggers stronger mandatory protection requirements.
That is the exposure limit value, which takes account of hearing protection and must not be exceeded.
Correct. The upper exposure action value is 85 dB(A) (and a peak of 137 dB(C)).
That is the WHO venue recommendation (LAeq over 15 minutes), not a UK workplace action value.

questions.workedExample:
HSE's table for the 2005 Regulations:

| | LEP,d | LCpeak |
|---|---|---|
| Lower action | 80 | 135 |
| Upper action | 85 | 137 |
| Limit | 87 | 140 |

At the upper action value (85 dB(A)) hearing protection and hearing protection zones are mandatory.

questions.prompt: A stage technician works 8 hours a day in an area averaging 88 dB(A), wearing hearing protection that reduces the level at the ear to about 75 dB(A). Under the Great Britain regulations, which statement is right?

options.text: The upper action value is exceeded, so protection and protection zones are mandatory; the daily exposure limit is not exceeded on the stated protected-level estimate
options.explanation: Correct. Action values use unprotected exposure; the 87 dB(A) limit value is assessed with the protection's reduction taken into account.

options.text: They're over the exposure limit value, because 88 > 87
options.explanation: The 87 dB(A) limit value takes account of the hearing protection, so the relevant figure is about 75 dB(A).

options.text: No duties apply because the protected level is below 80 dB(A)
options.explanation: Action values are judged on unprotected exposure. 88 dB(A) is above the upper action value, so duties apply.

options.text: Only the peak limit matters for an 8-hour shift
options.explanation: Both daily exposure and peak values apply.

questions.workedExample:
1. Unprotected daily exposure: 88 dB(A).
2. That's above the upper exposure action value (85 dB(A)), so the employer must provide hearing protection, enforce hearing protection zones and run a noise control programme.
3. The exposure limit value (87 dB(A)) is assessed *taking account of* hearing protection: about 75 dB(A), so the daily limit is not exceeded on this estimate; peak exposure still needs a separate assessment.
4. Action values aren't reduced by protection; the limit value is.

lessons.title: Noise dose and safe-listening guidance
lessons.summary: NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate.
lessons.body:
## Noise dose and listening guidance

**NIOSH (US) recommended exposure limit:** **85 dB(A)** averaged over an eight-hour day, with a **3 dB noise-dose exchange rate**: every 3 dB increase halves the allowed time. A 3 dB increase doubles the sound energy, so halving the time keeps the total energy (the dose) the same:

```formula
T = 480 / 2^{(L − 85) / 3}
where
T: the time to reach the NIOSH reference daily dose, in minutes (min)
480: eight hours, in minutes
L: the steady A-weighted exposure level, in dB(A)
85: the NIOSH recommended exposure limit for eight hours, in dB(A)
3: the noise-dose exchange rate, in decibels: each 3 dB step halves the time
2^{(L − 85) / 3}: 2 raised to the number of 3 dB steps above 85 dB(A)
In words: start from 8 hours at 85 dB(A) and halve the time for every 3 dB louder.
```

Worked example at a steady 100 dB(A):

```formula
T = 480 / 2^{(100 − 85) / 3}
T = 480 / 2^5
T = 480 / 32 = 15 min
where
T: the time to reach the reference dose, in minutes
min: minutes
In words: 100 dB(A) is five 3 dB steps above 85, so the time halves five times, from 480 to 15 minutes.
```

The same calculation for several levels, as a program:

```python
# Reference-dose time, not guaranteed safe.
for level in (85, 88, 91, 94, 97, 100):
    minutes = 480 / 2 ** ((level - 85) / 3)
    print(f"{level} dBA: "
          f"{minutes:5.0f} min")
```

```output
85 dBA:   480 min
88 dBA:   240 min
91 dBA:   120 min
94 dBA:    60 min
97 dBA:    30 min
100 dBA:    15 min
```

A steady 100 dB(A) exposure reaches the NIOSH reference daily dose in **15 minutes**, before adding other exposure that day. This is a risk-management limit, not a guarantee of no hearing damage.

**WHO:**
- The WHO–ITU standard for personal audio devices sets a reference weekly allowance of **80 dB for 40 hours a week** for adults (75 dB for children).
- The **WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events** (2022) recommends a maximum of **100 dB LAeq over any 15 minutes** for audiences, alongside monitoring, hearing protection, quiet zones and other measures. This is a ceiling, not a recommended operating target or a guarantee of safety for an entire event.

> [!warning] Protect your hearing while building and testing
> - Bring levels up gradually. A DIY synth can produce a full-scale square wave or a feedback screech the moment you change a line of code.
> - Set headphone and monitor volume *before* putting headphones on, and start low.
> - Use a limiter on the monitoring path while developing.
> - Wear musicians' earplugs at gigs and loud rehearsals; they reduce level fairly evenly across frequency.

## Key takeaways
- NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate.
- Other daily exposures add to the total dose.
- WHO venue and personal-device recommendations use different reference periods and additional protective measures.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)
- [Noise exposure and exchange rate — NIOSH](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/noise.html)
- [Personal-device reference sound allowances — WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening)
- [WHO–ITU personal-device reference allowances](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/standard-summary-make-listening-safe.pdf?sfvrsn=fc114686_14)

questions.prompt: Using the NIOSH recommendation (85 dBA for 8 hours, 3 dB noise-dose exchange rate), what duration at a steady 97 dBA reaches the reference daily dose, before any other exposure?

options.explanation: That's 91 dBA (two halvings).
Correct. 97 dBA is 12 dB, or four 3 dB steps, above 85 dBA, so the 8 hours halves four times, to 30 minutes.
That's 88 dBA (one halving).
This uses a linear reduction. The allowed time halves with every 3 dB.

questions.workedExample:
With a 3 dB noise-dose exchange rate, the time to reach the reference dose halves for every 3 dB above 85 dBA:

```formula
T = 480 / 2^{(L − 85) / 3}
T = 480 / 2^{(97 − 85) / 3}
T = 480 / 2^4
T = 480 / 16 = 30 min
where
T: the time to reach the reference daily dose, in minutes (min)
480: eight hours, in minutes
L: the steady exposure level, here 97 dBA (A-weighted decibels)
85: the NIOSH limit for eight hours, in dBA
3: the noise-dose exchange rate: every 3 dB halves the time
2^4: four copies of 2 multiplied together, 16
min: minutes
In words: 97 dBA is four 3 dB steps above 85, so the 480 minutes halves four times, to 30 minutes.
```

Each 3 dB doubles the sound energy, so the reference duration halves. Add other daily exposures; remaining below this dose does not guarantee no hearing harm.
