lessons.title: How microphone types produce voltage
lessons.summary: Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction.
lessons.body:
A moving-coil microphone resembles a moving-coil loudspeaker run backwards: a light diaphragm moved by sound pressure, connected to something that turns motion into voltage. The way it makes that conversion decides its sensitivity, noise, ruggedness and whether it needs power. The way sound reaches the diaphragm decides its directional pattern.

Even if you mostly record your synth by plugging it straight in (the sound-system units’ DI box), you'll mic amplifiers, voices and rooms, and you'll need to read microphone specifications.

## Three ways to make a voltage

### Dynamic (moving coil)

A small coil of wire is glued to the diaphragm and sits in the gap of a permanent magnet. Sound moves the diaphragm, the coil moves through the magnetic field, and **electromagnetic induction** generates a voltage proportional to its velocity.

- A traditional passive moving-coil mic needs no power; models with internal active electronics are exceptions.
- Rugged and tolerant of very high SPL (kick drums, guitar cabs, vocals on stage).
- The coil adds mass, so transient and high-frequency detail are usually less than a condenser's.
- Low output: typically around 1–3 mV per pascal. Needs plenty of preamp gain.

The Shure SM58 is the classic example.

### Condenser (capacitor)

The diaphragm is one plate of a **capacitor**; a fixed **backplate** is the other. Sound changes the gap, so the capacitance changes. A conventional capsule with an external polarising supply is charged through a very large resistance, so charge is approximately constant over the relevant audio timescale. An **electret** supplies a persistent electric polarisation. Changing capacitance then changes the capsule voltage; the readout electronics and capsule design still matter.

- The capsule has an extremely high impedance, so a conventional studio condenser microphone uses an **impedance converter** (a small amplifier). That needs power: usually phantom power, sometimes a battery or a dedicated supply for valve models.
- The diaphragm is very light, so condensers capture fast transients and high-frequency detail.
- Often higher output (for example 10–30 mV/Pa). A low-noise condenser can give a quieter recording of a quiet source, but compare the actual microphone and preamp specifications; the operating principle alone does not guarantee lower noise or lower maximum SPL.

### Ribbon

A very thin corrugated metal ribbon hangs in a magnetic field. Sound moves the ribbon, and induction generates a voltage, as in a dynamic mic. The ribbon has a tiny output and very low impedance, so passive ribbons use a step-up transformer.

- Open at front and back, a ribbon naturally has a **figure-8** pattern.
- Smooth, often darker high end.
- Physically fragile: a blast of air (wind, a kick drum port, blowing into it) can stretch the ribbon.

> [!warning] Ribbons and phantom power
> A correctly wired balanced cable puts phantom voltage equally on both signal pins, so an ideal floating passive output sees no differential DC. Damage can still happen with a faulty or miswired cable, with unbalanced adapters, or when hot-plugging with phantom on, because the pins don't make contact at the same instant. Switch phantom power **off** before connecting a passive ribbon (or anything that doesn't need it). Some modern "active" ribbons need phantom: follow the manufacturer's manual.

## Proximity effect

Directional (pressure-gradient) mics have a **bass boost when the source is very close**, within a few centimetres to tens of centimetres. Close to a small source, the pressure difference between the front and back of the diaphragm contains an extra component that is relatively strongest at low frequencies. The closer the source, the bigger the boost.

- Singers use it ("eating the mic" for a warm, big voice).
- It causes boomy, muddy recordings when you didn't want it.
- **Omnidirectional (pure pressure) mics have no proximity effect.**
- Many directional mics have a bass-cut switch to compensate.

## Key takeaways
- Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction.
- Condenser microphones need power for their impedance-converting electronics.
- Pressure-gradient microphones can show proximity bass boost; pure pressure microphones do not.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)
- [Ribbon microphone phantom precautions — Royer](https://royerlabs.com/faqs/)

questions.prompt: Which microphone type needs power for its internal electronics, typically supplied as phantom power?

options.explanation: Correct. A conventional condenser capsule's very high impedance needs an internal impedance converter and, for a design requiring external capsule bias, a polarising supply, so the microphone needs power.
A passive moving-coil mic generates voltage by induction without active electronics.
A passive ribbon generates its output by induction and uses a transformer, not active electronics.
Passive dynamics and passive ribbons work without external power.

questions.workedExample:
1. Dynamic and ribbon mics: a conductor moves in a magnetic field, so induction generates the voltage directly.
2. Condenser: capacitance changes with sound; turning that into a usable low-impedance signal needs an amplifier in the mic body.
3. That amplifier is usually powered by P48 phantom power over the mic cable.

questions.prompt: A vocalist moves from 30 cm to 3 cm away from a cardioid dynamic mic. Apart from getting louder, how does the tone change?

options.text: It gets thinner, with less bass
options.explanation: Close placement on a directional mic does the opposite: more bass.

options.text: It gets bass-heavier because of the proximity effect
options.explanation: Correct. Directional mics respond to a pressure gradient that, close to a small source, has extra low-frequency content.
Pressure-gradient mics show a distance-dependent bass boost.

options.text: It gets brighter because of the precedence effect
options.explanation: The precedence effect is about localisation in hearing, not microphone tone.

questions.workedExample:
1. A cardioid is a pressure-gradient (or partly gradient) mic.
2. Close to a small source the gradient includes a component that rises at low frequencies as distance falls.
3. So at 3 cm the bass is boosted compared with 30 cm.
4. An omnidirectional (pressure) mic wouldn't show this.

lessons.title: Read microphone patterns and their nulls
lessons.summary: Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses.
lessons.body:
## Polar patterns

How a mic responds to sound from different directions depends on how the diaphragm is exposed:

- **Pressure microphones** (diaphragm open only at the front, sealed behind) respond to pressure itself, which has no direction: **omnidirectional**.
- **Pressure-gradient** mics (open at front and back) respond to the *difference* in pressure between the two sides. Sound from the side reaches both sides equally, giving a null: **figure-8**.
- Combining the two (or using an acoustic delay network behind the diaphragm) gives the **cardioid family**.

All the common ("first-order") patterns are a mix of an omni part, which is the same in every direction, and a figure-8 part, which follows the cosine of the angle. One formula covers the whole family; only the mix changes:

```formula
r(θ) = A + (1 − A) cos(θ)
where
r(θ): the microphone's relative sensitivity to sound arriving from angle θ, as a fraction of its on-axis sensitivity; 1 means as sensitive as straight ahead, 0 means a null (no pickup), and a negative value means a lobe that picks up with inverted polarity
r: the relative sensitivity (see r(θ))
θ: theta, the angle between the sound's direction and the front axis of the mic, in degrees (°); 0° is straight ahead, 90° is the side, 180° is directly behind
A: the omni share of the mix, a pure number from 0 to 1; A = 1 is omni, A = 0 is figure-8, A = 0.5 is cardioid, about 0.37 is supercardioid and 0.25 is hypercardioid
cos: cosine, a function that is 1 at 0°, 0 at 90° and −1 at 180°
In words: the pickup in any direction is the fixed omni part plus the figure-8 part scaled by the cosine of the angle. Lowering A narrows the front but grows a rear lobe.
```

To compare directions you convert the ratio r into decibels relative to the front. Setting r to zero and solving gives the angle of the null:

```formula
L(θ) = 20 log_10(|r(θ)|)
cos(θ_null) = −A / (1 − A)
θ_null = arccos(−A / (1 − A))
where
L(θ): the pickup level from angle θ relative to straight ahead, in decibels (dB); 0 dB is the on-axis level, −6 dB is half the voltage
r(θ): the relative sensitivity from the formula above, a pure number
r: the relative sensitivity (see r(θ))
θ: theta, the angle from the front axis, in degrees (°)
θ_null: the angle at which the mic picks up nothing, in degrees (°)
A: the omni share of the mix, from 0 to 1
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 is used because r is a voltage (amplitude) ratio
|r(θ)|: the size of r ignoring its sign (absolute value), because a rear lobe with inverted polarity is still heard
cos: cosine
arccos: the inverse cosine: the angle whose cosine is the given number
dB: decibel, a logarithmic unit for a ratio
In words: turn the sensitivity ratio into decibels to compare directions, and the null sits where the cosine term exactly cancels the omni part.
```

The logarithmic pickup formula applies only where the sensitivity magnitude is nonzero; at an ideal null its limiting level is negative infinity. A real microphone has finite rejection. The null-angle expression applies only when the omni share is at most one half and less than one; a pure omni has no null.

Worked through for a cardioid with omni share 0.5 and a hypercardioid with omni share 0.25:

```formula
r_c(90°) = 0.5 + 0.5 × 0 = 0.5
L_c(90°) = 20 log_10(0.5) ≈ −6.0 dB
r_c(180°) = 0.5 + 0.5 × (−1) = 0
cos(θ_null) = −0.25 / 0.75 = −1/3
θ_null = arccos(−1/3) ≈ 109.5°
r_h(180°) = 0.25 − 0.75 = −0.5
L_h(180°) = 20 log_10(0.5) ≈ −6.0 dB
where
r_c: the cardioid's (A = 0.5) relative sensitivity at the angle in brackets, a pure number; 90° is the side, 180° directly behind
r_h: the hypercardioid's (A = 0.25) relative sensitivity at the angle in brackets, a pure number
L_c: the cardioid's pickup at that angle relative to the front, in decibels (dB)
L_h: the hypercardioid's pickup at that angle relative to the front, in decibels (dB)
θ_null: the hypercardioid's null angle, in degrees (°)
cos: cosine (cos 90° = 0, cos 180° = −1)
arccos: inverse cosine
log_10: base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: a cardioid is 6 dB down at the side and silent behind; a hypercardioid's nulls sit at about 110°, and its rear lobe is only 6 dB down (with inverted polarity).
```

The same sums in Python, for all three directional patterns (the code puts the absolute value in for you):

```python
import math

def rel_db(a, deg):
    # The pattern uses degrees; cos needs
    # rad.
    r = a + (1 - a) * math.cos(
        math.radians(deg))
    return 20 * math.log10(abs(r))

pats = {"cardioid": 0.5,
        "super": 0.366,
        "hyper": 0.25}
for name, a in pats.items():
    null = math.degrees(
        math.acos(-a / (1 - a)))
    print(f"{name}: 90deg "
          f"{rel_db(a, 90):5.1f} dB,"
          f" null {null:5.1f} deg")
```

```
cardioid: 90deg  -6.0 dB, null 180.0 deg
super: 90deg  -8.7 dB, null 125.3 deg
hyper: 90deg -12.0 dB, null 109.5 deg
```

| Pattern | Side (90°) | Null |
|---|---|---|
| Omni | 0 dB | none |
| Cardioid | −6 dB | 180° (rear) |
| Supercardioid | ≈ −8.7 dB | ≈ 125° |
| Hypercardioid | −12 dB | ≈ 110° |
| Figure-8 | null | 90° |

Super- and hypercardioids are narrower at the front but have a **rear lobe** (a hypercardioid is only −6 dB directly behind). That matters for stage monitors (the sound-system units): put a wedge at a cardioid's 180° null, but at the 110–125° nulls of a hyper- or supercardioid.

Real microphones only follow these shapes approximately. Their directionality can change substantially with frequency; a pressure-gradient design can retain low-frequency directionality, while a pressure microphone becomes more directional at high frequencies as its size matters. Check the polar plots in the datasheet.

## Key takeaways
- Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses.
- A cardioid’s rear null differs from the angled nulls of hypercardioid and supercardioid patterns.
- Measured polar plots vary with frequency and determine practical placement.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)

questions.prompt: A cardioid microphone points at a singer. From which direction does it reject sound most strongly?

options.explanation: A cardioid is only about 6 dB down at the sides.
That's the direction of maximum sensitivity.
Correct. Directly behind, the figure-8 part of a cardioid exactly cancels its omni part, so the response is zero: the null (see the worked example).
That describes an omnidirectional mic, which rejects nothing.

questions.workedExample:
A cardioid is an equal mix of omni and figure-8 pickup. Its relative sensitivity at each angle is:

```formula
r(θ) = 0.5 + 0.5 cos(θ)
r(0°) = 0.5 + 0.5 × 1 = 1 (0 dB)
r(90°) = 0.5 + 0.5 × 0 = 0.5 (−6 dB)
r(180°) = 0.5 + 0.5 × (−1) = 0
where
r(θ): the relative sensitivity from angle θ, as a fraction of the on-axis sensitivity; 1 is full sensitivity, 0 is a null
r: the relative sensitivity
θ: theta, the angle from the front of the mic, in degrees (°); 0° is in front, 180° is directly behind
cos: cosine, which is 1 at 0°, 0 at 90° and −1 at 180°
dB: decibel; 0.5 of the voltage is about −6 dB
In words: a cardioid is full sensitivity in front, half (−6 dB) at the sides and zero directly behind.
```

So place a floor monitor directly behind a cardioid mic.

questions.prompt: A singer uses a hypercardioid vocal mic on stage. Where should the floor wedge go to get the most gain before feedback?

options.explanation: A hypercardioid has a rear lobe; it's only about 6 dB down directly behind.

options.text: At about 110° off-axis, roughly in line with the null
options.explanation: Correct. A hypercardioid's null is at about 109.5° (see the worked example), so a wedge there is picked up least.
At 90° a hypercardioid is about 12 dB down, but its null is further round.

options.text: In front of the mic, facing the singer
options.explanation: That points the wedge into the mic's most sensitive direction.

questions.workedExample:
A hypercardioid is a quarter omni and three quarters figure-8. Find its null and its rear level:

```formula
r(θ) = 0.25 + 0.75 cos(θ)
cos(θ_null) = −0.25 / 0.75 = −1/3
θ_null = arccos(−1/3) ≈ 109.5°
r(180°) = 0.25 − 0.75 = −0.5
L = 20 log_10(0.5) ≈ −6 dB
where
r(θ): the relative sensitivity from angle θ, as a fraction of on-axis; a negative value is a lobe with inverted polarity
r: the relative sensitivity
θ: theta, the angle from the front of the mic, in degrees (°)
θ_null: the null angle, where r(θ) = 0, found by setting the formula to zero, in degrees (°)
cos: cosine (−1 at 180°)
arccos: inverse cosine, the angle whose cosine is the given number
L: the rear lobe's level relative to the front, in decibels (dB), using the size of r and ignoring its sign
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the nulls are about 110° off-axis, while directly behind there is a rear lobe only 6 dB down.
```

In practice a pair of wedges is often set either side, each near the null angle. Check the actual polar plot in the mic's datasheet, since real patterns vary with frequency.

lessons.title: Microphone sensitivity, noise and overload
lessons.summary: Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal.
lessons.body:
## Reading the specifications

### Sensitivity

The output voltage for a given sound pressure, normally at 1 kHz and **1 Pa (94 dB SPL)**:

- **mV/Pa**: millivolts of output per pascal of sound pressure, or
- **dBV/Pa**: the same figure in decibels relative to 1 volt per pascal.

Converting between the two is a voltage-ratio decibel calculation:

```formula
S_dBV = 20 log_10(S / (1 V/Pa))
S_dBV = 20 log_10((0.028 V/Pa) / (1 V/Pa))
S_dBV ≈ −31.1 dBV/Pa
where
S_dBV: the sensitivity in decibels relative to 1 volt per pascal (dBV/Pa); negative for these two microphones; a less negative value means greater output, and sufficiently sensitive active designs need not be negative
S: the sensitivity as a voltage ratio, in volts per pascal (V/Pa); here 28 mV/Pa = 0.028 V/Pa (a Neumann U 87 Ai)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
V: volt, the unit of voltage
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure; 1 Pa is about 94 dB SPL
dBV: decibels relative to 1 volt
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: sensitivity in dBV/Pa is 20 times the base-10 log of the output voltage per pascal; 28 mV/Pa comes out at about −31 dBV/Pa.
```

| Mic (manufacturer's figures) | mV/Pa | dBV/Pa |
|---|---|---|
| Shure SM58 (dynamic) | 1.6 | −56.0 |
| Neumann U 87 Ai, cardioid | 28 | ≈ −31 |

(The SM58 figures follow Shure’s user guide version 6.4 (2024-F), checked October 2026; the −56.0 dBV/Pa figure corresponds to about 1.585 mV/Pa, rounded to 1.6 mV/Pa. Older specifications quote different values, so confirm the revision for the microphone being used. Supercardioid definitions also vary a little between sources; an omni share of 0.366 is one common choice.)

How much more preamp gain does the less sensitive mic need for the same output? Take the ratio of the two sensitivities and convert it to decibels:

```formula
G = 20 log_10(S_A / S_B)
G = 20 log_10((28 mV/Pa) / (1.6 mV/Pa))
G = 20 log_10(17.5)
G ≈ 24.9 dB
where
G: the extra preamp gain mic B needs to match mic A's output, in decibels (dB)
S_A: the sensitivity of the more sensitive mic (here the U 87 Ai), in millivolts per pascal (mV/Pa)
S_B: the sensitivity of the less sensitive mic (here the SM58), in mV/Pa
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 because these are voltage ratios
mV: millivolt, a thousandth of a volt
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: the condenser puts out about 17.5 times the voltage, which is about 24.9 dB, so the dynamic needs about 25 dB more preamp gain.
```

So the dynamic needs about **25 dB** more preamp gain for the same output. Gain raises signal and input noise together. For quiet sources, compare microphone sensitivity, its own noise and the preamp’s equivalent input noise; a low-noise condenser often performs well.

### Self-noise

A condenser's electronics produce some noise even in a silent room. **Self-noise** (or "equivalent noise level") is quoted as the SPL that would produce the same output, usually A-weighted (dB-A). Neumann specifies the U 87 Ai's self-noise as **12 dB-A** in cardioid. Below about 10 dB-A is very quiet; above about 20 dB-A can become audible on quiet sources.

Passive dynamics and ribbons have no active electronics, but their winding and transformer resistance still generate thermal noise. That noise and the preamp’s input noise both contribute to the recorded noise floor.

### Maximum SPL and dynamic range

Max SPL is the level at which distortion reaches a stated figure (often 0.5% or 1% THD). Neumann gives **117 dB SPL** for the U 87 Ai (127 dB with its pre-attenuation pad). The dynamic range is the gap between self-noise and max SPL:

```formula
DR = L_max − L_noise
DR = 117 dB SPL − 12 dB SPL = 105 dB
where
DR: the microphone's dynamic range, in decibels (dB): how far the loudest clean sound is above its own noise
L_max: the maximum SPL, the sound level at which distortion reaches the stated limit, in dB SPL
L_noise: the self-noise expressed as an equivalent sound level, in dB SPL (A-weighted here)
dB: decibel
SPL: sound pressure level, measured relative to 20 µPa
In words: subtract the noise floor from the overload point; both are already in decibels, so subtraction gives the range.
```

Because the self-noise figure is A-weighted, this is an approximate, A-weighted range; with the pad engaged the top end rises to 127 dB SPL.

## Key takeaways
- Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal.
- Compare microphone noise and preamp noise together.
- Dynamic range requires both a noise reference and a stated overload criterion.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)
- [SM58 manufacturer specifications — Shure](https://pubs.shure.com/view/guide/SM58/en-US.pdf)

questions.prompt: Microphone sensitivity is conventionally quoted at which sound pressure?

options.explanation: That's the reference for dB SPL, far too quiet for a sensible sensitivity measurement.
Volts are the output, not the acoustic input.
Some calibrators produce 114 dB SPL (10 Pa), but sensitivity is normalised to 1 Pa.

options.text: 1 Pa, which is about 94 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. 1 Pa is 50,000 times the 20 µPa reference pressure, which works out at about 93.98 dB SPL (see the worked example).

questions.workedExample:
Sensitivity relates output voltage to sound pressure, normally at one kilohertz. The sound pressure level of 1 Pa is:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(p / p_0)
L = 20 log_10(1 Pa / 0.00002 Pa)
L = 20 log_10(50000) ≈ 93.98 dB SPL
where
L: the sound pressure level, in decibels relative to 20 µPa (dB SPL)
p: the sound pressure, in pascals (Pa); here 1 Pa
p_0: the reference pressure, 20 µPa = 0.00002 Pa, roughly the quietest sound a young listener can hear at 1 kHz
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 because pressure is an amplitude
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure
dB: decibel
SPL: sound pressure level
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 1 Pa is 50,000 times the reference pressure, which is about 94 dB SPL.
```

So "28 mV/Pa" means 28 mV out at 94 dB SPL.

questions.prompt: Mic A has a sensitivity of 28 mV/Pa and mic B 1.6 mV/Pa. Roughly how much more preamp gain does B need for the same output level?

options.explanation: 28/1.6 ≈ 17.5, but that's the voltage *ratio*, not decibels.
This treats the ratio as a power ratio (10 times the logarithm, about 12.4 dB). Sensitivity is a voltage ratio, so it takes 20 times the logarithm.
Correct. The voltage ratio is about 17.5, which is about 24.9 dB (see the worked example).
Gain is a ratio, best expressed in dB, not a voltage difference.

questions.workedExample:
Gain is a voltage ratio, so convert it with 20 × log_10:

```formula
G = 20 log_10(S_A / S_B)
G = 20 log_10(28 / 1.6)
G = 20 log_10(17.5) ≈ 24.9 dB
where
G: the extra preamp gain mic B needs to match mic A, in decibels (dB)
S_A: mic A's sensitivity, 28 millivolts per pascal (mV/Pa)
S_B: mic B's sensitivity, 1.6 mV/Pa
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: mic A gives about 17.5 times the voltage of mic B, which is about 25 dB.
```

Gain also raises input noise. Overall recording noise depends on the microphone’s own noise, sensitivity and the preamp’s input noise; low-noise condensers often suit quiet sources.

questions.prompt: Neumann specifies the U 87 Ai (cardioid) with 12 dB-A self-noise and 117 dB SPL maximum SPL without its pad. What's its approximate dynamic range?

options.explanation: Adding the two numbers doesn't give a range. The range is the difference.
That's the max SPL, measured from 0 dB SPL, not from the self-noise floor.
That's the self-noise alone.
Correct. 117 − 12 = 105 dB.

questions.workedExample:
Dynamic range is the gap between the loudest clean level and the noise floor:

```formula
DR = L_max − L_noise
DR = 117 dB − 12 dB = 105 dB
where
DR: the dynamic range, in decibels (dB)
L_max: the maximum SPL before the stated distortion, 117 dB SPL
L_noise: the self-noise as an equivalent sound level, 12 dB SPL (A-weighted)
dB: decibel
In words: both figures are already in decibels, so the range is simply the difference.
```

(The self-noise is A-weighted, so this is an approximate, A-weighted range. With the pre-attenuation pad, the max SPL rises to 127 dB.)

lessons.title: Understand phantom-power connections
lessons.summary: P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors.
lessons.body:
## Phantom power (P48)

Condenser microphones are powered through the same balanced cable that carries their signal. **IEC 61938** defines **P48**:

- **+48 V** fed through two matched **6.81 kΩ** resistors, one to each signal conductor (pins 2 and 3 of an XLR), with the shield (XLR pin 1) as the return.
- Closely matched feed resistors help preserve the impedance balance of the line.
- The standard allows up to **10 mA** per microphone. Lower-voltage P12 and P24 variants also exist.

The equal DC on the signal wires is common-mode, so it does not appear across an ideal floating dynamic coil. A preamp still needs suitable DC blocking, voltage ratings and transient protection: common-mode rejection alone does not make an arbitrary balanced input safe at 48 V.

The mic draws its current through both feed resistors at once. Two equal resistors side by side (in parallel) act like one of half the value, and the voltage lost across them follows Ohm's law:

```formula
R_feed = 6810 Ω / 2 = 3405 Ω
V_mic = V_s − I R_feed
V_mic = 48 V − 0.010 A × 3405 Ω
V_mic = 48 V − 34.05 V ≈ 14.0 V
where
R_feed: the combined resistance of the two 6.81 kΩ feed resistors in parallel, in ohms (Ω)
V_mic: the DC voltage left at the microphone, in volts (V)
V_s: the phantom supply voltage, 48 V for P48
I: the current the microphone draws, in amperes (A); here 10 mA = 0.010 A, the maximum the standard allows
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance
V: volt
A: ampere (amp), the unit of current
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: the more current the mic draws, the more voltage is dropped in the feed resistors, so a hungry mic sees much less than 48 V.
```

The same calculation for three currents, in Python:

```python
# Each matched leg carries half the current.
R_feed = 6810 / 2     # two in parallel
for i_ma in (0.8, 5, 10):
    v = 48 - i_ma / 1000 * R_feed
    print(f"{i_ma:>4} mA: "
          f"{v:5.1f} V at mic")
```

```
 0.8 mA:  45.3 V at mic
   5 mA:  31.0 V at mic
  10 mA:  14.0 V at mic
```

The feed resistors limit what the mic can draw: a low-current mic like the U 87 Ai (0.8 mA per Neumann) sees nearly the full 48 V; a hungry one sees much less. A supply that can't deliver enough current makes some mics distort earlier.

> [!warning] Phantom power and your synth
> As module 5 said, keep phantom **off** on any channel your synth or other line-level gear is plugged into. Phantom is for microphones and DI boxes designed for it.

## Key takeaways
- P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors.
- Feed resistance makes the microphone’s connector voltage depend on current draw.
- Use compatible inputs and correct cables; turn phantom off for equipment that does not require it.

## Further reading
- [Phantom supply and XLR contact diagrams — Schoeps CMC/MK manual, October 2015](https://schoeps.de/fileadmin/user_upload/user_upload/Downloads/Bedienungsanleitungen/SCHOEPS_Manual_CMC_MK_E_2015-10-03_1444311033__1_.pdf)
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)
- [Ribbon microphone phantom precautions — Royer](https://royerlabs.com/faqs/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about IEC 61938 P48 phantom power are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The standard allows up to 10 mA per microphone
options.explanation: Correct.

options.text: Phantom appears as a 48 V difference between XLR pin 2 and XLR pin 3
options.explanation: Phantom DC is common-mode on the two signal legs. A phantom-compatible input needs appropriate DC blocking and protection; differential amplification alone does not provide voltage tolerance.

options.text: +48 V is applied equally to XLR pins 2 and 3 through matched 6.81 kΩ resistors
options.explanation: Correct. That's the P48 definition.

options.text: The shield (XLR pin 1) is the return path
options.explanation: Correct. Interrupting the actual microphone pin-1 return breaks this circuit, but a DI ground-lift switch may preserve its phantom return.

questions.workedExample:
```
+48V --6.81k--> pin 2
+48V --6.81k--> pin 3
0 V  ----------> pin 1 (shield)
```

The DC is common-mode and does not appear across an ideal floating coil. The input must still be designed to tolerate and block phantom DC and transients. The mic draws its current through both resistors in parallel (3.4 kΩ).

questions.prompt: You're about to plug a vintage passive ribbon mic into a channel that has phantom power available. Which precautions are sensible? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the cable is correctly wired, for example no short from XLR pin 1 to XLR pin 2 or XLR pin 3
options.explanation: Correct. A fault can put phantom voltage across the mic's output.

options.text: Use an XLR-to-TS unbalanced adapter so phantom can't reach the mic
options.explanation: An unbalanced adapter typically ties one signal leg to ground, which with phantom on can put DC across the mic. It's one of the known damage routes.

options.text: Switch phantom off on that channel before connecting
options.explanation: Correct. Good practice for anything that doesn't need phantom.

options.text: Avoid hot-plugging into a live phantom input
options.explanation: Correct. Pins make contact at different instants, which can put a transient across the ribbon or preamp.

questions.workedExample:
With a correctly wired balanced cable, both signal contacts carry equal phantom DC, so an ideal floating passive output sees no differential DC. Schoeps recommends connecting microphones with phantom switched off; Royer also warns about miswired cables and live patch-bay connections.

1. Check that XLR pin 1 is the shield/phantom return and that XLR pin 2 and XLR pin 3 are the signal contacts, without faults between them.
2. Avoid unbalanced adapters that connect a signal leg to the return.
3. Switch phantom off, allow the interface's specified discharge time, and connect using the microphone maker's procedure.

A differential input still needs suitable DC blocking, component voltage ratings and transient protection.

lessons.title: Control leakage and comb filtering
lessons.summary: Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage.
lessons.body:
## Placement basics

- **Distance controls the direct-to-room balance.** Close placement gives more direct sound, less room, more proximity effect and more level variation as the performer moves. Further away captures more of the room.
- **Angle controls tone.** On a guitar cab, the centre of the cone is brighter; towards the edge it's darker. Small moves matter.
- Use **acoustic nulls**. Aim the null of a directional mic at what you *don't* want (a monitor, a neighbouring drum).
- Mind **sound reflections**. A music stand or desk near the mic adds a reflection a few milliseconds late, which comb-filters the sound.

### The 3:1 rule

When several mics are open at once, a source reaches its own mic and, more weakly and later, its neighbours. When the signals are mixed, the delayed copy comb-filters the direct one. The **3:1 rule** says the distance *between* mics should be at least **three times** the distance from each mic to its source.

Why it works: by the inverse square law, sound pressure falls in proportion to distance, so the leakage level drops by:

```formula
L_leak = 20 log_10(d_far / d_near)
L_leak = 20 log_10(3d / d)
L_leak = 20 log_10(3) ≈ 9.5 dB
where
L_leak: how far the leaked copy is below the direct sound, in decibels (dB)
d_far: the distance from the source to the neighbouring mic, in metres (m)
d_near: the distance from the source to its own mic, in metres (m)
d: the source-to-own-mic distance; the 3:1 rule makes d_far at least 3 × d
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 because pressure is an amplitude
dB: decibel
m: metre
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: three times further away means about a third of the pressure, which is about 9.5 dB quieter.
```

When a copy that much quieter is mixed with the direct sound, it can only nudge the sum up or down a little:

```formula
g = 10^{−L_leak/20} = 10^{−9.5/20} ≈ 0.335
L_peak = 20 log_10(1 + g) ≈ +2.5 dB
L_notch = 20 log_10(1 − g) ≈ −3.5 dB
where
g: the leaked copy's amplitude as a fraction of the direct sound, a pure number
L_leak: how far the leak is below the direct sound, in decibels (dB); here 9.5 dB
L_peak: the biggest boost, at frequencies where the copy arrives in phase, in dB
L_notch: the deepest cut, at frequencies where the copy arrives out of phase, in dB
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: convert the 9.5 dB gap back to an amplitude fraction, then add or subtract it from 1 to find the worst peak and notch.
```

That is about +2.5 dB at a peak and −3.5 dB at a notch, rather than the +6 dB peaks and perfect notches of equal-amplitude delayed copies.

```diagram
  src A      src B
   |          |
  0.3 m      0.3 m
   |          |
  mic A ---- mic B
     >= 0.9 m apart
```

It's a rule of thumb that assumes omni-like pickup and similar levels. Directional mics aimed well, or very different source levels, change the numbers.

## Key takeaways
- Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage.
- The three-to-one spacing rule is a practical starting estimate.
- Leakage ripple also depends on source geometry, microphone response and channel gains.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)

questions.prompt: Two cardioid mics are each 25 cm from their own singers. Following the 3:1 rule, what's the minimum spacing between the mics?

options.explanation: Correct. 3 × 25 cm = 75 cm.
This does not satisfy the rule. Actual leakage also depends on geometry, polar patterns and channel gains.
That's 2:1; the rule asks for 3:1.
That divides by three instead of multiplying.

questions.workedExample:
Apply the 3:1 rule, then check how much quieter the leakage is:

```formula
s ≥ 3d
s ≥ 3 × 25 cm = 75 cm
L_leak = 20 log_10(3) ≈ 9.5 dB
where
s: the spacing between the two mics, in centimetres (cm)
d: each mic's distance from its own singer, here 25 cm
L_leak: how far the leakage is below the direct sound, in decibels (dB), when the singer is three times further from the other mic
≥: is at least
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 because pressure falls in proportion to distance (inverse square law for intensity)
cm: centimetre
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: keep the mics at least three times as far apart as each is from its singer, which keeps the leakage about 9.5 dB down.
```

About 9.5 dB down limits comb filtering to roughly +2.5/−3.5 dB. These numerical leakage limits assume approximately equal gains and a source-to-distant-mic distance three times the source-to-near-mic distance; directional pickup changes the result.

questions.prompt: Two mics pick up a broadband source. Model the leakage into the second as a delayed copy, 9.5 dB below the direct signal at every frequency. With equal channel gains, roughly how large are the comb-filter peaks and notches?

options.text: About +2.5 dB peaks and −3.5 dB notches
options.explanation: Correct. 9.5 dB down is about 0.335 of the direct amplitude, so the sum swings between about 1.335 and 0.665 of the direct level: about +2.5 dB and −3.5 dB.
That's for two equal-level copies. 9.5 dB down limits both.
A nonzero delayed copy produces a comb response in this ideal broadband model; real microphone responses can change its shape.
The ripple is much smaller than the level difference itself.

questions.workedExample:
Convert the 9.5 dB gap back into an amplitude fraction, then add it to or subtract it from the direct sound:

```formula
g = 10^{−9.5/20} ≈ 0.335
L_peak = 20 log_10(1 + g) ≈ +2.5 dB
L_notch = 20 log_10(1 − g) ≈ −3.5 dB
where
g: the leak's amplitude as a fraction of the direct sound, a pure number
L_peak: the biggest boost, where the copy arrives in phase, in decibels (dB)
L_notch: the deepest cut, where the copy arrives out of phase, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 10^{x/20} undoes 20 × log_10
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a copy at about a third of the amplitude can only raise the sum by about 2.5 dB or cut it by about 3.5 dB.
```

That's the arithmetic behind the 3:1 rule: three times the distance gives about 9.5 dB of separation (inverse square law), which keeps the ripple to a few dB.

lessons.title: From voice-coil current to cone force
lessons.summary: A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force.
lessons.body:
A **loudspeaker driver** is the motor and diaphragm that actually move air. A loudspeaker *system* is one or more drivers plus an enclosure (the enclosure units) and usually a crossover (the crossover units). This lesson is about the driver: how it works, and how to read the numbers on its datasheet.

## The motor structure

Nearly all speakers you will meet are **moving-coil** (electrodynamic) drivers, a design dating from the 1920s.

```diagram
     surround          cone
   ,-----------.  /
  (             )/
   \  +-------+ /      spider
    \ | coil  |/  ===  (suspension)
  [N]=|=gap===|=[N]
  [S]  pole    [S]  <- magnet
       piece
```

The parts:

- **Magnet and pole pieces (the motor).** A permanent magnet (ferrite or neodymium) and steel parts concentrate a strong magnetic field in a narrow ring-shaped **magnetic gap**.
- **Voice coil.** A coil of fine wire wound on a light former, sitting in the gap. It's attached to the cone.
- **Cone (diaphragm).** Pushes the air. Paper, polypropylene, aluminium and composites are common. It must be light and stiff.
- **Driver suspension.** The **driver surround** at the outer edge and the **driver spider** behind the cone keep the coil centred in the gap and provide a restoring force that pulls the cone back to rest.
- **Basket (frame)** holds it all together.

## How current becomes sound

A current in a wire in a magnetic field feels a force (the Lorentz force; it's the motor principle). The voice coil is wound so the wire crosses the field at right angles everywhere in the gap, so the force on it is simply:

```formula
F = B l i
F = Bl i
where
F: the force on the voice coil (and so on the cone), in newtons (N)
B: the magnetic flux density in the gap, how strong the magnet's field is there, in tesla (T); around 1 T is typical
l: the length of voice-coil wire sitting in the field, in metres (m); often several metres of fine wire
i: the current through the voice coil, in amperes (A)
Bl: the product B × l, quoted on datasheets as the "force factor" or "BL", in tesla-metres (T·m); typically about 5–20 T·m
N: newton, the unit of force
T: tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density
m: metre
A: ampere, the unit of current
In words: the push on the cone is proportional to the current in this small-signal model; a stronger field or more wire in the gap gives more push per amp.
```

Datasheets quote the product **Bl** ("BL") because B and l only ever appear together. For example, with 1 A in the coil of a 7 T·m driver:

```formula
F = Bl i = 7 T·m × 1 A = 7 N
where
F: the force on the voice coil, in newtons (N)
Bl: the force factor, here 7 tesla-metres (T·m)
i: the voice-coil current, here 1 ampere (A)
T: tesla
m: metre
A: ampere
N: newton
In words: 7 T·m of force factor turns each amp into 7 newtons of push.
```

Audio current alternates, so the force alternates and the cone moves back and forth, pushing air (the acoustics units).

The cone, coil and the air it carries have **mass**; the suspension acts as a **spring**. Mass on a spring has a resonance. That's the driver's **free-air resonance, Fs**, one of the Thiele–Small parameters in the enclosure units. Below Fs the output falls away.

A driver is also an **electromagnetic generator**: a moving coil in a field produces a voltage (back-EMF), exactly as a dynamic mic does. That back-EMF is why the impedance changes so much near resonance.

## Key takeaways
- A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force.
- Moving mass and suspension compliance establish the driver’s free-air resonance.
- The moving coil also generates back electromotive force.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt: In a moving-coil driver, what produces the force that moves the cone?

options.text: Current in the voice coil sitting in the magnet's field
options.explanation: Correct. A current in a conductor in a magnetic field feels a force proportional to B, wire length and current.

options.text: The magnet attracting the cone directly
options.explanation: The cone isn't magnetic. The force acts on the current-carrying voice coil.
The enclosure's air acts as a spring on the cone, but it isn't the driving force.

options.text: Electric charge pulling the cone towards a fixed plate
options.explanation: Electrostatic loudspeakers use electric forces between charged structures. A moving-coil driver's motor instead uses current in a magnetic field.

questions.workedExample:
1. The motor concentrates a magnetic field in a narrow gap.
2. The voice coil sits in the gap and is attached to the cone.
3. Amplifier current through the coil produces a force:

```formula
F = B l i = Bl i
F = 6 T·m × 2 A = 12 N
where
F: the force on the voice coil, in newtons (N)
B: the magnetic flux density in the gap, in tesla (T)
l: the length of coil wire in the field, in metres (m)
i: the current in the coil, in amperes (A)
Bl: the force factor B × l from the datasheet, in tesla-metres (T·m); here 6 T·m
T: tesla
m: metre
A: ampere
N: newton, the unit of force
In words: the force is the force factor times the current, so 2 A through a 6 T·m motor pushes with 12 N.
```

4. Alternating current gives an alternating force, so the cone vibrates.

lessons.title: Read a driver’s impedance curve
lessons.summary: An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency.
lessons.body:
## Impedance: nominal vs reality

An "8 Ω" speaker isn't 8 Ω. Its impedance depends on frequency:

- At DC it's just the voice-coil resistance, **Re** (often around 5–7 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver).
- Near **Fs** it rises to a sharp peak, because the back-EMF of the resonating cone opposes the current.
- Above resonance it falls to a minimum, then rises again at high frequencies because the voice coil is an **inductor**.

A simple model adds up three parts: the coil's resistance, the coil’s inductive impedance (which grows with frequency in this simple model), and a "motional" part that peaks at resonance. Impedance is a complex number, because it also shifts the timing (phase) of the current; the *size* of the total is what an impedance plot shows.

```formula
Z(f) = R_e + Z_L + Z_m
Z_L = 2jπf L_e
Z_m = R_res / (1 + jx)
x = Q_ms (f / F_s − F_s / f)
R_res = (R_e Q_ms) / Q_es
where
Z(f): the driver's total impedance at frequency f, in ohms (Ω); a complex number whose size |Z| is what the impedance curve plots
f: the frequency of the signal, in hertz (Hz)
R_e: the DC resistance of the voice coil (Re on datasheets), in ohms (Ω); often 5–7 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver
Z_L: the impedance of the voice coil's inductance, in ohms (Ω); it rises in proportion to frequency
Z_m: the motional impedance caused by the cone's movement (back-EMF), in ohms (Ω); largest at resonance
L_e: the voice-coil inductance (Le on datasheets), in henries (H); often a fraction of a millihenry
R_res: the peak value of the motional part, reached exactly at F_s, in ohms (Ω)
x: how far the frequency is from resonance, scaled by Q_ms; a pure number, 0 at F_s
F_s: the free-air resonance frequency (Fs), in hertz (Hz)
Q_ms: the mechanical Q (Qms): how sharp the resonance is from suspension losses alone; a pure number, typically 1–10
Q_es: the electrical Q (Qes): how strongly the motor's electrical damping controls the resonance; a pure number, typically 0.2–1
j: the imaginary unit used in electrical engineering (j × j = −1); it marks the part of an impedance that shifts phase
π: pi, about 3.14159
Ω: ohm, the unit of impedance and resistance
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
H: henry, the unit of inductance
In words: the impedance is the coil's resistance, plus an inductive part that grows with frequency, plus a resonant part that peaks at F_s and dies away either side.
```

At resonance the frequency-offset variable is zero, so the motional part reaches its full peak. Purdue’s sample uses 6.6 Ω coil resistance, 0.48 mH inductance, 65 Hz free-air resonance, electrical Q of 0.436 and mechanical Q of 2.25:

```formula
R_res = 6.6 Ω × 2.25 / 0.436 ≈ 34.1 Ω
Z_L = j × 2π × 65 × 0.00048 ≈ j × 0.2 Ω
|Z(F_s)| ≈ 6.6 Ω + 34.1 Ω ≈ 40.7 Ω
where
R_res: the motional peak, in ohms (Ω)
Z_L: the coil inductance's impedance at 65 Hz, tiny here
|Z(F_s)|: the size of the total impedance at the resonance frequency F_s = 65 Hz, in ohms (Ω)
F_s: the free-air resonance frequency, 65 Hz
Z: impedance
j: the imaginary unit; a j × 0.2 Ω part adds almost nothing to the size
π: pi, about 3.14159
Ω: ohm
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: at 65 Hz the woofer looks like about 41 Ω, more than five times its "8 Ω" label.
```

The model is easier to sweep across frequency in Python (`2j` is Python's way of writing 2 × j):

```python
import math

Re, Le = 6.6, 0.48e-3
Fs, Qes, Qms = 65, 0.436, 2.25
Rres = Re * Qms / Qes  # motional peak

def z(f):
    x = Qms * (f / Fs - Fs / f)
    # Back-EMF adds frequency-dependent
    # load.
    zm = Rres / complex(1, x)
    return Re + 2j*math.pi*f*Le + zm

for f in (20, 65, 200, 600, 2000, 10000):
    mag = abs(z(f))
    print(f"{f:>5} Hz: {mag:5.1f} ohm")
```

```
   20 Hz:   8.9 ohm
   65 Hz:  40.7 ohm
  200 Hz:   8.9 ohm
  600 Hz:   6.7 ohm
 2000 Hz:   8.6 ohm
10000 Hz:  30.8 ohm
```

From 6.7 Ω to over 40 Ω across the band. (Real voice-coil inductance is lossy, so the high-frequency rise is usually gentler than this simple model shows.)

**Nominal impedance** is a single rounded label for the region above resonance. The loudspeaker standard IEC 60268-5 says the minimum impedance in the rated frequency range should not fall below **80% of the rated (nominal) impedance**:

```formula
Z_min ≥ 0.8Z_nom
Z_min ≥ 0.8 × 8 Ω = 6.4 Ω
where
Z_min: the lowest impedance in the rated frequency range, in ohms (Ω)
Z_nom: the rated (nominal) impedance on the label, in ohms (Ω)
≥: is at least (greater than or equal to)
Ω: ohm
In words: a speaker labelled 8 Ω shouldn't dip below 6.4 Ω in its working range.
```

 Not every manufacturer follows that rule, and real multi-way speakers with crossovers can dip well below their label, which is why amplifier makers care about the *minimum*, not the nominal (the power-amplifier units).

## Key takeaways
- An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency.
- Resonance, coil resistance and inductance shape the curve.
- Amplifier compatibility requires the load’s magnitude and phase, not just its nominal label.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt: An "8 Ω" loudspeaker is labelled with its nominal impedance. What does that label mean?

options.text: Its impedance is 8 Ω at every frequency
options.explanation: Impedance varies widely: a peak at resonance and a rise at high frequencies from coil inductance.

options.text: Its DC resistance is exactly 8 Ω
options.explanation: The DC resistance (Re) is usually lower than nominal, often around 5–7 Ω.

options.text: The maximum impedance the speaker ever presents
options.explanation: The maximum (at resonance) can be several times the nominal value.

options.text: A rounded figure for the region above resonance; IEC 60268-5 says the in-band minimum shouldn't fall below 80% of it
options.explanation: Correct. For an 8 Ω rating, that's 6.4 Ω.

questions.workedExample:
1. A speaker's impedance changes with frequency.
2. Nominal impedance labels the minimum region above resonance, rounded to a standard value.
3. IEC 60268-5: the minimum in the rated frequency range should be at least 80% of rated:

```formula
Z_min ≥ 0.8Z_nom
Z_min ≥ 0.8 × 8 Ω = 6.4 Ω
where
Z_min: the lowest impedance in the rated frequency range, in ohms (Ω)
Z_nom: the nominal (rated) impedance, here 8 Ω
≥: is at least
Ω: ohm, the unit of impedance
In words: an "8 Ω" speaker should not dip below 6.4 Ω in its working range.
```

4. Amplifier current demand depends on the dips, so the minimum matters most.

link.title: Rated impedance and IEC rule — Dynaudio

questions.prompt:
Purdue's sample woofer has a DC resistance (Re) of 6.6 Ω, an electrical Q (Qes) of 0.436 and a mechanical Q (Qms) of 2.25. Neglecting voice-coil inductance, the impedance peak at its resonance Fs is:

```formula
Z_max = R_e (1 + Q_ms / Q_es)
where
Z_max: the impedance at the resonance peak, in ohms (Ω)
R_e: the voice coil's DC resistance (Re), in ohms (Ω)
Q_ms: the mechanical Q (Qms), a pure number
Q_es: the electrical Q (Qes), a pure number
Ω: ohm
In words: the peak is the coil resistance multiplied up by one plus the ratio of the two Qs.
```

Roughly what is it?

options.explanation: That's just the DC resistance, missing the motional part.
Correct. The ratio of the two Qs is about 5.16, so the peak is about 6.6 Ω × 6.16 ≈ 40.7 Ω.
The specified calculation gives 40.7 Ω, not 15 Ω. Reversing the ratio of the Qs would instead give about 7.9 Ω.
That's the nominal rating, not the peak at resonance.

questions.workedExample:
Substitute the datasheet values:

```formula
Q_ms / Q_es = 2.25 / 0.436 ≈ 5.16
Z_max = 6.6 Ω × (1 + 5.16)
Z_max ≈ 40.7 Ω
where
Q_ms: the mechanical Q, 2.25
Q_es: the electrical Q, 0.436
Z_max: the impedance peak at resonance, in ohms (Ω)
Ω: ohm
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the motional part adds about five times the coil resistance at resonance, so the peak is about 41 Ω.
```

At Fs, the cone's motion generates a large back-EMF, so little current flows: the impedance peaks. That's also how Fs and the Qs are measured, from the impedance curve.

lessons.title: Compare speaker sensitivity references
lessons.summary: Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts.
lessons.body:
## Sensitivity and the maths of power vs SPL

**Loudspeaker sensitivity** is the SPL on-axis at 1 m for a reference input. Two conventions:

- **dB SPL @ 1 W / 1 m.** One watt into the *nominal* impedance.
- **dB SPL @ 2.83 V / 1 m.** 2.83 V is 1 W into 8 Ω.

Why 2.83 V? The power a voltage delivers into a resistance is:

```formula
P = V^2 / R
P = (2.83 V)^2 / 8 Ω ≈ 1.0 W
P = (2.83 V)^2 / 4 Ω ≈ 2.0 W
where
P: the electrical power delivered, in watts (W)
V: the RMS voltage across the speaker, in volts (V)
R: the load's (nominal) impedance, treated as a plain resistance, in ohms (Ω)
W: watt, the unit of power
Ω: ohm
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: power is voltage squared divided by resistance, so the same 2.83 V pushes twice the power into 4 Ω as into 8 Ω.
```

Using nominal impedance to define the test voltage, the two references agree for 8 Ω. For **4 Ω**, 2.83 V corresponds to **2 W nominal**, and doubling the power adds about 3 dB (the following power-and-distance unit derives the relationship), making its voltage-sensitivity figure about **3 dB higher**. Actual electrical power varies with complex impedance and frequency; compare the measurement conditions.

## Key takeaways
- Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts.
- The voltage reference corresponds to about one watt nominal into eight ohms, and two into four ohms.
- In the linear regime, doubling power gives approximately three decibels.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt: A driver is rated 90 dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m. In its linear range, what SPL does it give at 1 m with 2 W?

options.explanation: Decibels don't multiply with power.
+6 dB needs four times the power (or double the voltage).
Correct. Doubling power adds about 3 dB, so 90 dB becomes about 93 dB.
More power gives more output, until the driver's limits.

questions.workedExample:
Add the decibels gained by using more than 1 W:

```formula
SPL = S + 10 log_10(P / 1 W)
SPL = 90 + 10 log_10(2 W / 1 W)
SPL = 90 dB + 3.01 dB ≈ 93 dB SPL
where
SPL: the sound pressure level at 1 m, in dB SPL
S: the sensitivity, 90 dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m
P: the power into the speaker, here 2 W
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 10 × log_10 because power is already a power quantity
W: watt, the unit of power
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: twice the power is only about 3 dB louder.
```

Doubling the *voltage* (four times the power into the same load) would give +6 dB.

link.title: Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue

questions.prompt: A 4 Ω speaker is specified as "88 dB SPL @ 2.83 V / 1 m". What is its sensitivity for 1 W / 1 m?

options.explanation: Correct. 2.83 V into 4 Ω delivers about 2 W, so 1 W gives 3 dB less: 85 dB.
2.83 V into 4 Ω is 2 W, not 1 W.
That's the wrong direction: 1 W is less power than 2.83 V delivers into 4 Ω.
That subtracts 6 dB; halving power is 3 dB.

questions.workedExample:
Work out the power that 2.83 V actually delivers into 4 Ω:

```formula
P = V^2 / R = (2.83 V)^2 / 4 Ω ≈ 2.0 W
L = 10 log_10(1 W / 2 W) ≈ −3 dB
88 dB − 3 dB = 85 dB
where
P: the power delivered, in watts (W)
V: the test voltage, 2.83 volts (V)
R: the nominal impedance, 4 ohms (Ω)
L: the level change from using 1 W instead of 2 W, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
W: watt, the unit of power
Ω: ohm
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 2.83 V into 4 Ω is 2 W; half that power is 3 dB less, so 85 dB at 1 W / 1 m.
```

When comparing speakers of different impedance, convert both specs to the same reference.

lessons.title: Work backwards from required listener level
lessons.summary: Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction.
lessons.body:
## Power, distance and efficiency

To predict how loud a speaker will be, start from its sensitivity, add the decibels gained by using more than 1 W, and subtract the decibels lost by listening further away than 1 m. For a fixed signal spectrum in the linear range, use this approximate on-axis free-field, far-field estimate (neglecting air absorption and power compression):

```formula
SPL = S + 10 log_10(P / 1 W)
      − 20 log_10(r / 1 m)
where
SPL: the sound pressure level at the listener, in decibels (dB SPL)
S: the speaker's sensitivity, in dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m; typically 84–90 dB for hi-fi, over 100 dB for PA horns
P: the amplifier power into the speaker's nominal impedance, in watts (W)
r: the listening distance from the speaker, in metres (m); in the actual source’s far field; one metre is a reference distance, not a universal far-field boundary
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
W: watt
m: metre
dB: decibel
In words: every doubling of power adds about 3 dB (10 × log_10 because power is already a power quantity), and every doubling of distance takes away about 6 dB (20 × log_10, the inverse square law for pressure).
```

Each **doubling of power adds only 3 dB**; ten times the power adds 10 dB. For an 87 dB/1 W/1 m speaker at 1 m (so the distance term is zero):

```formula
SPL = 87 + 10 log_10(100 W / 1 W)
SPL = 87 dB + 20 dB = 107 dB SPL
P = 1 W × 10^{(L_t − S)/10}
P = 1 W × 10^{(105 − 87)/10} ≈ 63 W
where
SPL: the level at 1 m, in dB SPL
P: the amplifier power, in watts (W)
L_t: the target level, here 105 dB SPL
S: the sensitivity, here 87 dB at 1 W / 1 m
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
10^{…}: ten to the power of the bracket; it undoes 10 × log_10, turning decibels back into a power ratio
W: watt
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 100 W gives 20 dB more than 1 W; going the other way, reaching 105 dB SPL needs 18 dB more than 1 W, which is about 63 W.
```

The same in Python:

```python
import math

sens = 87  # dB SPL, 1 W / 1 m
for p in (1, 2, 10, 100):
    # Power ratio is relative to one watt.
    spl = sens + 10 * math.log10(p)
    print(f"{p:>3} W: {spl:5.1f} dB @ 1 m")

# power for 105 dB SPL at 1 m:
print(round(10 ** ((105 - sens) / 10), 1))
```

```
  1 W:  87.0 dB @ 1 m
  2 W:  90.0 dB @ 1 m
 10 W:  97.0 dB @ 1 m
100 W: 107.0 dB @ 1 m
63.1
```

Worked example (from Purdue's notes): you want 90 dB SPL at 4 m outdoors from an 86 dB/1 W/1 m speaker. Work backwards: first the distance loss, then the level needed at 1 m, then the power.

```formula
D = 20 log_10(4 m / 1 m) ≈ 12 dB
L_1 = 90 dB + 12 dB = 102 dB SPL
L_1 − S = 102 dB − 86 dB = 16 dB
P = 1 W × 10^{16/10} ≈ 40 W
where
D: the level lost between 1 m and 4 m, in decibels (dB)
L_1: the level needed at 1 m, in dB SPL
S: the speaker's sensitivity, 86 dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m
P: the amplifier power needed, in watts (W)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
10^{…}: ten to the power of the bracket, turning decibels back into a power ratio
m: metre
W: watt
dB: decibel
SPL: sound pressure level
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 4 m costs about 12 dB, so you need 102 dB at 1 m, 16 dB above the 1 W figure, which is about 40 times the power: **40 W**, before any headroom for peaks.
```

Every 3 dB of sensitivity halves the amplifier power needed for the same level. Sensitivity is closely related to **loudspeaker efficiency**, the fraction of electrical power that comes out as sound:

```formula
η = P_ac / P_el
P_ac = 0.01 × 40 W = 0.4 W
where
η: eta, the efficiency, a fraction (or percentage); around 0.01 (1%) for a typical home loudspeaker
P_ac: the acoustic power radiated as sound, in watts (W)
P_el: the electrical power from the amplifier, in watts (W)
W: watt
In words: efficiency is sound power out divided by electrical power in; at 1%, 40 W of amplifier power makes only about 0.4 W of sound.
```

The rest becomes heat, mostly in the voice coil.

## Key takeaways
- Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction.
- Distance loss can demand much more power than a sensitivity comparison alone suggests.
- Leave appropriate peak margin while respecting driver excursion and thermal limits.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt: A speaker rated 90 dB SPL at 1 W/1 m is driven with 50 W. Assuming on-axis far-field spreading from 1 m, negligible air absorption, room reflections and power compression, roughly what level reaches a listener at 4 m?

options.explanation: That's the level at 1 m. You still need to subtract the distance loss.
Correct. 50 W adds about 17 dB over 1 W, and 4 m costs about 12 dB, so 90 + 17 − 12 ≈ 95 dB.
This subtracts only 6 dB for distance; 4 m is two doublings (12 dB).
This uses 20 times the logarithm for the power term (+34 dB). Power is a power quantity, so it takes 10 times the logarithm (+17 dB).

questions.workedExample:
Start from the sensitivity, add the power gain, subtract the distance loss:

```formula
SPL = S + 10 log_10(P / 1 W)
      − 20 log_10(r / 1 m)
G_P = 10 log_10(50 W / 1 W)
G_P ≈ +16.99 dB
L_r = 20 log_10(4 m / 1 m) ≈ 12.04 dB
SPL = 90 + 16.99 − 12.04 ≈ 94.95 dB
where
SPL: the sound pressure level at the listener, in dB SPL
S: the sensitivity, 90 dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m
P: the amplifier power, 50 W
r: the listening distance, 4 m
G_P: the decibels gained by using 50 W instead of 1 W
L_r: the decibels lost between 1 m and 4 m (inverse square law)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
W: watt, the unit of power
m: metre
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 50 W is about 17 dB more than 1 W; 4 m is about 12 dB down on 1 m; so about 95 dB SPL.
```

Indoors, reflections can raise or lower the level at a particular position and frequency; at high power, voice-coil heating (power compression) would lower it.

questions.prompt: Speaker A is 84 dB/1 W/1 m and speaker B is 90 dB/1 W/1 m. To get the same SPL, how much more power does A need?

options.explanation: 6 dB isn't 6×. Decibels are logarithmic: convert 6 dB back to a power ratio (about 4).
Twice the power is only 3 dB.
Correct. A 6 dB difference is a power ratio of about 3.98.
This treats the 6 dB as a percentage of 84 dB, which isn't meaningful.

questions.workedExample:
Find the sensitivity gap, then turn it back into a power ratio:

```formula
ΔS = 90 dB − 84 dB = 6 dB
ratio = 10^{ΔS/10} = 10^{6/10} ≈ 3.98
where
Δ: delta, "the difference in"
ΔS: the difference in sensitivity between the two speakers, in decibels (dB)
S: sensitivity, in dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m
ratio: how many times more power the less sensitive speaker needs, a pure number
10^{…}: ten to the power of the bracket; 10^{x/10} undoes 10 × log_10 for a power ratio
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 6 dB of sensitivity is worth about four times the amplifier power.
```

So a 25 W amp on B does what a 100 W amp does on A. Sensitivity differences are expensive in amplifier power.

link.title: Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue

questions.prompt: You want 90 dB SPL at 4 m outdoors from a speaker with 86 dB/1 W/1 m sensitivity. Assume on-axis far-field spreading from 1 m, negligible air absorption and linear response. Before allowing headroom for peaks, about how much amplifier power do you need?

options.explanation: Correct. 4 m costs about 12 dB, so you need 102 dB at 1 m: 16 dB above 86 dB, a power ratio of about 40, so about 40 W.
This only covers the 4 dB between the 90 dB target and the 86 dB sensitivity (4 dB is a power ratio of about 2.5) and ignores the 12 dB distance loss.
16 is the number of dB needed, not watts.
That's 26 dB above 1 W; the distance loss is about 12 dB, not 22.

questions.workedExample:
Work backwards from the listener to the amplifier:

```formula
D = 20 log_10(4 m / 1 m) ≈ 12.0 dB
L_1 = 90 dB + 12 dB = 102 dB
L_1 − S = 102 dB − 86 dB = 16 dB
P = 1 W × 10^{16/10} ≈ 39.8 W
where
D: the level lost between 1 m and 4 m, in decibels (dB)
L_1: the level needed at 1 m, in dB SPL
S: the sensitivity, 86 dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m
P: the amplifier power needed, in watts (W)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
10^{…}: ten to the power of the bracket, turning decibels back into a power ratio
m: metre
W: watt, the unit of power
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 4 m costs 12 dB, so you need 16 dB more than the 1 W figure, which is about 40 W.
```

For a signal with a ten-decibel peak-to-RMS crest factor, an average forty watts into a resistor requires this ideal peak capability:

```formula
V_rms = √(P_avg R)
V_pk = V_rms × 10^{CF/20}
P_sine = V_pk^2 / (2R)
P_sine = (40 W × 10) / 2 = 200 W
where
V_rms: the signal's RMS voltage, in volts (V)
P_avg: its average power, here 40 watts (W)
R: the resistive load, in ohms (Ω)
V_pk: its peak voltage, in volts (V)
CF: peak-to-RMS crest factor, here 10 decibels (dB)
P_sine: continuous sine-wave amplifier rating that reaches the same peak voltage, in watts (W), before additional margin
√: square root
W: watt, the unit of power
In words: ten decibels of crest factor makes peak instantaneous power ten times average; a sine rating is half that peak power, so 40 W average needs 200 W of ideal sine-rated peak capability.
```

This is an ideal voltage calculation, not a safe amplifier recommendation. Check current capability, extra margin, driver excursion and thermal limits, gain and protection.

lessons.title: Driver response, dispersion and limits
lessons.summary: A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency.
lessons.body:
## Frequency response

A frequency response plot shows on-axis SPL (at a fixed input) against frequency. Look for:

- The **usable range**, often given as ±3 dB limits, with the low-frequency limit set mainly by Fs and the enclosure.
- **Smoothness**: narrow peaks often come from cone breakup or cabinet resonance.
- **Off-axis curves**: how the response changes at 30° or 60°. Because of diffraction, a driver radiates widely when its wavelength is large compared with the cone, and shows **beaming** (narrower dispersion) when the wavelength becomes comparable with the cone.

Where does beaming start? Treat the cone as a flat, rigid disc (a "piston"). Directivity becomes significant when the cone's circumference is about one wavelength, which corresponds to a dimensionless wavenumber-radius product of one:

```formula
ka = 1
k = (2πf) / c
f_beam = c / (2πa)
where
k: the wavenumber, 2π divided by the wavelength, in radians per metre (rad/m); higher frequency means bigger k
a: the effective radius of the cone (half its effective diameter), in metres (m)
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_beam: the frequency above which the cone starts to focus sound forwards instead of spreading it, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
π: pi, about 3.14159
In words: the bigger the cone, the lower the frequency at which it starts beaming. Double the radius and beaming starts an octave lower.
```

Worked for a woofer with a 13 cm effective diameter and a 25 mm tweeter dome:

```formula
f_beam = 343 / (2π × 0.065) ≈ 840 Hz
f_beam = 343 / (2π × 0.0125) ≈ 4.4 kHz
where
f_beam: the frequency where beaming becomes significant, in hertz (Hz)
π: pi, about 3.14159
Hz: hertz, cycles per second; kHz is a thousand hertz
kHz: kilohertz
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the 6.5 cm-radius woofer beams from about 840 Hz; the 12.5 mm-radius tweeter stays wide up to about 4.4 kHz.
```

(343 is the speed of sound in m/s; 0.065 m and 0.0125 m are the two radii.) The piston model stops being reliable once the cone breaks up (below), so check measured off-axis curves.

That beaming is one reason multi-way speakers hand high frequencies to smaller drivers.

## Power handling

Two separate limits:

- **Driver power handling** (thermal). The voice coil heats up. Too much *average* power for too long burns the coil or its adhesive. Ratings are usually based on long tests with band-limited noise, and the method (and so the number) differs between standards and manufacturers, so read what method a figure refers to.
- **Mechanical (excursion).** At low frequencies the cone must move a long way. **Xmax** describes an excursion limit under a specified geometric or distortion criterion; definitions vary. Motor, suspension and other nonlinearities can limit it. Beyond the useful linear range, distortion increases; far beyond it, the coil can strike the motor structure or the suspension can tear. A driver can be over-excursed at low frequencies with modest power, especially below a ported box's tuning frequency (the enclosure units).

> [!tip] Power ratings are not targets
> A "100 W" speaker doesn't need 100 W, and isn't safe with any 100 W signal. A clipped signal from a small amplifier can damage a tweeter (the power-amplifier units), while the required clean peak capacity and suitable protection must be chosen from actual limits.

## Driver types

| Driver | Typical job | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Subwoofer | Below ~80–120 Hz | Long excursion, big cone |
| Woofer | Bass (and mids in 2-way) | 13–38 cm common |
| Midrange | ~300 Hz–3 kHz | Covers the vocal region |
| Tweeter | Above ~2–3 kHz | Light dome, 19–28 mm |
| Compression driver + horn | Mid/high in PA | Very high sensitivity |

In a **compression driver**, a diaphragm pressurises a small chamber; sound passes through **phase-plug** channels into a narrow **horn throat**, and the **loudspeaker horn** flares out to the room. The horn improves the match between the diaphragm and the air, so far more of the electrical power becomes sound. It also controls dispersion, which PA designers use to aim sound at the audience and away from walls. Horn-loaded systems can reach sensitivities around 110 dB SPL at 2.83 V/1 m; a typical hi-fi speaker is in the mid-80s to around 90 dB.

## Cone breakup

At low frequencies a cone moves as a rigid **rigid piston**. As frequency rises, the cone stops moving as one piece: bending waves travel across it, and different parts move with different phase. This is **cone breakup**. It causes:

- Peaks and dips in the response, often a sharp peak near the top of the driver's range.
- Changes in dispersion, and sometimes audible coloration and distortion.

Stiff, light cones (aluminium, ceramic) push breakup higher but often produce a stronger, sharper peak when it happens. Softer, well-damped cones break up earlier but more gently. Either way, the crossover (the crossover units) is chosen so the driver isn't asked to play much in its breakup region.

## Key takeaways
- A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency.
- Cone breakup invalidates a rigid-piston prediction; use measured off-axis data.
- Thermal power and cone excursion are separate limits.
- Driver types trade displacement, bandwidth, dispersion and efficiency.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt:
Using the rigid-piston approximation, a cone or dome starts to become noticeably directional around:

```formula
f = c / (2πa)
where
f: the frequency where beaming becomes significant, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
π: pi, about 3.14159
a: the radius of the cone or dome (half its diameter), in metres (m)
In words: beaming starts when the cone's circumference is about one wavelength, so bigger drivers beam from lower frequencies.
```

Around what frequency does a 25 mm (diameter) tweeter dome start to become noticeably directional?

options.explanation: That's what a radius of 12.5 cm (ten times too big) would give.
This uses the full 25 mm diameter as a; the formula needs the radius (12.5 mm).

options.text: It is omnidirectional at all audible frequencies
options.explanation: Every finite piston beams once the wavelength becomes comparable with its size.
Correct. With the 12.5 mm radius the formula gives about 4.37 kHz (see the worked example).

questions.workedExample:
Halve the diameter to get the radius in metres, then substitute:

```formula
a = 0.025 m / 2 = 0.0125 m
f = 343 / (2π × 0.0125)
f ≈ 4367 Hz ≈ 4.4 kHz
where
a: the dome radius, in metres (m)
f: the beaming frequency, in hertz (Hz)
π: pi, about 3.14159
m: metre
Hz: hertz, cycles per second; kHz is a thousand hertz
kHz: kilohertz
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the 12.5 mm-radius tweeter stays wide up to about 4.4 kHz (343 is the speed of sound in m/s).
```

Compare a woofer with a 13 cm effective diameter (radius 0.065 m): the same formula gives about 840 Hz. That's why the tweeter takes over above a few kilohertz: it keeps dispersion wide where the woofer would beam.

link.title: Baffled-piston directivity — Dan Russell, Penn State

questions.prompt: Which are genuine ways a driver can be damaged or driven into gross distortion? Select all that apply.

options.text: Too much average power overheating the voice coil
options.explanation: Correct. That's the thermal limit.

options.text: Excessive cone excursion at low frequencies beyond Xmax
options.explanation: Correct. That's the mechanical limit; it can happen at modest power at low frequencies.

options.text: Reducing the input while keeping the signal within every applicable thermal and excursion limit
options.explanation: Operating within all applicable limits does not itself cause overload. A power number alone is not enough to establish those limits.

options.text: Sustained heavy clipping that adds high-frequency energy, especially for tweeters
options.explanation: Correct. Clipping adds harmonics and raises average power, which can overheat a tweeter.

questions.workedExample:
Two independent limits:

1. **Thermal**: the voice coil heats with average power. Long, loud, compressed or clipped signals push it.
2. **Mechanical**: excursion grows as frequency falls (for the same SPL). Beyond Xmax, distortion rises; well beyond, the coil can bottom out.

Clipping matters for tweeters because it adds high-frequency harmonics that the crossover passes straight to them (the power-amplifier units).

link.title: Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue

questions.prompt: A frequency response plot of a 16 cm aluminium-cone woofer shows a sharp +8 dB peak at 5 kHz. Which statements are likely true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The peak means the woofer will play bass better
options.explanation: Breakup is a high-frequency effect and doesn't help low-frequency output.

options.text: A rigid-piston model predicts narrowing at 5 kHz, but breakup makes actual off-axis measurements necessary
options.explanation: Correct. The rigid-piston beaming point for a 13 cm effective diameter is near 840 Hz. Above breakup, the rigid-piston approximation no longer predicts the actual radiation reliably.

options.text: The peak is probably cone breakup: the cone has stopped behaving as a rigid piston
options.explanation: Correct. Stiff metal cones tend to show a sharp breakup peak near the top of their range.

options.text: A crossover that lets the woofer play up to 4–5 kHz at full level would expose that peak
options.explanation: Correct. The crossover should roll the woofer off well below its breakup region.

questions.workedExample:
1. Breakup: bending waves cross the cone and parts move out of phase; stiff, light cones break up high but with sharp peaks.
2. Directivity: the rigid-piston model puts the start of beaming at:

```formula
f = c / (2πa)
f = 343 / (2π × 0.065) ≈ 840 Hz
where
f: the frequency where beaming becomes significant, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 m/s
π: pi, about 3.14159
a: the effective cone radius, 0.065 m (13 cm effective diameter)
Hz: hertz
≈: approximately equal to
In words: this woofer starts to beam from about 840 Hz, far below its 5 kHz peak.
```

The model predicts narrowing, but breakup changes the radiation and requires measured polar data.

3. Both say the same thing: cross over to a tweeter well below 5 kHz, often around 2–3 kHz for this size, with a slope steep enough to suppress the peak.
