lessons.title: Separate front and rear radiation
lessons.summary: A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies.
lessons.body:
Hold a bare woofer in the air, play a bass line through it, and you get a thin, tinny sound. Mount the same driver in a box and the bass appears. This lesson explains why, and how the box's design shapes the bass response.

It's a deep subject with decades of published theory. The goal here is the concepts and enough of the maths to read a driver datasheet and understand what box-modelling software tells you.

## The acoustic short circuit

When the cone moves forward, it compresses the air in front and rarefies the air behind. The two sides radiate **equal and opposite** pressure waves: the bare driver is a **dipole** (Dan Russell's radiation demo in Further reading shows the field).

At high frequencies the wavelength is short compared with the path from front to back around the cone's edge, so the two waves don't meet in time to cancel much. At low frequencies the wavelength is long, the rear wave easily diffracts round the edge, and it **cancels the front wave**. Air just sloshes from front to back. This is the **acoustic short circuit**, and it's why a bare driver has almost no bass.

```diagram
 bare driver:   front (+)  )  (  rear (-)
                 \_ air sloshes round _/
 on a baffle:   front (+) |  rear (-)
                  longer path, less cancel
```

The cure is to separate front from back:

- A **baffle** (a flat board) lengthens the path, so cancellation starts at a lower frequency.
- An **enclosure** (a box) traps the rear wave completely, or redirects it so it helps.

## Baffle step

Even in a box, the front baffle has a finite size. At high frequencies, where the baffle is large compared with the wavelength, the driver radiates into the **half-space** in front: half a sphere of directions. At low frequencies, where the wavelength is much larger than the baffle, sound diffracts around the cabinet and radiates into the **full space**: the whole sphere.

Engineers often call these "2π" and "4π" radiation, after the solid angle each one covers:

```formula
Ω_full = 4π sr
Ω_half = 2π sr
where
Ω_full: the solid angle of a whole sphere, which a driver fills when it radiates in all directions (full space)
Ω_half: the solid angle of half a sphere, which a driver on a large flat baffle fills (half-space)
π: pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159
sr: steradian, the unit of solid angle: how much of the space around a point a cone of directions covers
In words: half-space is exactly half of all possible directions, so "2π" means "in front of a big wall" and "4π" means "floating in free space".
```

For the same cone motion, radiating into half-space gives twice the sound pressure of full space: the baffle acts like a mirror, adding a coherent "image" source. Doubling pressure is a 6 dB rise, because sound pressure level is 20 times the base-10 logarithm of a pressure ratio:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(p_half / p_full)
ΔL = 20 log_10(2)
ΔL ≈ 6.02 dB
where
ΔL: the difference in on-axis level between half-space and full-space radiation, in decibels (dB)
p_half: the on-axis sound pressure for fixed cone volume velocity when radiating into ideal half-space, in pascals (Pa)
p_full: the on-axis sound pressure for the same cone motion in full space, in pascals (Pa); here p_half = 2 × p_full
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: log_10(x) is the power you raise 10 to in order to get x; log_10(2) ≈ 0.301
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, a logarithmic unit for comparing two levels
In words: twice the pressure is about 6 dB louder, so losing the baffle's mirror effect costs about 6 dB.
```

So as frequency falls and the radiation spreads into full space, a speaker's on-axis response steps down by up to **6 dB** going from high to low frequencies. The transition happens where the wavelength is comparable with the baffle width: a few hundred hertz for a typical bookshelf speaker. This is the ideal figure: the real step is smoother, and nearby walls and floors change it.

Designers compensate with **baffle step compensation**: usually a gentle shelf in the crossover that reduces everything above the step. In a real room, placing the speaker near a wall gives back some of the lost bass, which is why compensation is a judgement call.

## Key takeaways
- A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies.
- A baffle separates the front and rear paths.
- For fixed cone motion, a finite baffle can produce an approximately six-decibel transition; boundary placement changes it.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)

questions.prompt: Why does a bare woofer held in the air produce so little bass?

options.text: The rear wave, opposite in polarity, diffracts around the cone at low frequencies and cancels the front wave
options.explanation: Correct. This is the acoustic short circuit: long wavelengths diffract easily round the small driver.

options.text: Woofers need an enclosure to receive power
options.explanation: Electrically, the driver works the same in or out of a box.

options.text: Air can't carry low frequencies without a box
options.explanation: Air carries low frequencies perfectly well; the problem is cancellation.

options.text: The magnet is too weak without a cabinet
options.explanation: The motor's strength doesn't depend on the cabinet.

questions.workedExample:
1. Cone forward: compression in front, rarefaction behind. The two sides radiate opposite-polarity waves (a dipole).
2. At low frequencies the wavelength is much longer than the driver, so the rear wave reaches the front almost in time to cancel it.
3. A baffle lengthens the path; a sealed box removes the rear wave altogether.

link.title: Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue

questions.prompt: A bookshelf speaker has an approximately 6 dB bass shelf consistent with its finite-baffle diffraction transition. Assume baffle step causes this measured shelf. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: This is the baffle step: below a frequency set by baffle width, the speaker radiates into full space instead of half space
options.explanation: Correct. For the same cone motion, that loses up to 6 dB on-axis.

options.text: A crossover shelf (baffle step compensation) can level it, at the cost of some sensitivity
options.explanation: Correct. Compensation reduces everything above the step to match the bass.

options.text: Placing the speaker near a wall can restore some of the bass
options.explanation: Correct. The wall reflects the low frequencies back towards the listener, partly undoing the step.

options.text: It means the woofer is faulty
options.explanation: The assumed effect is baffle diffraction, which does not itself imply a faulty woofer. A bass deficit without further measurements would not establish its cause.

questions.workedExample:
1. High frequencies: the baffle is large compared with the wavelength, so the driver radiates into half-space (half a sphere, often called "2π").
2. Low frequencies: the wavelength is much larger than the baffle, so it radiates into full space (the whole sphere, "4π").
3. For the same cone motion, half-space radiation doubles the on-axis pressure (the baffle acts like a mirror):

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(p_half / p_full)
ΔL = 20 log_10(2) ≈ 6 dB
where
ΔL: the level difference between half-space and full-space radiation, in decibels (dB)
p_half: the on-axis sound pressure in half-space, in pascals (Pa)
p_full: the on-axis sound pressure in full space for the same cone motion, in pascals (Pa); p_half is twice this
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: log_10(x) is the power you raise 10 to in order to get x; log_10(2) ≈ 0.301
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, a logarithmic unit for comparing levels
In words: double the pressure is about 6 dB, and that is what the bass loses when it diffracts around the cabinet.
```

4. Designers pick how much to compensate depending on expected room placement.

link.title: Acoustic treatment and boundary interference — Genelec

lessons.title: Choose an enclosure’s operating principle
lessons.summary: Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes.
lessons.body:
## Four ways to box a driver

### Sealed (closed box, acoustic suspension)

The rear wave is trapped. The air inside acts as an extra **spring** on the cone, which raises the system resonance above the driver's free-air Fs.

- Below the system resonance, Fc, the response falls at **12 dB per octave** (a second-order high-pass).
- Transient behaviour depends on system Q. Sealed boxes are relatively simple to model, and the trapped air adds restoring force at very low frequencies.
- Less efficient in the bass than a ported box of the same size.

### Ported (bass reflex, vented)

A **port tube** (tube) connects the box air to the outside. The air in the port is a mass, the air in the box is a spring: a **Helmholtz resonator**, tuned to a frequency Fb. Around Fb, the port radiates strongly and in phase with the cone's front, adding bass output while the cone barely moves.

- More bass extension or output from the same box volume than sealed.
- Below Fb the response falls at **24 dB per octave** (fourth-order), steeper than sealed.
- **Below Fb the box provides progressively less air-spring loading on the cone**: the suspension and motor still act, but the port increasingly relieves box pressure, so excursion can become excessive. Many ported systems use a subsonic high-pass filter to protect the driver.
- Ports can make noise ("chuffing") if the air speed is too high, usually because the port is too narrow for the output.

### Open baffle

No box at all: the driver sits on a flat panel, open at the back. It stays a **dipole**, radiating front and back with opposite polarity and a null at the sides.

- No box resonances; many listeners like the spacious presentation.
- Front-to-back cancellation adds about **6 dB per octave** of low-frequency roll-off relative to monopole radiation. The driver’s own response also matters: below its mechanical resonance, an unequalised ideal voltage-driven dipole can approach **18 dB per octave** in total. Large baffles, displacement capability and EQ may be needed.
- The rear wave reflects off the wall behind, so placement matters even more.

### Transmission line

The rear wave travels down a long, folded, damped duct before leaving through a vent. The line length is typically chosen as a **quarter wavelength** at the lowest frequency the design targets (often near the driver's resonance), so the line's output reinforces the front at low frequencies while the damping absorbs higher frequencies.

To see how long that is, divide the wavelength by four:

```formula
L_line = c / (4f_t)
L_line = (343 m/s) / (4 × 40 Hz)
L_line ≈ 2.14 m
where
L_line: the length of the transmission line, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
f_t: the target frequency the line is tuned for, in hertz (Hz); here 40 Hz
m: metre, the unit of length
s: second, the unit of time
Hz: hertz, the unit of frequency: one cycle per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a line tuned to 40 Hz needs to be about 2.1 m long, which is why lines are folded inside the cabinet.
```

That is a starting estimate: stuffing slows the sound in the line and tapered lines behave differently, so real lines are tuned in modelling software. They're more complex to design and build than sealed or ported boxes.

| Type | Roll-off | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Sealed | 12 dB/oct | Compact, controlled |
| Ported | 24 dB/oct | More output; excursion below Fb |
| Open baffle | Additional ~6 dB/oct dipole loss | Driver roll-off also contributes |
| Transmission line | varies | Complex build |

## Key takeaways
- Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes.
- A port reduces cone movement near tuning but unloads it progressively below tuning.
- Open baffles and damped transmission lines use rear radiation differently.

## Further reading

lessons.title: Read the driver’s small-signal parameters
lessons.summary: Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance.
lessons.body:
## Thiele–Small parameters

A driver datasheet lists **Thiele–Small (T/S) parameters**, measured at low levels where the driver behaves linearly. The three you use most:

- **Fs**: the free-air resonance (moving mass on the suspension spring).
- **Qts**: the total Q at Fs: how damped the resonance is. Purdue's notes put most drivers between about 0.2 and 0.5.
- **Vas**: the volume of air with the same springiness (compliance) as the driver's suspension.

### Fs: a mass on a spring

The cone, voice coil and the air they carry are a mass; the surround and spider are a spring. Like any mass on a spring, they have one natural frequency:

```formula
Fs = 1 / (2π √(Mms Cms))
Fs = 1 / (2π √(0.02 kg × 0.001 m/N))
Fs ≈ 35.6 Hz
where
Fs: the driver's free-air resonance frequency, in hertz (Hz)
Mms: the total moving mass (cone, coil and the air load moving with them), in kilograms (kg); here 20 g = 0.02 kg
Cms: the mechanical compliance of the suspension: how far it moves per newton of force, in metres per newton (m/N); here 1 mm/N = 0.001 m/N. Higher compliance means a softer suspension
π: pi, about 3.14159
√: square root
kg: kilogram, the unit of mass
m: metre, the unit of length
N: newton, the unit of force
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a heavier cone or a softer suspension gives a lower resonance; four times the mass halves Fs.
```

### Qts: how damped the resonance is

Two things damp the resonance. The suspension loses some energy as heat (the mechanical Q, **Qms**). The voice coil moving in the magnet generates a voltage that the amplifier's low output impedance loads through a low-resistance circuit, which brakes the cone (the electrical Q, **Qes**). They combine like resistors in parallel:

```formula
Qts = (Qms Qes) / (Qms + Qes)
Qts = (4 × 0.4) / (4 + 0.4)
Qts ≈ 0.36
where
Qts: the total Q of the driver at Fs (no unit); lower means more damped
Qms: the mechanical Q, set by losses in the suspension (no unit); typically several, e.g. 4
Qes: the electrical Q, set by braking from the motor and amplifier (no unit); typically 0.2 to 1, e.g. 0.4
In words: the total Q is always lower than either part, and the smaller one (usually Qes) dominates.
```

With mechanical Q four and electrical Q 0.4, total Q is close to the electrical Q. That is typical: the motor does most of the damping. Q has no unit because it is a ratio (stored energy to energy lost per cycle, roughly).

### Vas: the suspension expressed as air

Vas turns the suspension's springiness into "the volume of air that would be just as springy" under the same cone:

```formula
Vas = ρc^2 Sd^2 Cms
Vas = 1.2 kg/m^3 × (343 m/s)^2
      × (0.022 m^2)^2 × 0.001 m/N
Vas ≈ 0.068 m^3 = 68 L
where
Vas: the equivalent compliance volume, in cubic metres (m^3) or litres (L); 1 m^3 = 1000 L
ρ: rho, the density of air, about 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m^3) at 20 °C
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
Sd: the effective radiating area of the cone, in square metres (m^2); here 0.022 m^2, roughly an 8-inch woofer
Cms: the suspension compliance, in metres per newton (m/N); here 0.001 m/N
m: metre, the unit of length
s: second, the unit of time
kg: kilogram, the unit of mass
N: newton, the unit of force; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s^2, which is why the units cancel down to m^3
L: litre, a volume of 0.001 m^3
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a softer suspension or a bigger cone gives a larger Vas; doubling the cone area quadruples Vas.
```

So for a fixed cone area, larger Vas means a softer suspension. Because Vas grows with cone area squared, it is not a stiffness comparison across arbitrary driver sizes: a big woofer can have a large Vas with a stiff suspension.

## Key takeaways
- Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance.
- Mechanical and electrical damping combine into total Q.
- Equivalent compliance volume depends on both cone area and suspension compliance.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)

options.explanation: Correct. Purdue's notes give that typical tolerance.

options.text: Fs is the frequency where the driver's impedance is lowest
options.explanation: At Fs the impedance peaks; the minimum is above it.

options.text: Qts is Qms × Qes divided by (Qms + Qes)
options.explanation: Correct. Total Q combines mechanical and electrical Q like resistors in parallel.

options.text: They describe the driver at small signal levels, where it behaves linearly
options.explanation: Correct. Large-signal behaviour (Xmax, thermal compression) needs other parameters.

questions.workedExample:
- Qts combines the mechanical and electrical Q like resistors in parallel:

```formula
Qts = (Qms Qes) / (Qms + Qes)
Qts = (4 × 0.4) / (4 + 0.4) ≈ 0.36
where
Qts: the total Q of the driver at its resonance (no unit)
Qms: the mechanical Q, from suspension losses (no unit); here 4
Qes: the electrical Q, from motor and amplifier damping (no unit); here 0.4

In words: the total is always below the smaller of the two, so a low Qes dominates.
```

- T/S parameters are small-signal values, measured from the impedance curve near resonance.
- Tolerances: about ±15% on Fs, ±20–30% on Vas (Purdue).
- Impedance: maximum at Fs, minimum above it.

lessons.title: Estimate a sealed box’s resonance and Q
lessons.summary: Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide.
lessons.body:
## Driver choice and sealed-box alignment

### Efficiency bandwidth product

A rough rule of thumb uses the **efficiency bandwidth product** (EBP):

```formula
EBP = Fs / Qes
EBP = 30 Hz / 0.5
EBP = 60 Hz
where
EBP: the efficiency bandwidth product, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz); here 30 Hz
Qes: the electrical Q (no unit); here 0.5
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: drivers with an EBP around 50 tend to suit sealed boxes and those around 100 suit ported ones.
```

An EBP of 60 Hz sits near the sealed end. It's a starting point, not a design method: always model the full parameter set.

Manufacturing tolerances are loose: Purdue's notes give typical factory tolerances of about ±15% for Fs and ±20–30% for Vas. Measure your own driver if accuracy matters.

### The sealed-box equations

Put a driver in a sealed box. The air trapped in the box is a second spring pushing on the cone, alongside the suspension. A smaller box is a stiffer spring. The **compliance ratio** says how stiff the box air is compared with the suspension, and both the resonance and its Q rise with the square root of the total stiffness. These are the closed-box results (Small, 1972), used when you choose a box size:

```formula
α = Vas / Vb
Fc = Fs √(1 + α)
Qtc = Qts √(1 + α)
where
α: alpha, the compliance ratio (no unit): how many times stiffer the box air is than the driver's suspension
Vas: the driver's equivalent compliance volume, in litres (L)
Vb: the internal volume of the box, in litres (L)
Fc: the resonance frequency of the driver in the box, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the driver's free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz)
Qtc: the total Q of the driver in the box (no unit); it sets the shape of the bass roll-off
Qts: the driver's total Q in free air (no unit)
√: square root
L: litre, a unit of volume; 1 L = 0.001 m^3
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: a smaller box (bigger α) pushes the resonance up and makes it less damped, both by the same factor √(1 + α).
```

Consider a driver with 30 Hz free-air resonance, total Q of 0.35 and 60 L equivalent compliance volume, in a 20 L box:

```formula
α = 60 L / 20 L = 3
√(1 + α) = √(4) = 2
Fc = 30 Hz × 2 = 60 Hz
Qtc = 0.35 × 2 = 0.70
where
α: alpha, the compliance ratio (no unit)
√: square root
L: litre, a unit of volume
Fc: the in-box resonance, in hertz (Hz)
Qtc: the in-box total Q (no unit)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: a 20 L box makes this driver resonate at 60 Hz with a Q of 0.70, close to maximally flat.
```

These equations ignore box losses and stuffing, and they assume the box is small compared with the wavelength (true in the bass).

The sealed-box **total Q** sets the shape of the bass roll-off. The box-and-driver is a second-order high-pass filter, and for that filter the level exactly at Fc depends only on Qtc:

```formula
L_Fc = 20 log_10(Qtc)
L_Fc = 20 log_10(0.707)
L_Fc ≈ −3 dB
where
L_Fc: the response at Fc, relative to the flat level well above Fc, in decibels (dB)
Qtc: the in-box total Q (no unit); here 0.707
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: log_10(x) is the power you raise 10 to in order to get x
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, a logarithmic unit for comparing levels
In words: A total Q of 0.5 gives −6 dB at resonance, 0.707 gives −3 dB, and 1.0 gives 0 dB with a hump above resonance.
```

| Qtc | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| 0.5 | Critically damped, −6 dB at Fc |
| 0.707 | Butterworth: maximally flat, −3 dB at Fc |
| ~1.0–1.1 | Peak before roll-off, "boomier" |

The same sum for three box sizes, as code:

```python
import math

def sealed(fs, qts, vas, vb):
    a = vas / vb
    # Box air raises resonance and total Q.
    k = math.sqrt(1 + a)
    return fs * k, qts * k

for vb in (10, 20, 40):
    fc, qtc = sealed(30, 0.35, 60, vb)
    print(f"{vb:>2} L: Fc={fc:5.1f} Hz,"
          f" Qtc={qtc:.2f}")
```

```
10 L: Fc= 79.4 Hz, Qtc=0.93
20 L: Fc= 60.0 Hz, Qtc=0.70
40 L: Fc= 47.4 Hz, Qtc=0.55
```

The 20 L box gives a near-Butterworth alignment (a Qtc of about 0.7) with a 60 Hz resonance. A smaller box gives higher, peakier bass; a bigger one lower, more damped bass. Deep bass extension, reference efficiency and enclosure volume are coupled. “Pick two” summarizes the trade-off; real driver excursion, losses and power limits still constrain the design.

(Filling the box with absorbent material can make it behave as if it were somewhat larger: Purdue's notes say up to about 15% in apparent volume, while also adding some effective moving mass.)

## Key takeaways
- Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide.
- A smaller sealed box raises both resonance and Q in the ideal model.
- Real losses, stuffing and measured driver parameters affect the finished alignment.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)

options.explanation: Vas is about suspension compliance, not magnet strength (that relates to Bl and Qes).

options.text: It has a high resonant frequency
options.explanation: A soft suspension tends to give a lower Fs for the same moving mass, not higher.
Power handling is set by thermal and excursion limits, not Vas.

options.text: A softer suspension; for the same Qts and target Qtc, a larger sealed box
options.explanation: Correct. At fixed cone area, equivalent acoustic compliance grows with suspension compliance. Box volume also depends on Qts and the target alignment.

questions.workedExample:
1. Vas is the volume of air whose springiness equals the suspension's.
2. In a sealed box, the compliance ratio says how much the box air stiffens the system:

```formula
α = Vas / Vb
Vb = Vas / α
where
α: alpha, the compliance ratio (no unit); it is fixed once you choose Qts and a target Qtc
Vas: the driver's equivalent compliance volume, in litres (L)
Vb: the internal box volume, in litres (L)
L: litre, a unit of volume
In words: for a fixed compliance ratio, the box volume is directly proportional to Vas.
```

3. For the same Qts and target Qtc, the required ratio is the same, so a driver with twice the Vas needs twice the box.

questions.prompt: A driver has a free-air resonance of 30 Hz, total Q of 0.35 and equivalent compliance volume of 60 L. In the ideal sealed-box model, what are the system resonance and total Q in a 20 L box?

options.explanation: This multiplies by the compliance ratio itself (3). The formula multiplies by the square root of 1 plus the ratio, which is 2.
Correct. The compliance ratio is 60 L / 20 L = 3, so the multiplier is the square root of 4, which is 2.
The box air adds stiffness, so both rise above the driver's free-air values.
This multiplies by the square root of the ratio alone (about 1.73) instead of the square root of 1 plus the ratio.

questions.workedExample:
The box air stiffens the system; the closed-box equations scale both the resonance and the Q by the same factor.

```formula
α = Vas / Vb = 60 L / 20 L = 3
k = √(1 + α) = √(4) = 2
Fc = Fs k = 30 Hz × 2 = 60 Hz
Qtc = Qts k = 0.35 × 2 = 0.70
where
α: alpha, the compliance ratio (no unit): how much stiffer the box air is than the suspension
Vas: the driver's equivalent compliance volume, in litres (L); here 60 L
Vb: the internal box volume, in litres (L); here 20 L
k: the scaling factor the box applies to both resonance and Q (no unit)
√: square root
Fc: the resonance of the driver in the box, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the driver's free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz); here 30 Hz
Qtc: the total Q in the box (no unit)
Qts: the driver's total Q in free air (no unit); here 0.35
L: litre, a unit of volume
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: a box one third of Vas doubles both the resonance and the Q.
```

A Qtc of about 0.707 is the Butterworth (maximally flat) alignment, 3 dB down at the box resonance, so 0.70 is very close to it.

questions.prompt: A driver has total Q of 0.5, equivalent compliance volume of 40 L and free-air resonance of 50 Hz. Roughly what ideal sealed-box volume gives a system total Q of 0.707?

options.explanation: A 20 L box gives a compliance ratio of 2, so the Q becomes 0.5 times the square root of 3, about 0.87: too high.
An 80 L box gives a compliance ratio of 0.5, so the Q becomes 0.5 times the square root of 1.5, about 0.61: below the target.
Correct. The box must raise the Q by 0.707 ÷ 0.5, about 1.414 (the square root of 2), so the compliance ratio is 1 and the box equals Vas: 40 L.

options.text: Any volume: Qtc depends only on the driver
options.explanation: Qtc depends on the box volume through α.

Work backwards from the target Q to the compliance ratio, then to the box volume.

```formula
Qtc / Qts = √(1 + α)
0.707 / 0.5 ≈ 1.414 = √(1 + α)
1 + α ≈ 1.414^2 ≈ 2.0
α = 1.0
Vb = Vas / α = 40 L / 1.0 = 40 L
Fc = Fs √(1 + α)
Fc = 50 Hz × 1.414 ≈ 70.7 Hz
where
Qtc: the target total Q in the box (no unit); here 0.707, the Butterworth value
Qts: the driver's total Q in free air (no unit); here 0.5
√: square root
α: alpha, the compliance ratio Vas / Vb (no unit)
Vb: the internal box volume, in litres (L)
Vas: the driver's equivalent compliance volume, in litres (L); here 40 L
Fc: the resonance in the box, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz); here 50 Hz
L: litre, a unit of volume
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: to raise Q from 0.5 to 0.707 the box must be as stiff as the suspension, so the box volume equals Vas; the resonance rises to about 71 Hz.
```

questions.prompt: A driver datasheet gives free-air resonance of 65 Hz and electrical Q of 0.436. Using efficiency bandwidth product (free-air resonance divided by electrical Q) as a rough initial guide, which enclosure type does it suggest?

options.explanation: Compute it: 65 Hz divided by 0.436 is about 149 Hz, nowhere near 50.

options.text: Ported: EBP is about 149, well above 100
options.explanation: Correct. Purdue's rule of thumb: sealed around 50, vented around 100. This is only a starting point.

options.text: Open baffle, because EBP is exactly 100
options.explanation: The value isn't 100, and EBP isn't a guide to open baffles.

Divide the free-air resonance by the electrical Q:

where

lessons.title: Estimate a port’s tuning frequency
lessons.summary: Box air acts as a spring and the port air as a moving mass.
lessons.body:
## Port tuning: Helmholtz intuition

A port behaves like the neck of a bottle. The air plug in the port is a mass bouncing on the springy air in the box. That is a **Helmholtz resonator**, and its resonance (the box tuning) is:

```formula
Fb = (c / (2π)) √(A / (Vb Leff))
where
Fb: the box tuning frequency, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
π: pi, about 3.14159
√: square root
A: the port's cross-sectional area, in square metres (m^2); for a round port, π × r^2 where r is its radius
Vb: the internal box volume, in cubic metres (m^3); 1 L = 0.001 m^3
Leff: the port's effective length, in metres (m): its physical length plus an end correction (see below)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: a bigger box or a longer port lowers the tuning; a wider port raises it.
```

The air just beyond each open end of the port moves with the plug too, so the port acts longer than it is. That extra is the **end correction**:

```formula
Leff = Lp + kr
where
Leff: the effective acoustic length of the port, in metres (m)
Lp: the physical length of the port tube, in metres (m)
k: the total end-correction factor for both ends (no unit): about 0.61 for an end that stops in free air, about 0.85 for an end flush with a flat panel; one of each gives about 1.46
r: the port's radius, in metres (m)
In words: add roughly one and a half port radii to the tube length when one end is flush with the baffle and the other is free inside the box.
```

Because the area is under the square root and divided by the length, a wider port must also be longer to keep the same Fb. Worked example: a 30 L box with a 5 cm diameter port, 15 cm long, with a total radius-based end-correction factor of 1.46:

```formula
A = π(0.025 m)^2 ≈ 0.00196 m^2
Leff = 0.15 m + 1.46 × 0.025 m
Leff ≈ 0.1865 m
Vb Leff = 0.03 m^3 × 0.1865 m
Vb Leff ≈ 0.005595 m^4
Fb = ((343 m/s) / (2π))
     × √(0.00196 m^2 / 0.005595 m^4)
Fb ≈ (54.6 m/s) × (0.592 / m)
Fb ≈ 32.3 Hz
where
A: the port's cross-sectional area, in square metres (m^2); the radius is half of 5 cm, 0.025 m
π: pi, about 3.14159
Leff: the effective port length, in metres (m)
Vb: the box volume, in cubic metres (m^3); 30 L = 0.03 m^3
Fb: the box tuning frequency, in hertz (Hz)
√: square root
m: metre, the unit of length
s: second, the unit of time
Hz: hertz, cycles per second; m/s divided by √(m^2) gives 1/s, which is Hz
≈: approximately equal to
In words: this 30 L box with a 5 cm × 15 cm port tunes to about 32 Hz; without end corrections it would be about 36 Hz.
```

The same sum as code:

```python
import math

c = 343
def fb(vb_litres, d, length, k=0.0):
    a = math.pi * (d / 2) ** 2
    # Include air moving just beyond the
    # ends.
    leff = length + k * (d / 2)
    return (c / (2 * math.pi)) * math.sqrt(
        a / (vb_litres / 1000 * leff))

# 30 L box, 5 cm port, 15 cm long
print(round(fb(30, 0.05, 0.15), 1))
# with end corrections ~1.46 x radius
print(round(fb(30, 0.05, 0.15, 1.46), 1))
```

```
36.1
32.3
```

End correction moves the tuning by several hertz here. Real designs are modelled in software and checked by measurement (the impedance curve of a ported box has two peaks with a dip at Fb, which is an easy way to find the true tuning).

## Key takeaways
- Box air acts as a spring and the port air as a moving mass.
- Tuning depends on port area, box volume and effective length.
- End corrections are geometry-dependent; model and measure the actual cabinet.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)

questions.prompt: A port tunes a box to a frequency Fb that is proportional to the square root of (port area ÷ (box volume × effective port length)). Keep the port the same and make the box four times bigger. What happens to the tuning frequency?

options.explanation: Larger volume lowers the tuning, not raises it.
Fb depends on the square root of volume, not volume itself.
The box air is the spring; a bigger box is a softer spring and a lower resonance.
Correct. The tuning is proportional to 1 over the square root of the box volume, and the square root of 4 is 2, so it halves.

questions.workedExample:
Only the box volume changes, so everything else in the Helmholtz formula is a constant.

```formula
Fb ∝ √(A / (Vb Leff))
Fb ∝ 1 / √(Vb)
Fb_new = Fb / √(4) = Fb / 2
Fb_new ≈ 32 Hz / 2 = 16 Hz
where
Fb: the original box tuning frequency, in hertz (Hz); here about 32 Hz
Fb_new: the tuning after making the box four times bigger, in hertz (Hz)
∝: "is proportional to": the two sides change by the same factor
√: square root
A: the port's cross-sectional area, in square metres (m^2); unchanged
Vb: the internal box volume, in cubic metres (m^3); multiplied by 4
Leff: the port's effective length, in metres (m); unchanged
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: four times the box volume is a spring four times softer, which halves the tuning.
```

Example: a 30 L box with a 5 cm × 15 cm port tunes to about 32 Hz with end correction; in 120 L the same port gives about 16 Hz.

questions.prompt: You need a port with the same tuning but twice the cross-sectional area (to reduce port noise). Ignoring end corrections, how must the port length change?

options.explanation: Correct. The tuning depends on the square root of port area divided by port length, so doubling the area needs double the length to keep that ratio, and the tuning, the same.
With more area, the tuning would rise unless the port is longer.
Then the area-to-length ratio doubles and the tuning rises by the square root of 2, about 1.41 times.

options.text: Multiply it by the square root of 2
options.explanation: The area-to-length ratio itself must stay constant (it sits inside the square root), so the length must double, not rise by about 1.41.

questions.workedExample:
Ignoring end corrections, the tuning depends on the port only through the ratio of area to length:

```formula
Fb ∝ √(A / (Vb L))
A_new / L_new = A / L
(2A) / (2L) = A / L
where
Fb: the box tuning frequency, in hertz (Hz)
∝: "is proportional to": the two sides change by the same factor
√: square root
A: the port's cross-sectional area, in square metres (m^2)
Vb: the internal box volume, in cubic metres (m^3)
L: the port length, in metres (m)
A_new: the new port area, in square metres (m^2); here 2 × A
L_new: the new port length, in metres (m); it must be 2 × L
In words: to keep the tuning when the port gets twice as wide in area, make it twice as long.
```

That's why low-tuned ports with low air speed get long, and designers fold them or use slot ports or passive radiators.

lessons.title: Check alignment and cabinet construction
lessons.summary: An alignment specifies a target bass response from driver and enclosure parameters.
lessons.body:
## Alignments, conceptually

The driver plus box is a **high-pass filter**: second-order for sealed, fourth-order for ported. An **box alignment** is a choice of driver parameters, box volume and tuning that gives a particular filter shape, borrowed from electrical filter theory. Thiele (1961) and Small (1972–73) published tables of these; Butterworth (maximally flat), Chebyshev (some ripple, more extension) and quasi-Butterworth variants are common names. Modern practice is to simulate the response, excursion and port air speed in software, then measure.

## Cabinet resonance and bracing

The box's walls are panels that vibrate. If they resonate at frequencies the driver produces, the cabinet itself radiates sound, smearing and colouring the output. Remedies:

- **Stiff, dense material**: MDF and birch plywood are common choices.
- **Bracing**: internal struts or shelves that stiffen large panels, pushing their resonances higher and reducing their amplitude.
- **Damping**: lining or filling the box with absorbent material reduces internal standing waves between parallel walls and can damp panels.
- **Seal everything**: air leaks in a sealed box change its behaviour and can whistle.

> [!tip] If you build one
> Woodworking has its own hazards: control MDF dust with effective extraction and add suitable, correctly fitted respiratory protection where needed; a mask is not a substitute for extraction. Use power-tool guards and eye protection. Keep any amplifier electronics separate from the box-building and follow the power-amplifier units’ safety notes.

## Key takeaways
- An alignment specifies a target bass response from driver and enclosure parameters.
- Cabinet panels can radiate unwanted resonances.
- Use bracing, appropriate damping and controlled workshop methods; keep amplifier electronics separate.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)
- [MDF dust controls — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/woodworking/faqs.htm)

questions.prompt: An enclosure model gives the desired bass alignment, but the finished cabinet has a strong panel resonance. What addresses that separate construction problem?

options.text: Brace the vibrating panels and evaluate suitable damping, then measure again
options.explanation: Correct. Panel stiffness and vibration are separate from the ideal air-volume and driver alignment.

options.text: Assume the alignment makes every cabinet wall rigid
options.explanation: The ideal model does not establish that real panels cannot vibrate.

options.text: Open the mains amplifier and change its power supply
options.explanation: That does not address the cabinet panel and is outside this low-voltage learning scope.

options.text: Ignore the resonance because only the cone can radiate sound
options.explanation: Vibrating cabinet walls also radiate sound and can colour the output.

questions.workedExample:
1. The model describes a driver, air volume and any port under stated assumptions.
2. A real wall can bend and resonate independently.
3. Bracing increases panel stiffness; appropriate damping dissipates vibration or internal acoustic energy.
4. Recheck the assembled cabinet by measurement. Control woodworking dust with extraction and appropriate protection. Keep amplifier electronics separate.

lessons.title: Crossover architectures, order and slope
lessons.summary: Passive networks filter speaker-level signals; active filters precede driver amplifiers.
lessons.body:
A single driver faces substantial trade-offs in covering 20 Hz to 20 kHz at useful levels and with controlled dispersion. A woofer big enough for bass beams and breaks up in the treble (the loudspeaker-driver units); a tweeter small enough to disperse treble widely would be destroyed by bass excursion. So most speakers use two or more drivers, and a **crossover** sends each one only the frequencies it handles well.

You already met filters in module 2 (synth filters). Crossovers use the same maths, with one extra demand: the outputs must **add back together** in the air into a smooth response.

## Passive, active and DSP

```diagram
 PASSIVE:
  amp ---> [LC filter] ---> woofer
       \-> [LC filter] ---> tweeter

 ACTIVE / DSP:
  source -> [filter] -> amp -> woofer
         \-> [filter] -> amp -> tweeter
```

- **Passive crossovers** are inductors, capacitors and resistors between one power amplifier and the drivers. They carry full speaker-level current, so parts are large and the filter's behaviour depends on the drivers' impedance. Most hi-fi speakers use them.
- **Active crossovers** filter at line level (op-amp circuits), *before* a separate amplifier for each driver. Filter behaviour is predictable, each amp sees one driver, and a clipping woofer amp can't send its distortion to the tweeter.
- **DSP** crossovers are active crossovers done in software, as in most powered studio monitor loudspeakers and PA processors. They add delay, EQ and limiters per driver at little extra cost, and you can even use linear-phase (FIR) filters, with delay and latency determined by the design.

## Order and slope

For the conventional analogue all-pole low-pass and corresponding high-pass families below, order sets the **asymptotic** stopband slope and total phase change. Arbitrary filters with additional zeros, delays or FIR structures need separate analysis:

| Order | Slope | Total phase rotation |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 6 dB/octave | 90° |
| 2nd | 12 dB/octave | 180° |
| 3rd | 18 dB/octave | 270° |
| 4th | 24 dB/octave | 360° |

The table follows one simple rule. Each order (each "pole" of the filter) adds 6 dB/octave of slope and 90° of phase rotation, so you can work out any row from the order alone:

```formula
slope = 6n dB/octave
φ_total = 90°n
slope = 4 × 6 dB/octave = 24 dB/octave
φ_total = 4 × 90° = 360°
where
slope: how fast the output falls in the stopband, far from the corner, in decibels per octave
n: the filter order (1, 2, 3, 4 ...); higher means steeper and more complex
dB: decibel, a logarithmic measure of level ratio; −6 dB is about half the voltage
octave: a doubling (or halving) of frequency, for example 1 kHz to 2 kHz
φ_total: the total phase rotation the filter adds across the whole band, in degrees (°)
In words: every extra order makes the filter fall another 6 dB per octave, and twists the phase another quarter turn.
```

Why 6 dB? Far above its corner, a first-order low-pass halves its output voltage every time the frequency doubles, and halving the voltage is −6 dB (20 dB per *decade*, a tenfold change in frequency, says the same thing). A fourth-order filter approaches another 24 dB of attenuation per octave far into its stopband. Its absolute level one octave from the corner depends on the filter family. These are asymptotes: near the corner the real curve is gentler.

Steeper slopes protect drivers better (a tweeter crossed with 24 dB/octave sees much less energy at its resonance than with 6 dB/octave) and reduce the overlap where both drivers play. The cost: more phase rotation, more complex circuits and, passively, more expensive parts.

## Key takeaways
- Passive networks filter speaker-level signals; active filters precede driver amplifiers.
- For the conventional families discussed, each order contributes roughly six decibels per octave asymptotically.
- Electrical filter response and actual driver response jointly determine the acoustic result.

## Further reading
- [Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab](https://www.linkwitzlab.com/crossovers.htm)
- [Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note160.html)
- [Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab](https://linkwitzlab.com/filters.htm)

questions.prompt: Why do most full-range loudspeakers use two or more drivers with a crossover?

options.text: Because a driver large enough for bass beams and breaks up at high frequencies, and a small tweeter can't handle bass excursion
options.explanation: Correct. Splitting the band lets each driver work where it performs well.

options.text: To make the speaker look more expensive
options.explanation: There are real acoustic reasons: no single driver covers the whole band well.

options.text: Because amplifiers can only drive one frequency at a time
options.explanation: Amplifiers handle the whole audio band at once.
Impedance isn't the reason; the crossover is about frequency ranges.

questions.workedExample:
A big cone moves enough air for bass, but it starts to **beam** (focus its sound into a narrowing forward beam) once the wavelength gets close to the cone size. A rough guide to where that starts:

```formula
f_beam ≈ c / (2πa)
f_beam ≈ (343 m/s) / (2π × 0.065 m)
f_beam ≈ 840 Hz
where
f_beam: the frequency above which the cone starts to beam, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
π: pi, about 3.14159
a: the cone's effective radius (half its diameter), in metres (m); here 0.065 m for a 13 cm cone
≈: approximately equal to
m: metres
s: seconds
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: bigger cones beam at lower frequencies; a 13 cm woofer already narrows its dispersion above about 840 Hz, and it breaks up higher still.
```

A small dome tweeter disperses treble widely but can't make the large excursion bass needs. A crossover routes lows to the woofer and highs to the tweeter, so each driver works where it performs well.

questions.prompt: What asymptotic stopband slope does a conventional fourth-order Butterworth or Linkwitz–Riley low-pass filter have?

options.explanation: That's first order.
That's second order.
Correct. Each order adds 6 dB/octave: 4 × 6 = 24.
That's eighth order (for example LR8).

questions.workedExample:
Each order (pole) of a conventional filter adds 6 dB/octave of asymptotic slope:

```formula
slope = 6n dB/octave
slope = 4 × 6 dB/octave
slope = 24 dB/octave
where
slope: how fast the output falls far into the stopband, in decibels per octave
n: the filter order, here 4
dB: decibel, a logarithmic measure of level ratio; −6 dB is about half the voltage
octave: a doubling of frequency
In words: a fourth-order filter falls four times as steeply as a first-order one: 24 dB for each doubling of frequency.
```

The 6 dB comes from a first-order filter halving its voltage each octave far from the corner (the same slope is often quoted as 20 dB per decade, a tenfold frequency change). So 1st order is 6, 2nd is 12, 3rd is 18 and 4th is 24 dB/octave.

questions.prompt: What's the main difference between a passive and an active crossover?

options.text: Passive crossovers need mains power; active ones don't
options.explanation: It's the reverse: passive networks need no power; active ones contain powered electronics.

options.text: Active crossovers only work with subwoofers
options.explanation: Active crossovers are used for every band, from studio monitor loudspeakers to PA systems.

options.text: There's no difference in where they sit in the chain
options.explanation: Where they sit is the defining difference.

options.text: Passive crossovers sit after one power amp at speaker level; active crossovers filter at line level before a separate amp for each driver
options.explanation: Correct.

questions.workedExample:
```
passive: amp -> LC network -> drivers
active:  filters -> amp per driver
```

Active and DSP crossovers aren't affected by driver impedance and can add delay, EQ and limiting per driver.

lessons.title: Why crossover phase matters
lessons.summary: At a crossover both driver outputs contribute.
lessons.body:
## Making the outputs add up

The low-pass and high-pass outputs have to sum to a flat response. Magnitude alone isn't enough: at the crossover frequency both drivers contribute, so their relative **phase shift** decides whether they add or cancel.

Crossover levels are quoted in decibels, which come from the voltage (amplitude) ratio. These are the numbers you'll meet below:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(A)
20 log_10(0.707) ≈ −3 dB
20 log_10(0.5) ≈ −6 dB
20 log_10(1) = 0 dB
20 log_10(1.414) ≈ +3 dB
where
L: the level change, in decibels (dB); negative means quieter
A: the amplitude ratio, output voltage divided by input voltage (no unit); 1 means unchanged, 0.5 means half
log_10: the base-10 logarithm, which asks "10 to what power gives this number?"
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: half the voltage is −6 dB, about 71 % of it (1/√2) is −3 dB, and 1.414 times (√2) is +3 dB.
```

### First order

A first-order low-pass and high-pass at the same frequency are each −3 dB at the crossover, and they sum *exactly* to the input. Filter designers write a filter as a fraction of the input using the variable *s*:

```formula
LP = 1 / (1 + s)
HP = s / (1 + s)
LP + HP = (1 + s) / (1 + s) = 1
where
LP: the low-pass output as a fraction of the input (its transfer function); no unit
HP: the high-pass output as a fraction of the input; no unit
s: the normalised complex frequency (the Laplace variable). For a steady sine wave it equals j times the frequency divided by the crossover frequency, where j is the imaginary unit (the square root of −1) that tracks phase. At the crossover the normalised variable equals the imaginary unit
In words: the low-pass and high-pass pieces share the same bottom line, so their tops add up to that bottom line and the sum is exactly the input, at every frequency.
```

At the crossover, each output's size is about 0.707 of the input (−3 dB), but the two are 90° apart in phase, which is why two 0.707s can still add up to exactly 1. The catch: the two outputs are 90° apart at the crossover, the 6 dB/octave slopes give the drivers a lot of out-of-band signal to handle, and the perfect sum only holds on one axis with ideal drivers.

### Butterworth

A Butterworth filter is maximally flat in its passband and −3 dB at its corner. For a **second-order Butterworth** crossover, the low-pass and high-pass outputs are 180° apart at the crossover, so:

- Wired with the same polarity, they **cancel**: a deep notch at the crossover.
- With one driver's polarity reversed, they sum with a **+3 dB peak** at the crossover (two −3 dB outputs adding in phase).

```formula
A_sum = A_LP + A_HP
A_sum = 0.707 + 0.707 = 1.414
L_sum = 20 log_10(1.414) ≈ +3 dB
where
A_sum: the size of the summed output at the crossover, as a fraction of the input (no unit)
A_LP: the low-pass output's size at the crossover; 0.707 (−3 dB) for a Butterworth
A_HP: the high-pass output's size at the crossover; also 0.707
L_sum: the summed level, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: two outputs that are each 71 % of the input, added in step, give 141 % of the input: a 3 dB bump.
```

This simple addition only works because, with one polarity flipped, the two outputs are exactly in step at the crossover.

## Key takeaways
- At a crossover both driver outputs contribute.
- A matched first-order pair sums exactly in the ideal aligned model.
- A second-order Butterworth pair needs a polarity choice and does not give a flat magnitude sum.

## Further reading
- [Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab](https://www.linkwitzlab.com/crossovers.htm)
- [Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note160.html)
- [Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab](https://linkwitzlab.com/filters.htm)

questions.prompt: Assume ideal drivers with equal sensitivity and equal path lengths to the listener. A second-order Butterworth crossover is used, with the tweeter's polarity reversed. What does the summed on-axis response look like near the crossover frequency?

options.explanation: Each output is −3 dB at the crossover frequency; adding them in phase gives +3 dB, not 0 dB.
That's what happens with the *same* polarity: the outputs are 180° apart.
Correct. Two −3 dB (0.707) outputs in phase add to 1.414, which is +3 dB.
That's the level of each Linkwitz–Riley output at the crossover frequency, not a Butterworth sum.

questions.workedExample:
Each second-order Butterworth output is 0.707 of the input (−3 dB) at the crossover, and the two are 180° apart. Inverting one driver brings them into step, so their sizes simply add:

```formula
A_sum = A_LP + A_HP
A_sum = 0.707 + 0.707 = 1.414
L_sum = 20 log_10(1.414) ≈ +3 dB
where
A_sum: the size of the summed output at the crossover, as a fraction of the input (no unit)
A_LP: the low-pass output's size at the crossover, 0.707
A_HP: the high-pass output's size at the crossover, 0.707
L_sum: the summed level, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: two 71 % outputs added in step make 141 %: a 3 dB bump at the crossover.
```

Linkwitz–Riley fixes this by making each output 0.5 (−6 dB) at the crossover, so the in-step sum is 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0, which is 0 dB.

lessons.title: Why Linkwitz–Riley can sum flat
lessons.summary: Cascaded Butterworth sections give each Linkwitz–Riley output half amplitude at crossover.
lessons.body:
## Linkwitz–Riley summation

### Linkwitz–Riley

Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley's fix (1976) was to cascade **two Butterworth filters** of the same order on each side. Each output is then **−6 dB** at the crossover, half the voltage, and the two halves add to exactly 0 dB:

```formula
A_LR = A_BW^2
A_LR = 0.707 × 0.707 ≈ 0.5
A_sum = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1
L_sum = 20 log_10(1) = 0 dB
where
A_LR: the size of one Linkwitz–Riley output at the crossover, as a fraction of the input (no unit)
A_BW: the size of one Butterworth section's output at the crossover: 0.707 (−3 dB)
A_sum: the size of the summed output (in-phase outputs), as a fraction of the input
L_sum: the summed level, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: putting two −3 dB filters in a row gives −6 dB (half the voltage), and two halves added in step make exactly the original level.
```

- **LR2** (two first-order sections): 12 dB/octave, outputs 180° apart, so one driver is reversed in polarity. Sums flat.
- **LR4** (two second-order Butterworths): 24 dB/octave. At the crossover the low-pass is at −180° and the high-pass at +180°, which is a **360° difference: the outputs are in phase at every frequency**. They sum to a flat magnitude, and the total behaves as an **all-pass** filter: flat amplitude with smoothly changing phase.

Why does LR4 sum flat at *every* frequency, not just at the crossover? Write each output as a transfer function, using the same normalised frequency variable as the first-order example, and compare the sizes of the top and bottom of the sum:

```formula
D = s^2 + √(2)s + 1
LP = 1 / D^2
HP = s^4 / D^2
LP + HP = (1 + s^4) / D^2
s = ju
|1 + s^4| = 1 + u^4
|D|^2 = (1 − u^2)^2 + 2u^2
|D|^2 = 1 + u^4
|LP + HP| = (1 + u^4) / (1 + u^4) = 1
where
D: the denominator (bottom line) of a second-order Butterworth filter; no unit
s: the normalised complex frequency (the Laplace variable); for a steady sine it equals j × u
LP: the LR4 low-pass output as a fraction of the input (two Butterworth low-passes in a row, so D is squared)
HP: the LR4 high-pass output as a fraction of the input
j: the imaginary unit, the square root of −1; it keeps track of phase. j^4 = 1, so s^4 = u^4
u: normalised frequency, the normalised frequency: the actual frequency divided by the crossover frequency (no unit); u = 1 at the crossover
√: square root
| |: the magnitude (size) of a complex number, ignoring its phase
In words: the top and the bottom of the summed transfer function always have the same size, so the sum's size is exactly 1 (0 dB) at every frequency; only its phase changes.
```

The denominator polynomial has odd powers that the numerator lacks, so they are not identical polynomials and the sum’s phase still rotates. That's exactly what an all-pass filter is.

| Crossover | Each output at crossover | Sum at crossover |
|---|---|---|
| BW2, one driver inverted | −3 dB | +3 dB peak |
| LR2, one driver inverted | −6 dB | 0 dB |
| LR4 | −6 dB | 0 dB, in phase |

LR4 is a very common choice in active and DSP crossovers, including PA processors.

## Key takeaways
- Cascaded Butterworth sections give each Linkwitz–Riley output half amplitude at crossover.
- The correctly aligned LR4 sum has flat magnitude and varying phase.
- Ideal mathematical summation assumes suitable driver responses and equal path lengths.

## Further reading
- [Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab](https://www.linkwitzlab.com/crossovers.htm)
- [Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note160.html)
- [Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab](https://linkwitzlab.com/filters.htm)

questions.prompt: Which statements about LR4 (fourth-order Linkwitz–Riley) crossovers are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The low-pass and high-pass outputs are in phase at all frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. They're 360° apart, which is in phase.

options.text: The summed output has a +3 dB peak at the crossover
options.explanation: That's the second-order Butterworth result; LR4 sums flat.

options.text: Each side is two cascaded second-order Butterworth filters
options.explanation: Correct. That's why it's sometimes called 'Butterworth squared'.

options.text: Each output is −6 dB at the crossover frequency

questions.workedExample:
- An LR4 is two second-order Butterworth filters in series on each side: 24 dB/octave.
- At the crossover the low-pass is at −180° and the high-pass at +180°: a 360° difference, so in phase.
- The total behaves as an all-pass: flat magnitude, rotating phase.

The levels at the crossover:

```formula
A_LR = A_BW^2
A_LR ≈ 0.707 × 0.707
A_LR = 0.5
A_sum = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1
L_sum = 20 log_10(1) = 0 dB
where
A_LR: the size of each LR4 output at the crossover, as a fraction of the input (no unit); 0.5 is −6 dB
A_BW: the size of one Butterworth section's output at the crossover, 0.707 (−3 dB)
A_sum: the size of the two outputs added in phase
L_sum: the summed level, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: two −3 dB stages in a row give −6 dB (half), and two in-phase halves add to exactly the original level.
```

questions.prompt:
An LR4 crossover's outputs can be written as:

```formula
D = s^2 + √(2)s + 1
LP = 1 / D^2
HP = s^4 / D^2
s = ju
where
D: the denominator (bottom line) of a second-order Butterworth filter
LP: the low-pass output as a fraction of the input (transfer function)
HP: the high-pass output as a fraction of the input
s: the normalised complex frequency (Laplace variable)
j: the imaginary unit, the square root of −1; it tracks phase
u: normalised frequency, frequency divided by the crossover frequency (no unit)
√: square root
In words: each LR4 output is a squared Butterworth filter; s carries both frequency and phase.
```

Why does the crossover sum to a flat magnitude?

options.text: Because the numerator and denominator are identical polynomials at every complex frequency
options.explanation: They're not equal as polynomials; D² has odd-power terms. Only their magnitudes match on the ju axis.

options.text: Because the numerator and denominator magnitudes match on the imaginary-frequency axis, so their ratio has magnitude one
options.explanation: Correct. The sum is an all-pass: flat magnitude with varying phase.

options.text: Because each output is −3 dB at the crossover frequency
options.explanation: LR outputs are −6 dB at the crossover frequency; −3 dB is Butterworth.

options.text: It doesn't: LR4 has a +3 dB bump
options.explanation: The bump is a Butterworth property; LR4 sums flat.

questions.workedExample:
Add the outputs, then compare the size (magnitude) of the top and the bottom of the sum for a steady sine wave:

```formula
LP + HP = (1 + s^4) / D^2
|1 + s^4| = 1 + u^4
|D|^2 = (1 − u^2)^2 + 2u^2
|D|^2 = 1 + u^4
|LP + HP| = |1 + s^4| / |D|^2 = 1
where
LP: the low-pass output as a fraction of the input
HP: the high-pass output as a fraction of the input
s: the normalised complex frequency, equal to j × u for a steady sine
D: the Butterworth denominator s^2 + √2 × s + 1
u: normalised frequency, frequency divided by the crossover frequency (no unit)
| |: the magnitude (size) of a complex number, ignoring its phase
In words: because j^4 = 1, the top is 1 + u^4, and the bottom's size works out to the same thing, so the sum has size 1 (0 dB) at every frequency.
```

The phase of the sum still rotates (an all-pass), so LR4 isn't phase-linear, but its magnitude is perfectly flat with ideal, aligned drivers.

lessons.title: Align drivers and protect the tweeter
lessons.summary: Distance offsets create frequency-dependent phase error.
lessons.body:
## Driver offset and phase

The preceding units’ ideal sums assume both drivers' sound starts from the same point. Real drivers don't: a woofer's **acoustic centre** usually sits further back than a tweeter's on a flat baffle. A path difference becomes a time delay, and a time delay becomes a frequency-dependent phase shift that ruins the neat summation:

```formula
t = d / c
φ = 360°ft
t = 0.02 m / (343 m/s) ≈ 58 µs
t = 0.08 m / (343 m/s) ≈ 233 µs
φ = 360° × 2000 Hz × 233 µs ≈ 168°
where
t: the time delay between the two drivers' sound, in seconds (s) or microseconds (µs, millionths of a second)
d: the path difference: how much further one acoustic centre is from the listener, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
φ: the phase error the delay causes, in degrees (°); 360° is one whole cycle
f: the frequency in question, here the 2 kHz crossover, in hertz (Hz)
m: metres
s: seconds
µs: microseconds
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: sound covers about 3.4 mm every 10 µs, and a fixed delay is a bigger slice of a cycle at higher frequencies; 233 µs is almost half a 2 kHz cycle (500 µs).
```

The script below adds that delay to the woofer of an ideal 2 kHz LR4 crossover and prints the on-axis sum in dB.

```python
import cmath, math

def lr4(f, fc):
    s = 1j * f / fc
    # Square each Butterworth transfer.
    d = s * s + math.sqrt(2) * s + 1
    return 1 / d**2, s**4 / d**2

def summed_db(f, fc, lag=0.0):
    lp, hp = lr4(f, fc)
    # woofer (low-pass) arrives late
    lp *= cmath.exp(-2j * math.pi * f * lag)
    db = 20 * math.log10(abs(lp + hp))
    return round(db, 1) + 0.0

fc = 2000
print("  f     0cm   2cm   8cm")
for f in (500, 1000, 1500, 2000,
          2500, 4000):
    row = [summed_db(f, fc, cm / 100 / 343)
           for cm in (0, 2, 8)]
    print(f"{f:>5}" + "".join(
        f"{v:6.1f}" for v in row))
```

```
  f     0cm   2cm   8cm
  500   0.0   0.0   0.0
 1000   0.0   0.0  -0.5
 1500   0.0  -0.2  -3.8
 2000   0.0  -0.6 -19.6
 2500   0.0  -0.8  -6.4
 4000   0.0  -0.5   0.0
```

With the woofer 2 cm behind (58 µs), the dip is under 1 dB. At 8 cm (233 µs, almost half a period at 2 kHz) there's a deep on-axis hole at the crossover. Remedies:

- **DSP delay** on the earlier driver (easy in active/DSP systems).
- **Stepped or sloped baffles** to line up acoustic centres physically.
- Choosing the crossover frequency and filter shapes so the *acoustic* responses (filter × driver) hit the target, and checking the result by measurement.

Even when on-axis is perfect, moving up or down changes the path lengths to the two drivers. That's **lobing**: the summed response changes with vertical angle. LR crossovers with aligned drivers keep the main radiation lobe pointing straight ahead, which is one reason they're popular.

## Filter choice also protects a driver

The first-order and LR4 filters from the preceding units pass very different amounts of signal below the crossover. At half the crossover frequency, the ideal first-order high-pass is about seven decibels down, while LR4 is about twenty-five decibels down. The question works through the transfer-function calculation.

This reduces the tweeter’s out-of-band input for the same source level. It does not establish a safe crossover or power rating: use the exact driver’s recommended filter type, minimum crossover and excursion and thermal limits, then measure the acoustic result.

## Key takeaways
- Distance offsets create frequency-dependent phase error.
- Delay or physical alignment can improve the target-axis sum.
- Steeper high-pass attenuation reduces out-of-band tweeter input but does not establish safe operating power.

## Further reading
- [Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab](https://www.linkwitzlab.com/crossovers.htm)
- [Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note160.html)
- [Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab](https://linkwitzlab.com/filters.htm)

questions.prompt: A tweeter's acoustic centre is 3 cm in front of the woofer's. Roughly what time offset is that, and what phase error at a 2 kHz crossover?

options.explanation: Correct. Sound takes about 87.5 µs to cover 3 cm at 343 m/s, and that is about 63° of a 2 kHz cycle.
That's ten times too small; 3 cm (0.03 m) divided by 343 m/s is about 87.5 µs, not 8.7 µs.
Ten times too large.

options.text: No error: crossovers correct for offsets automatically
options.explanation: Unless you add delay or align the drivers, the offset remains.

questions.workedExample:
Turn the distance into a time, then the time into a fraction of one cycle at the crossover frequency:

```formula
t = d / c
t = 0.03 m / (343 m/s)
t ≈ 0.0000875 s = 87.5 µs
φ = 360°ft
φ = 360° × 2000 Hz × 0.0000875 s
φ ≈ 63°
where
t: the time offset between the drivers' sound, in seconds (s) or microseconds (µs, millionths of a second)
d: the distance between the acoustic centres, 3 cm = 0.03 metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
φ: the phase error, in degrees (°); 360° is one full cycle
f: the crossover frequency, 2000 hertz (Hz)
m: metres
s: seconds
µs: microseconds
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a 3 cm offset is an 87.5 µs delay, which is about a sixth of a 2 kHz cycle (500 µs): 63° of phase.
```

DSP crossovers fix this by delaying the tweeter by about 87 µs. The same delay is a bigger phase error at higher frequencies.

questions.prompt: A DSP crossover lets you choose a steep LR4 at 2 kHz or a gentle first-order at 2 kHz for a small dome tweeter with a free-air resonance of 900 Hz. Which is safer for the tweeter, and why?

options.text: LR4, because at 1 kHz it attenuates much more than first-order (roughly 24 dB/octave vs 6 dB/octave), keeping energy away from the tweeter's resonance and excursion limits
options.explanation: Correct. One octave below the crossover frequency, LR4 is far lower than a first-order filter.

options.text: First-order, because it has less phase shift
options.explanation: Less phase shift doesn't protect the tweeter; it passes far more energy near its resonance.

options.text: They're equally safe because both cross at 2 kHz
options.explanation: The slope decides how much out-of-band energy reaches the tweeter.

options.text: First-order, because the tweeter's impedance peak at Fs blocks the bass
options.explanation: The impedance peak doesn't protect the tweeter, and with a passive network it can even shift the filter.

questions.workedExample:
One octave below 2 kHz is 1 kHz, so the normalised frequency is 0.5. Compare the two high-pass sizes there:

```formula
A_1 = u / √(1 + u^2)
A_1 = 0.5 / √(1 + 0.5^2) ≈ 0.447
L_1 = 20 log_10(0.447) ≈ −7 dB
A_4 = u^4 / (1 + u^4)
A_4 = 0.0625 / 1.0625 ≈ 0.059
L_4 = 20 log_10(0.059) ≈ −25 dB
where
u: normalised frequency, the frequency divided by the crossover frequency (no unit): 1 kHz / 2 kHz = 0.5
A_1: the first-order high-pass output's size, as a fraction of the input
A_4: the LR4 high-pass output's size, as a fraction of the input
L_1: the first-order level, in decibels (dB)
L_4: the LR4 level, in decibels (dB)
√: square root
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: an octave below the crossover, a first-order filter only takes about 7 dB off, while an LR4 takes about 25 dB off.
```

Near its resonance a small dome has little excursion to spare, so steeper slopes protect it and lower distortion. This compares attenuation at the same input level; check the tweeter manufacturer’s minimum crossover, filter type and power limits before choosing a real design.

lessons.title: Calculate passive values and recognise their limits
lessons.summary: The textbook values assume fixed resistive driver loads.
lessons.body:
## A first-order passive crossover, worked

The textbook calculation treats each driver as a plain resistor equal to its nominal impedance. An inductor's opposition to current (its reactance) rises with frequency, and a capacitor's falls. A first-order filter's corner is where the part's reactance equals the driver's resistance, which gives:

```formula
X_L = 2πf L
X_C = 1 / (2πf C)
L = R / (2πf_c)
C = 1 / (2πf_c R)
where
X_L: the inductor's reactance (its opposition to alternating current), in ohms (Ω); it rises with frequency, so a series inductor attenuates treble into a suitable load
X_C: the capacitor's reactance, in ohms (Ω); it falls with frequency, so a series capacitor attenuates bass into a suitable load
f: any frequency, in hertz (Hz)
L: the inductance of the series inductor feeding the woofer (low-pass), in henries (H); a few tenths of a millihenry (mH) is typical
C: the capacitance of the series capacitor feeding the tweeter (high-pass), in farads (F); a few microfarads (µF) is typical
R: the driver's impedance treated as a fixed resistance, in ohms (Ω); usually the nominal 4 Ω or 8 Ω
f_c: the crossover (corner) frequency, in hertz (Hz), where X_L or X_C equals R
π: pi, about 3.14159
In words: set the inductor's or capacitor's reactance equal to the driver's resistance at the crossover frequency and solve; a higher crossover or a lower driver impedance needs a smaller inductor, while a higher crossover or higher impedance needs a smaller capacitor.
```

```diagram
 amp+ --+--L------ woofer ------+
        |                      |
        +--C------ tweeter -----+-- amp-
```

Worked example: crossover at 3 kHz, 8 Ω drivers.

```formula
L = R / (2πf_c)
L = 8 Ω / (2π × 3000 Hz)
L ≈ 0.000424 H = 0.424 mH
C = 1 / (2πf_c R)
C = 1 / (2π × 3000 Hz × 8 Ω)
C ≈ 0.00000663 F = 6.63 µF
where
L: the woofer's series inductor, in henries (H)
C: the tweeter's series capacitor, in farads (F)
R: the driver impedance, taken as a fixed 8 ohms (Ω)
f_c: the crossover frequency, 3000 hertz (Hz)
π: pi, about 3.14159
≈: approximately equal to
H: henry, the unit of inductance
mH: millihenry, a thousandth of a henry
F: farad, the unit of capacitance
µF: microfarad, a millionth of a farad
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance and impedance
In words: for a 3 kHz crossover on 8 Ω drivers, the woofer needs about 0.42 mH in series and the tweeter about 6.6 µF.
```

So a 0.42 mH inductor in series with the woofer and a 6.6 µF capacitor in series with the tweeter (nearest standard values in practice).

### Why it won't behave as calculated

The formula assumes a constant 8 Ω resistor. The loudspeaker-driver units showed real drivers aren't:

- **The impedance varies with frequency.** If the tweeter can be approximated by a constant 6 Ω resistance throughout this region, the high-pass corner moves to about **4 kHz** (calculated below). A single impedance measurement at 3 kHz cannot establish the real corner. The woofer's impedance *rises* through the crossover region because of coil inductance, so its inductor filters less than intended.
- **The tweeter's resonance.** Near its Fs (for a dome tweeter typically somewhere around 0.5–1.5 kHz; check the datasheet) the tweeter's impedance peaks and it can't handle much power. A gentle 6 dB/octave filter still feeds it a lot of energy there.
- **The drivers' own roll-offs add to the filter's.** What matters is the *acoustic* slope: electrical filter × driver response. A woofer that's already falling off adds its own slope and phase.
- **Sensitivity differences.** Tweeters are often more sensitive than woofers, so a resistor network (L-pad) is needed to bring the tweeter down.

Here is the tweeter corner with the 6.63 µF capacitor from the 8 Ω design, when the tweeter is really closer to 6 Ω:

```formula
f_c = 1 / (2πRC)
f_c = 1 / (2π × 6 Ω × 6.63 µF)
f_c ≈ 4000 Hz = 4 kHz
where
f_c: the high-pass corner frequency, in hertz (Hz) and kilohertz (kHz, thousands of hertz)
R: the tweeter's actual resistance in this region, 6 ohms (Ω)
C: the series capacitor, 6.63 microfarads (µF), i.e. 0.00000663 farads (F)
π: pi, about 3.14159
≈: approximately equal to
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
µF: microfarads, millionths of a farad
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
kHz: kilohertz, thousands of hertz
In words: the corner frequency scales inversely with resistance, so 6 Ω instead of 8 Ω pushes the 3 kHz corner up by 8/6 to about 4 kHz.
```

This still assumes a constant resistance; a real driver's impedance is complex and changes with frequency, so only the full measured curve gives the true corner.

Designers fix some of this with impedance-compensation networks (a **Zobel** network across the woofer flattens the rising impedance) and by designing from *measured* driver impedance and frequency response in simulation software, then measuring the built speaker. For a DIY project, using published, tested crossover designs, or a DSP crossover where everything can be measured and adjusted, is far more forgiving than calculating a passive one from nominal values.

> [!note] Passive crossover safety
> Passive crossovers sit after the power amplifier, at speaker-level voltages and currents. High-power speaker outputs can themselves present hazardous voltages and currents. Never open the amplifier; switch it off before changing speaker wiring and follow its discharge and connection instructions (the power-amplifier units).

## Key takeaways
- The textbook values assume fixed resistive driver loads.
- Real impedance, driver roll-off, sensitivity and acoustic-centre offsets change the result.
- Design from measurements and follow the amplifier’s safe connection guidance.

## Further reading
- [Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab](https://www.linkwitzlab.com/crossovers.htm)
- [Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note160.html)
- [Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab](https://linkwitzlab.com/filters.htm)
