questions.prompt: You calculate a first-order high-pass for an 8 Ω tweeter at 3 kHz: C ≈ 6.6 µF. Now approximate the tweeter as a constant 6 Ω resistance across the crossover region. Where does this simplified model put the corner?

options.explanation: The corner depends on the actual load resistance: a lower resistance with the same capacitor moves the corner up.
That would be the case if the impedance rose to about 10.7 Ω.
That's far too low and would endanger the tweeter near its resonance.
Correct. With 6 Ω and 6.63 µF the corner is about 4.0 kHz; see the worked example.

questions.workedExample:
First the capacitor from the nominal 8 Ω design, then the corner it actually gives with 6 Ω:

```formula
C = 1 / (2πf_c R)
C = 1 / (2π × 3000 Hz × 8 Ω)
C ≈ 6.63 µF
f = 1 / (2πRC)
f = 1 / (2π × 6 Ω × 6.63 µF)
f ≈ 4000 Hz
where
C: the series capacitor, in farads (F); here in microfarads (µF, millionths of a farad)
f_c: the intended crossover frequency, 3000 hertz (Hz)
R: the tweeter's resistance: 8 ohms (Ω) nominal, then 6 Ω in the simplified model
f: the actual high-pass corner frequency, in hertz (Hz)
π: pi, about 3.14159
≈: approximately equal to
µF: microfarads
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
Ω: ohms
In words: the corner scales inversely with resistance, so 6 Ω instead of 8 Ω pushes 3 kHz up by 8/6 to about 4 kHz.
```

That's why passive crossovers are designed with measured impedance data, not nominal values. A real frequency-dependent complex impedance requires the full measured curve; its value at one frequency is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Which are reasons a crossover calculated from nominal impedance and textbook formulas will differ from the real speaker? Select all that apply.

options.text: The drivers' own acoustic roll-offs and phase add to the electrical filter's
options.explanation: Correct. The acoustic slope is filter × driver response.

options.text: Acoustic centres of the drivers are at different distances
options.explanation: Correct. The offset adds delay and phase error near the crossover.

options.text: Ideal linear capacitors and inductors change their component values merely because the signal level rises
options.explanation: Ideal linear component values do not depend on signal level. Real components can depart from that ideal through saturation, heating or voltage dependence, which should also be checked.

options.text: Driver impedance varies with frequency (resonance peak, rising coil inductance)
options.explanation: Correct. The filter's corner depends on the actual load at each frequency.

questions.workedExample:
Textbook passive formulas assume a constant resistive load and ideal drivers. Real systems:

1. Load varies: Re at DC, peak at Fs, inductive rise.
2. Drivers have their own response: you design the acoustic target, not just the electrical filter.
3. Offsets move phase.

So designers measure each driver in the cabinet, simulate, build, then measure again.

lessons.title: Voltage gain, current and load power
lessons.summary: An amplifier supplies output voltage and the current required by its load within its limits.
lessons.body:
Your synth's line output can swing a volt or two into 10 kΩ or more (module 5). A loudspeaker needs tens of volts into a few ohms: amps of current and tens or hundreds of watts. A **power amplifier** bridges that gap.

> [!warning] Safety: conceptual lesson only
> Power amplifiers contain **mains wiring** and, inside, **high-voltage supply rails and large capacitors** that can stay charged after unplugging. Valve (tube) amps run at hundreds of volts. Speaker terminals on a large amp can carry voltages that are dangerous to touch at full power. This lesson is about understanding and choosing amplifiers. **Don't open, modify or build mains-powered amplifiers.** Connect speakers with the amp switched off and the volume down, and leave repairs to qualified technicians.

## What a power amp does

A power amp is a **voltage amplifier with a very low output impedance** that can deliver large currents:

- It multiplies the input voltage by a fixed **voltage gain**.
- It holds that output voltage steady whatever the speaker's impedance does (within its limits), by supplying whatever current the load demands.
- Power is a *result*. The amp sets the voltage; the speaker's impedance decides the current and so the power.

For a resistive load, Ohm's law and the power formula tell you the current and power from the voltage:

```formula
I_rms = V_rms / R
P = V_rms^2 / R
I_rms = 20 V / 8 Ω = 2.5 A
P = (20 V)^2 / 8 Ω = 400 / 8 = 50 W
where
I_rms: the RMS current through the speaker, in amperes (A)
V_rms: the RMS (root-mean-square, an "effective average") output voltage, in volts (V)
R: the load resistance, in ohms (Ω); a nominal speaker is typically 4 Ω or 8 Ω
P: the average power delivered to the load, in watts (W)
A: amperes (amps), the unit of current
V: volts, the unit of voltage
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: power rises with the square of voltage, so doubling the voltage gives four times the power, and halving the resistance doubles it.
```

That's exact only for a resistor. A real speaker has complex impedance, so sinusoidal real power also depends on the voltage–current phase difference.

### Voltage gain vs power

Amplifier gain is usually quoted in dB (voltage), or as **input sensitivity**: the input voltage that produces full rated output. To use a dB gain, turn it back into a multiplier:

```formula
G = 10^{G_dB / 20}
G = 10^{26 / 20} ≈ 19.95
V_in = 0.7746 V × 10^{4 / 20} ≈ 1.228 V
V_out = V_in G
V_out = 1.228 V × 19.95 ≈ 24.5 V
P = (24.5 V)^2 / 8 Ω ≈ 75 W
V_sens = √(P_max R) / G
V_sens = √(100 W × 8 Ω) / 19.95 ≈ 1.42 V
where
G: the voltage gain as a plain multiplier (no unit)
G_dB: the voltage gain in decibels (dB), here 26 dB
V_in: the RMS input voltage, in volts (V); +4 dBu (professional line level) is 0.7746 V × 10^(4/20) ≈ 1.228 V
V_out: the RMS output voltage, in volts (V)
P: the average power into the load, in watts (W)
R: the load resistance, 8 ohms (Ω)
V_sens: the input sensitivity: the input voltage that gives the rated maximum power, in volts (V)
P_max: the rated maximum power, here 100 W
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to
V: volts
W: watts
Ω: ohms
dB: decibel; dividing by 20 converts a voltage decibel figure back to a ratio
In words: 26 dB is a voltage gain of about 20, so a +4 dBu line signal comes out at about 24.5 V, which is 75 W into 8 Ω; you'd need about 1.42 V in to reach 100 W.
```

So an amp with 26 dB gain fed a +4 dBu signal gives about 24.5 V RMS: 75 W into 8 Ω. Gain and maximum output power are separate specifications. Higher power may require greater voltage swing, greater current capacity or both; different models may also have different gain. (26 dB is used here as an illustration: real amps range widely, and many quote sensitivity instead. Read the manual.)

## Key takeaways
- An amplifier supplies output voltage and the current required by its load within its limits.
- Gain and maximum clean output are different specifications.
- The simple voltage-squared power calculation assumes a resistive load.

## Further reading
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)


lessons.title: Amplifier classes and heat
lessons.summary: Amplifier class describes output-device conduction.
lessons.body:
## Amplifier classes

The **amplifier class** describes how the output transistors (or valves) conduct over the signal cycle. It's a broad guide to efficiency and linearity.

### Class A

The output devices conduct over the **whole** cycle, biased at a high standing current even with no signal.

- Very linear: no switching between devices, so no crossover distortion.
- **Inefficient**: the ideal sine-wave amplifier power-stage efficiency depends on topology: 25% for a simple resistively loaded stage, and up to 50% in suitable inductively coupled or push-pull output-stage designs. Real designs at typical listening levels are far lower. Most of the power drawn from the mains becomes heat, all the time.

### Class B and AB

A **push-pull pair**: one device handles the positive half of the waveform, the other the negative.

- Class B (each device conducts exactly half the cycle) has a maximum theoretical efficiency of **78.5%** (see below), but suffers **crossover distortion** where one device hands over to the other.
- **Class AB** adds a small bias current so both devices conduct briefly around the handover, removing most crossover distortion. Efficiency sits just below class B's. It's been the standard design for linear hi-fi and PA amplifiers for decades.

The class B figure comes from an ideal amplifier power stage swinging a full sine wave right up to its supply rails:

```formula
η = P_out / P_in
η_max = π / 4 ≈ 0.785 = 78.5 %
where
η: eta, efficiency: the fraction of the power drawn from the supply that reaches the speaker (no unit, often given as a percentage)
P_out: the audio power delivered to the speaker, in watts (W)
P_in: the power drawn from the power supply, in watts (W)
η_max: the best possible efficiency of an ideal class B stage at full sine-wave output
π: pi, about 3.14159
≈: approximately equal to
In words: even a perfect class B stage turns at least about a fifth of its supply power into heat at full output, and much more at lower levels.
```

### Class D

The output devices act as **switches**, fully on or fully off, switching far above the audio band (often at hundreds of kilohertz). The audio is encoded in the switching pattern (for example pulse-width modulation), and in conventional designs an **output low-pass filter** attenuates the switching carrier. Some low-power filterless designs instead use suitable modulation and the speaker’s electrical/mechanical filtering; external filtering and wiring constraints depend on the device.

- A perfect switch dissipates no power (either no voltage across it or no current through it), so class D is **very efficient**: over 80% is common and over 90% achievable with MOSFETs.
- Small, light, cool-running: the norm in powered speakers, PA amplifiers, car audio and portable devices.
- Trade-offs: the output filter's response can depend on the speaker load, the switching causes EMI that must be contained, and design quality varies. Good modern class D measures extremely well.

Efficiency decides how much heat the amp makes. Everything drawn from the supply that doesn't reach the speaker becomes heat:

```formula
P_in = P_out / η
P_heat = P_in − P_out
P_heat = 100 W / 0.25 − 100 W = 300 W
P_heat = 100 W / 0.90 − 100 W ≈ 11 W
where
P_in: the power drawn from the supply, in watts (W)
P_out: the audio power delivered to the speaker, here 100 W
η: eta, the efficiency as a fraction (0.25 means 25 %)
P_heat: the power wasted as heat in the amplifier power stage, in watts (W)
≈: approximately equal to
W: watts, the unit of power
In words: at 25 % efficiency you burn three watts of amplifier power-stage heat for every watt of electrical load power; at 90 % you burn about one ninth of a watt.
```

The same sum for four efficiencies, as Python:

```python
for name, eff in (("A, typical max", 0.25),
                  ("A, transformer", 0.50),
                  ("B, max", 0.785),
                  ("D, good", 0.90)):
    # Supply input minus electrical output.
    heat = 100 / eff - 100
    print(f"{name:<15} {heat:5.0f} W heat")
```

```
A, typical max    300 W heat
A, transformer    100 W heat
B, max             27 W heat
D, good            11 W heat
```

Illustrative amplifier power-stage heat to deliver 100 W at the assumed efficiencies. The class D value is a practical example; these figures exclude power-supply and other losses. Heat means heatsinks, fans, weight and power bills, which is why class D dominates where size and power matter.

## Key takeaways
- Amplifier class describes output-device conduction.
- Ideal class-A limits depend on topology; class B reaches about 78.5 percent at full sine output.
- Class D reduces amplifier power-stage losses through switching; total system losses still matter.

## Further reading
- [Class-D output filtering — Texas Instruments, SLAA701B](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/sloa119b/sloa119b.pdf)
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Class-A power-stage efficiency — ADI university course](https://wiki.analog.com/university/courses/engineering_discovery/lab_10)
- [Class-A resistive and transformer coupling limits — ACS College of Engineering, pages 65–67](https://www.acsce.edu.in/acsce/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Analog-Circuits-module-3.pdf)

lessons.title: Interpret amplifier power specifications
lessons.summary: Compare power ratings at stated load, bandwidth, distortion and test conditions.
lessons.body:
## Power ratings

- **Continuous (average) power**, often called **"RMS power"**, is the meaningful figure: the average power the amp can deliver continuously into a stated load, over a stated bandwidth, at a stated distortion. "RMS power" is a loose name: it's the average power calculated from RMS voltage and current, not the RMS of the power waveform.
- **Peak power.** For a sine wave, peak instantaneous power is **twice** the average. A "200 W peak" amp may be a 100 W continuous amp.
- **PMPO** ("peak music power output") has no reliable conversion to continuous power without a defined test method and conditions. Treat an unexplained PMPO number as unsuitable for comparison.

Where the factor of two for peak power comes from: a sine wave's instantaneous power swings between zero and a peak, and spends as long below the halfway line as above it.

```formula
p = V_pk^2 sin^2(2πft) / R
p_peak = V_pk^2 / R
P_avg = V_pk^2 / (2R) = V_rms^2 / R
V_rms = V_pk / √(2)
where
p: the instantaneous power at time t, in watts (W)
V_pk: the sine wave's peak voltage, in volts (V)
sin: the sine function; sin^2 (sine squared) swings between 0 and 1 and averages exactly 0.5
f: the frequency of the sine, in hertz (Hz)
t: time, in seconds (s)
π: pi, about 3.14159
R: the load resistance, in ohms (Ω)
p_peak: the highest instantaneous power, in watts (W)
P_avg: the average (continuous) power, in watts (W)
V_rms: the RMS voltage, the peak divided by √2 (about 0.707 of the peak)
√: square root
In words: for a sine into a resistor, the average power is half the peak instantaneous power, and it equals the RMS voltage squared over the resistance.
```

Example: a sine of 40 V peak into 8 Ω peaks at 1600 ÷ 8 = 200 W but averages 100 W, so "200 W peak" and "100 W continuous" can describe the same amp. This only holds for a steady sine into a resistive load.

A complete specification looks like: *"100 W continuous into 8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, at 0.1% THD"*. Missing conditions usually hide something, such as a rating taken at 10% distortion or at 1 kHz only.

## Key takeaways
- Compare power ratings at stated load, bandwidth, distortion and test conditions.
- Sine-wave instantaneous peak power is twice average into a resistor.
- A marketing peak label alone does not establish continuous output.

## Further reading
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)

lessons.title: Parallel loads and bridged outputs
lessons.summary: Lower impedance demands greater current at the same output voltage.
lessons.body:
## Load impedance and matching amp to speaker

A solid-state amp is a voltage source, so **lower impedance draws more current and more power**:

```formula
V_rms = √(PR)
V_rms = √(100 W × 8 Ω) ≈ 28.3 V
I_rms = 28.3 V / 8 Ω ≈ 3.5 A
P = (28.3 V)^2 / 4 Ω ≈ 200 W
I_rms = 28.3 V / 4 Ω ≈ 7.1 A
where
V_rms: the RMS output voltage, in volts (V)
P: the average power into the load, in watts (W)
R: the load resistance, in ohms (Ω)
I_rms: the RMS current, in amperes (A)
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to
V: volts
W: watts
Ω: ohms
A: amperes
In words: the voltage that gives 100 W into 8 Ω would push twice the current, and so twice the power, into 4 Ω.
```

That's why amps quote power at several loads ("100 W into 8 Ω, 160 W into 4 Ω"). In practice power doesn't quite double into half the impedance, because the supply sags and the output devices have current limits.

Matching rules of thumb:

- **Check the minimum load.** If an amp is rated for 4 Ω minimum, don't connect two 4 Ω speakers in parallel (2 Ω). Speakers' actual impedance dips below nominal (the loudspeaker-driver units), so nominal 4 Ω loads are already demanding.
- **Parallel speakers halve impedance** (two 8 Ω = 4 Ω); series doubles it.
- **Power headroom.** An amplifier’s clean capacity should accommodate the required peaks, but a higher rating can also destroy a driver. Avoid clipping and set gain and appropriate protection from the actual signal, driver limits and manufacturer’s guidance. Many manufacturers give a recommended amplifier power range; follow it.
- **Bridged (BTL) mode** drives one speaker from two channels in opposite polarity, doubling the voltage swing: in theory four times the power into the same load, but each channel sees half the load impedance, so bridging into 4 Ω asks each side to drive 2 Ω. Check the manual's bridged minimum load.

The parallel and bridged rules come from these relations (for resistive loads):

```formula
R_par = (R_1 R_2) / (R_1 + R_2)
R_par = (8 Ω × 8 Ω) / (8 Ω + 8 Ω) = 4 Ω
P_bridge = (2V)^2 / R = 4V^2 / R
R_ch = R / 2
where
R_par: the combined resistance of two loads in parallel, in ohms (Ω)
R_1: the first speaker's impedance, in ohms (Ω)
R_2: the second speaker's impedance, in ohms (Ω)
P_bridge: the power into the speaker in bridged mode, in watts (W)
V: the RMS voltage one channel can swing on its own, in volts (V)
R: the bridged speaker's impedance, in ohms (Ω)
R_ch: the load each channel effectively sees in bridged mode, in ohms (Ω)
Ω: ohms
In words: two equal speakers in parallel give half the impedance; bridging doubles the voltage, so in theory four times the power, but each channel then works as if it were driving half the speaker's impedance.
```

> [!tip] Valve amps are different
> Valve amps with output transformers *do* need the right load: running them with no speaker connected can damage the output transformer or valves. Always connect a speaker (or a proper load) before powering a valve guitar or hi-fi amp.

## Key takeaways
- Lower impedance demands greater current at the same output voltage.
- Two identical parallel speaker loads have half the impedance of one.
- Bridging doubles voltage swing ideally while each channel effectively drives half the load impedance.

## Further reading
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Example valve-amplifier load warning — Fender 65 Twin Reverb manual, rear panel](https://www.fmicassets.com/Damroot/Original/10001/021730_gamp_manual_all_revE.pdf)

questions.prompt: An amp rated for a 4 Ω minimum load drives one 8 Ω speaker. You add a second identical 8 Ω speaker in parallel on the same output. What does the amp now see?

options.text: 16 Ω, so the amp is under-loaded
options.explanation: Parallel loads reduce impedance; series would give 16 Ω.
Each speaker draws its own current, so the total load impedance halves.

options.text: 4 Ω nominal, and twice the current at the same output voltage
options.explanation: Correct for two identical impedance curves in parallel. Check the amplifier’s compatibility guidance for the combined load.
Two 8 Ω in parallel is 4 Ω, not 2 Ω (that's two 4 Ω in parallel).

questions.workedExample:
Two loads in parallel combine like this:

```formula
R_par = (R_1 R_2) / (R_1 + R_2)
R_par = (8 Ω × 8 Ω) / (8 Ω + 8 Ω)
R_par = 4 Ω
where
R_par: the combined impedance the amp sees, in ohms (Ω)
R_1: the first speaker's nominal impedance, 8 Ω
R_2: the second speaker's nominal impedance, 8 Ω
Ω: ohms
In words: two equal speakers in parallel present half the impedance of one.
```

At the same output voltage the current doubles. An amplifier’s nominal load rating is not necessarily a hard impedance floor at every frequency. Follow its load and wiring guidance; impedance magnitude and phase both matter.

questions.prompt: You bridge a two-channel amp (each channel rated 4 Ω minimum) to drive one speaker. What's the smallest speaker impedance you should use in bridged mode, and why?

options.text: 8 Ω, because each channel effectively sees half the speaker's impedance
options.explanation: Correct. An 8 Ω speaker bridged presents 4 Ω to each side, which is their minimum.

options.text: 2 Ω, because bridging halves the minimum load
options.explanation: Bridging halves the load each channel sees, so the minimum load goes *up*, not down.
In bridged mode each channel sees half of the speaker's impedance.

options.text: Any impedance: bridging removes load limits
options.explanation: Bridging makes the amp work harder, not easier.

questions.workedExample:
In bridged (BTL) mode the two channels drive the speaker in opposite polarity:

```formula
V_spk = 2V_ch
Z_ch = Z_spk / 2
Z_ch = 8 Ω / 2 = 4 Ω
where
V_spk: the voltage across the speaker, in volts (V)
V_ch: the voltage one channel swings on its own, in volts (V)
Z_ch: the load each channel effectively sees, in ohms (Ω)
Z_spk: the bridged speaker's impedance, in ohms (Ω)
Ω: ohms
In words: bridging doubles the voltage across the speaker, but each channel works as if it were driving half the speaker's impedance.
```

So with a 4 Ω per-channel minimum, use at least 8 Ω bridged. The manual normally states the bridged minimum load: follow it.

lessons.title: Understand damping factor and cable loss
lessons.summary: Damping factor compares load impedance with amplifier source impedance.
lessons.body:
## Damping factor

**Damping factor** is the ratio of the speaker's nominal impedance to the amp's **output impedance**:

```formula
DF = Z_load / Z_out
DF = 8 Ω / 0.01 Ω = 800
where
DF: damping factor, a plain ratio (no unit); bigger means the amp holds the driver more firmly
Z_load: the speaker's nominal impedance, in ohms (Ω)
Z_out: the amplifier's output impedance, in ohms (Ω); typically a few hundredths of an ohm for a solid-state amp
Ω: ohms
In words: damping factor says how many times smaller the amp's own internal impedance is than the speaker's.
```

So an amp with 0.01 Ω output impedance into 8 Ω has a damping factor of 800. A low output impedance lets the amp's back-EMF path control the driver's motion near resonance (the loudspeaker-driver units: the driver is also a generator). Above a modest value (tens) the audible benefit is small, because the **speaker cable** and the driver's own voice-coil resistance dominate. The cable's resistance adds to the amp's output impedance:

```formula
R_c = (ρL_w) / A_w
R_c = (1.68 × 10^{-8} Ω·m × 20 m)
      / (1.5 × 10^{-6} m^2)
R_c ≈ 0.224 Ω
DF_spk = Z_load / (Z_out + R_c)
DF_spk = 8 Ω / (0.01 Ω + 0.224 Ω) ≈ 34
where
R_c: the resistance of the speaker cable (both conductors), in ohms (Ω)
ρ: rho, the resistivity of the conductor material, in ohm-metres (Ω·m); assume 1.68 × 10^−8 Ω·m for this illustrative copper-wire calculation; actual resistivity depends on material and temperature
L_w: the total length of conductor the current flows through (out and back), in metres (m): 20 m for a 10 m cable
A_w: the cross-sectional area of each conductor, in square metres (m^2); 1.5 mm² is 1.5 × 10^−6 m^2
DF_spk: the damping factor seen at the speaker, including the cable (no unit)
Z_load: the speaker's nominal impedance, 8 ohms (Ω)
Z_out: the amplifier's output impedance, 0.01 Ω
m: metres
Ω: ohms, the unit of resistance
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a long, thin cable adds far more resistance than a good amp's amplifier power stage, so it sets the real damping factor.
```

Ten metres of 1.5 mm² cable (20 m of conductor) turns DF 800 into about 34. Use thicker cable for long runs, and treat very high DF claims as marketing.

## Key takeaways
- Damping factor compares load impedance with amplifier source impedance.
- Both cable conductors contribute resistance.
- Long thin cable can dominate the amplifier’s own output resistance.

## Further reading
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)

options.explanation: Correct. The 20 m of conductor is about 0.224 Ω, which swamps the amp's 0.01 Ω: 8 Ω ÷ 0.234 Ω ≈ 34.
That ignores the cable, which dominates.
That's ten times too low; check the cable resistance calculation.
That counts only 10 m of conductor (0.112 Ω): 8 / (0.01 + 0.112) ≈ 66. The current flows out and back, so it passes through 20 m of wire.

```formula
Z_out: the amp's output impedance, 0.01 Ω
Ω: ohms

In words: the cable adds over twenty times the amp's own output impedance, so the damping factor at the speaker falls from 800 to about 34.
```

Thicker or shorter cable helps more than a higher-DF amp.

lessons.title: How clipping changes driver power
lessons.summary: At equal peak voltage, a square wave dissipates twice a sine’s average power into a resistor.
lessons.body:
## Clipping and why it can kill tweeters

An amplifier can't output more voltage than its supply rails allow. Ask for more and the output shows **clipping**: the waveform's peaks are flattened.

```diagram
  clean:      /\      /\
             /  \    /  \
            /    \  /    \
  clipped:   ____      ____
            /    \    /    \
           /      \__/      \
```

Why that's dangerous for **tweeters**:

- **More average power.** A sine wave clipped hard towards a square wave carries up to **twice** the average power of the clean sine with the same peak voltage (worked out below).
- **High-frequency harmonics.** A square wave contains odd harmonics at 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental's amplitude (about −9.5, −14 and −16.9 dB, worked out below). Clip a loud bass or middle-frequency note and those harmonics land in the tweeter's band. The crossover passes them straight to a driver that normally receives only a small fraction of the total power, and its small voice coil overheats.

A square wave sits at its peak voltage all the time, while a sine only touches its peak briefly:

```formula
P_sine = V_pk^2 / (2R)
P_square = V_pk^2 / R = 2P_sine
L_n = 20 log_10(1 / n)
L_3 = 20 log_10(1/3) ≈ −9.5 dB
L_5 = 20 log_10(1/5) ≈ −14 dB
L_7 = 20 log_10(1/7) ≈ −16.9 dB
where
P_sine: the average power of a clean sine wave, in watts (W)
P_square: the average power of a square wave with the same peak voltage, in watts (W)
V_pk: the peak voltage, in volts (V)
R: the load resistance, in ohms (Ω)
L_n: the level of the nth harmonic relative to the square wave's fundamental, in decibels (dB)
n: the harmonic number (3, 5, 7 ...): the multiple of the fundamental frequency; a square wave has only odd ones
L_3: the 3rd harmonic's level
L_5: the 5th harmonic's level
L_7: the 7th harmonic's level
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: hard clipping can double the average power at the same peak voltage, and pushes strong harmonics at three, five and seven times the note's frequency into the tweeter's range.
```

For example, a 1.5 kHz note clipped to a square wave puts its 3rd harmonic at 4.5 kHz, its 5th at 7.5 kHz and its 7th at 10.5 kHz: all above a typical 2–3 kHz crossover.

So sustained clipping can overheat a tweeter; a larger clean amplifier can also damage it if level, spectrum or duration exceeds its limits. Watch for clip indicators, leave headroom, and use limiters in PA systems.

## Key takeaways
- At equal peak voltage, a square wave dissipates twice a sine’s average power into a resistor.
- Symmetric clipping adds odd harmonics.
- Driver damage depends on signal spectrum, duration, filtering and actual limits.

## Further reading
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)

The waveform shape changes the average power even at the same peak.
Even a full square wave only doubles it.

Compare average powers at the same peak voltage, then the harmonic levels:

```formula
A_1 = (4 / π)V_pk ≈ 1.273V_pk

L_5 = 20 log_10(1/5) ≈ −14 dB
L_7 = 20 log_10(1/7) ≈ −16.9 dB
where
P_sine: the average power of the clean sine, in watts (W)
P_square: the average power of the square wave, in watts (W)
V_pk: the shared peak voltage, in volts (V)
A_1: the square wave's fundamental peak amplitude, in volts (V)
π: pi, about 3.14159
R: the load resistance, in ohms (Ω)
L_n: the nth harmonic's level relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB)
n: the harmonic number (odd only for a square wave: 3, 5, 7 ...)
L_3: the 3rd harmonic's level
L_5: the 5th harmonic's level
L_7: the 7th harmonic's level
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
In words: hard clipping doubles the average power and adds strong odd harmonics at 3, 5 and 7 times the note's frequency.
```

Those harmonics of a middle-frequency note fall in the tweeter's band, so the tweeter suddenly receives far more power than normal music would send it.

lessons.title: Match a headphone output to its load
lessons.summary: Required voltage and current depend on headphone impedance and sensitivity.
lessons.body:
## headphone drive stages

Headphones need far less power than speakers, but they vary enormously in impedance (roughly 16 Ω to several hundred ohms) and sensitivity:

- **Low-impedance headphones** need current; **high-impedance** ones need voltage. 10 mW is 0.57 V RMS into 32 Ω but 1.73 V RMS into 300 Ω (worked out below).
- A headphone drive stage should have a **low output impedance**, much lower than the headphones'. A high output impedance forms a divider with the headphones' frequency-varying impedance and changes their frequency response.
- Laptop and phone outputs can struggle with some headphones; compare required voltage/current and sensitivity with the source’s rated capabilities. A suitable dedicated amp or interface can help.

The voltage needed for a given power comes from rearranging the power formula:

```formula
V_rms = √(PR)
V_rms = √(0.01 W × 32 Ω) ≈ 0.57 V
V_rms = √(0.01 W × 300 Ω) ≈ 1.73 V
where
V_rms: the RMS voltage the amp must supply, in volts (V)
P: the power wanted in the headphones, here 10 milliwatts (mW) = 0.01 watts (W)
R: the headphones' impedance, treated as a resistance, in ohms (Ω)
√: square root
≈: approximately equal to
V: volts
W: watts
Ω: ohms
In words: the same power needs about three times the voltage into 300 Ω headphones as into 32 Ω ones, but far less current.
```

The output impedance and the headphones form a voltage divider:

```formula
V_hp = V_src Z_hp / (Z_out + Z_hp)
V_hp = V_src × 32 Ω / (10 Ω + 32 Ω)
V_hp ≈ 0.76V_src  (≈ −2.4 dB)
V_hp = V_src × 64 Ω / (10 Ω + 64 Ω)
V_hp ≈ 0.86V_src  (≈ −1.3 dB)
where
V_hp: the voltage that actually reaches the headphones, in volts (V)
V_src: the voltage the amp generates internally, before its own output impedance, in volts (V)
Z_hp: the headphones' impedance at a given frequency, in ohms (Ω)
Z_out: the amplifier's output impedance, in ohms (Ω)
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibel, the unit of level ratio
Ω: ohms
In words: the bigger the amp's output impedance compared with the headphones', the more voltage is lost, and if the headphone impedance changes with frequency, so does the loss.
```

In this illustrative example, 32 Ω headphones whose impedance rises to 64 Ω at their resonance, driven from a 10 Ω output, get about 1.1 dB more level at the resonance than elsewhere. From a 1 Ω output the difference would be well under 0.3 dB. (This treats the impedances as plain resistances; real ones also have phase.)

> [!warning] Ears first
> Headphone amps can produce hearing-damaging levels very easily (the hearing units). Turn the level down before plugging in or switching sources.

> [!note] Verification gap
> The earlier historical headphone-output standard recommendation and broad output-impedance range are omitted because their original standard text and representative measurement basis were not reliably verified. Use the actual product specifications.

## Key takeaways
- Required voltage and current depend on headphone impedance and sensitivity.
- Source and load impedances form a voltage divider.
- A varying load can colour frequency response when source impedance is significant.

## Further reading
- [Headphone amplifier load and output impedance — Texas Instruments, TIDUAW1](https://www.ti.com/lit/ug/tiduaw1/tiduaw1.pdf)
- [Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown](https://www.crownaudio.com/en-US/faq_categories/1)
- [Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which are good reasons for a headphone drive stage to have a low output impedance? Select all that apply.

options.text: A low output impedance stops the headphones drawing any current
options.explanation: The headphones still draw current; low output impedance just means little is lost inside the amp.

options.text: It keeps electrical control of the drivers, much as damping factor does for speakers
options.explanation: Correct. The same principle applies at smaller scale.

options.text: Headphone impedance varies with frequency, so a high source impedance forms a frequency-dependent divider that colours the sound
options.explanation: Correct for headphones with frequency-varying impedance: the divider ratio then changes with frequency.

options.text: Low-impedance headphones need current, which a high source impedance wastes as voltage drop
options.explanation: Correct. A significant source impedance consumes some of the available voltage; most is lost there only if it exceeds the load impedance.

questions.workedExample:
A headphone drive stage and the headphones form a voltage divider:

```formula
V_hp = V_src Z_hp / (Z_out + Z_hp)
V_hp = V_src × 32 Ω / (10 Ω + 32 Ω)
V_hp ≈ 0.76V_src
where
V_hp: the voltage that reaches the headphones, in volts (V)
V_src: the voltage the amp generates internally, in volts (V)
Z_hp: the headphones' impedance at a given frequency, in ohms (Ω)
Z_out: the amp's output impedance, in ohms (Ω)
≈: approximately equal to
Ω: ohms
In words: the headphones get the fraction Z_hp ÷ (Z_out + Z_hp) of the voltage; if Z_out is tiny, that fraction stays near 1 whatever the headphones' impedance does.
```

In this illustrative example a 10 Ω output loses about a quarter of the voltage into 32 Ω, and the loss changes wherever the headphone impedance changes with frequency. If Z_out is much smaller than Z_hp at every frequency, the divider stays near 1 and flat. Check the actual output-impedance and headphone-load curves.

lessons.title: Follow a console channel and its sends
lessons.summary: Each system stage has noise and overload limits.
lessons.body:
Up to now we've looked at parts: microphones, drivers, boxes, crossovers, amplifiers. A **sound system** connects them so that a source (your synth, a voice, a drum) reaches listeners at the right level, with the right balance and without noise, distortion or feedback. Whether it's a desk in your bedroom or a festival PA, the principles are the same.

## The chain

```flow
Source: synth, mic or instrument
DI box or mic: to balanced mic/line level
Console: preamp gain, EQ, routing, mix
Processing: system EQ, delay, crossover
Power amplifiers (or powered speakers)
Loudspeakers
Room and listeners
```

Every stage has a **noise floor** below the signal and a **clipping point** above it. The job is to keep the signal comfortably between them at every stage.

## The mixing console

A console (mixer, desk) combines many inputs into a few outputs, with independent control over each. Digital consoles and DAWs (Ableton's mixer included) copy the analogue layout, so learning one teaches you the others.

### The channel strip

Signal flows from top to bottom of a typical channel:

1. **Input and preamp gain (trim).** Brings mic or line level up to the console's internal operating level. This is the most important control on the desk for noise and headroom. Phantom power and a pad switch usually live here.
2. **High-pass filter.** Removes rumble and handling noise below the useful range of the source. Engage it only where removing those frequencies suits the source and the intended sound.
3. **Insert point.** A send and return that loops the channel's signal out to an external processor (a compressor, say) and back, in series.
4. **EQ.** Shelving and parametric bands for tone and to make room for other sources.
5. **Dynamics processing** (on many digital desks): gate and compressor.
6. **Aux sends.** Copies of the channel at an adjustable level to separate **aux buses**, used for monitor mixes and effects.
   - **Pre-fader** sends ignore the channel fader: right for **monitor mixes**, so the front-of-house engineer's fader moves don't change what the performer hears.
   - **Post-fader** sends follow the fader: right for effects like reverb, so the wet signal fades with the dry.
7. **Panning** places the signal in the stereo bus.
8. **Fader** sets the channel's level in the mix.
9. **Signal routing** assigns the channel to the main mix and/or **subgroups**.

### Buses and subgroups

A **mix bus** is any point where signals are summed. The main L/R mix is a bus; so are aux sends and subgroups.

- **Subgroups** sum related channels (all drums, all backing vocals) to one fader, so you can ride a whole section, or compress it together, with one control.
- **VCA or DCA groups** (on many consoles) are a variation: one fader remotely controls the faders of its member channels without summing audio.

## Key takeaways
- Each system stage has noise and overload limits.
- Pre-fader sends can keep monitor mixes independent of channel fader moves.
- Subgroups sum audio; VCA and DCA groups control channel gains.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: Which kind of aux send should feed a performer's monitor wedge, and why?

options.text: Pre-fader, so the monitor mix is independent of the channel fader
options.explanation: Correct. Monitor mixes use pre-fader sends.

options.text: Post-fader, so monitors follow the front-of-house mix
options.explanation: Then every FOH fader move would change what the performer hears, which is distracting and can cause feedback.
Inserts loop the channel through a processor in series; they're not mix sends.
That's the audience mix, not a separate monitor mix.

questions.workedExample:
- **Pre-fader**: taps the signal before the channel fader. Used for monitors.
- **Post-fader**: follows the fader. Used for effects (reverb, delay) so wet and dry stay balanced.

The FOH engineer can then mix freely without changing the stage sound.

questions.prompt: You put a reverb on vocals using an aux send. Which send type should it be, and why?

options.text: Post-fader, so the reverb level follows the vocal fader
options.explanation: Correct. The wet/dry balance stays constant as you ride the vocal.

options.text: Pre-fader, so the reverb stays at a constant level
options.explanation: Then pulling the vocal fader down leaves the reverb behind on its own.

options.text: An insert, so the reverb replaces the dry signal
options.explanation: Inserts are in series; reverb is usually blended in parallel via a send.
It matters whenever you move the fader.

lessons.title: Plan gain across the whole system
lessons.summary: Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom.
lessons.body:
## Gain staging across the system

Module 1 covered gain staging inside a digital synth. In a system, the same idea applies at every box:

1. **Set the preamp gain first**, with the performer at their loudest. Aim for healthy levels with headroom to spare: on a digital desk, nominal levels around −18 to −20 dBFS leave room for peaks (module 1); on an analogue desk, follow its meter calibration and overload-warning guidance, allowing headroom for unexpectedly loud peaks rather than deliberately clipping. The system's signal-to-noise ratio is largely fixed here: noise added at the mic preamp is amplified by everything after it.
2. **Keep faders near their unity (0 dB) mark** for normal levels, so there's travel in both directions.
3. **Set outboard gear to unity** where possible, passing the full signal without clipping.
4. **Set amplifier input sensitivity** as part of the system’s gain and protection plan. One approach maps the maximum clean system output to the required amplifier output; that output must also respect speaker and audience limits. Amp input controls are attenuators that set sensitivity, not "power" controls.

To work out how much preamp gain a mic needs, start from its sensitivity (its output voltage at a reference sound pressure of 1 pascal, which is 94 dB SPL), add however far the real source is above that reference, convert to dBu, and subtract from the level the console wants. Example: an SM58 (sensitivity −56.0 dBV/Pa) picks up a singer at 104 dB SPL, which is 10 dB above 1 Pa:

```formula
V_v = S + (L_p − 94)
V_v = −56.0 + (104 − 94) = −46.0 dBV
V_u = V_v + 20 log_10(1 / 0.7746)
V_u ≈ −46.0 + 2.2 = −43.8 dBu
G = L_nom − V_u
G = 4 − (−43.8) = 47.8 dB
where
V_v: the mic's output level, in dBV (decibels relative to 1 volt)
S: the mic's sensitivity, in dBV per pascal (dBV/Pa): its output at 94 dB SPL; −56.0 dBV/Pa for an SM58, about 1.6 millivolts
L_p: the sound pressure level at the mic, in dB SPL; here 104 dB SPL
94: the sound pressure level of 1 pascal (Pa), in dB SPL: the reference at which sensitivity is measured
V_u: the same output level expressed in dBu (decibels relative to 0.7746 volts)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number
0.7746: the voltage used as the dBu reference, 0.7746 volts (V); 20 × log_10(1 / 0.7746) ≈ 2.2 dB is the fixed gap between dBV and dBu
G: the preamp gain needed, in decibels (dB)
L_nom: the console's nominal operating level, here +4 dBu
dB: decibels, a logarithmic ratio; every 20 dB is a factor of 10 in voltage
dBV: decibels relative to 1 volt
dBu: decibels relative to 0.7746 volts
In words: the singer is 10 dB louder than the sensitivity reference, so the mic puts out 10 dB more than its rated sensitivity; the preamp must make up the gap between that and the console's +4 dBu working level.
```

About 48 dB of preamp gain. A condenser about 25 dB more sensitive (the microphone units) would need only around 23 dB.

> [!warning] Two common mistakes
> - Low preamp gain "made up" with faders pushed to the top: the console's noise is amplified as much as the signal.
> - Preamp gain set with the singer warming up quietly: the first chorus clips the input, and no fader can undo clipping that happened upstream.

## Key takeaways
- Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom.
- A fader cannot repair clipping at an earlier stage.
- Coordinate amplifier sensitivity, limiter settings and speaker and audience limits.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: On a console channel, which control most affects the channel's noise and headroom?

options.explanation: The fader comes after the preamp; it can't fix a signal that's too quiet or clipped at the input.
Pan only distributes the signal between left and right.
Sends only affect the copies sent to aux buses.
Correct. It sets the level everything after it works with; noise added here is amplified by everything downstream.

```formula
V_u ≈ −46.0 + 2.2 = −43.8 dBu
G = L_nom − V_u
G = 4 − (−43.8) ≈ 47.8 dB
where
V_v: the mic's output level, in dBV (decibels relative to 1 volt)
S: the mic's sensitivity, −56.0 dBV per pascal (dBV/Pa) for an SM58
L_p: the sound pressure level at the mic, 104 dB SPL
94: the level of 1 pascal (Pa), in dB SPL: the sensitivity reference
V_u: the mic's output level in dBu (decibels relative to 0.7746 volts)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
0.7746: the voltage used as the dBu reference, in volts (V); the 20 × log_10(1 / 0.7746) term is about 2.2 dB
G: the preamp gain needed, in decibels (dB)
L_nom: the target nominal level, +4 dBu

In words: the singer is 10 dB above the reference, so the mic gives −46.0 dBV (−43.8 dBu), and the preamp must add about 48 dB.
```

questions.prompt: The console has a maximum clean sine-wave output of +18 dBu RMS. The power amp reaches its rated maximum clean sine output at +5.1 dBu RMS with input attenuation at zero. Assume no limiter. How do these gain limits compare?

options.text: None: more headroom at the console is always better
options.explanation: The issue is the amp: it reaches full power long before the console approaches its own limit.

options.text: The amplifier reaches its clean-output limit about 13 dB before the console reaches its own limit
options.explanation: Correct. About 13 dB of input attenuation would align those stated limits; the actual system may need a lower target output and suitable protection.

options.text: The speakers will be too quiet
options.explanation: They'll be loud; the problem is clipping and tweeter risk.

options.text: The console will clip before the amp
options.explanation: The console has about 13 dB more range than the amp needs.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the two clean-output limits in the same unit (dBu):

```formula
H = L_con − L_amp
H = 18 − 5.1 = 12.9 dB
where
H: how far the console can go above the level that drives the amp to full clean power, in decibels (dB)
L_con: the console's maximum clean output, +18 dBu RMS
L_amp: the input level that drives the amp to rated maximum clean output, +5.1 dBu RMS
dB: decibels
In words: the amp runs out of clean power about 13 dB before the console does.
```

About 13 dB of amplifier input attenuation aligns these clean sine-wave limits. Music peak metering, limiter thresholds, speaker limits and audience exposure still need separate consideration.

lessons.title: Connect an instrument through a DI
lessons.summary: A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input.
lessons.body:
## DI boxes

A **DI (direct input) box** connects an instrument or line-level source to a console's balanced **mic input**:

- It accepts an instrument or line-level signal and provides a **low-impedance, balanced, mic-level** output. Passive guitar pickups often need a high input impedance; synth and keyboard line outputs are usually low impedance and may already be balanced. Choose the DI or direct line connection to suit both devices.
- That lets the signal travel down a long multicore to the desk with good noise rejection (module 5's balanced lines).
- Most DIs have a **ground lift** switch to break a ground loop between stage gear and the desk's ground (module 3), and many have a pad.

Two types:

- **Passive DIs** use a transformer. No power needed; robust; the transformer gives galvanic isolation.
- **Active DIs** use a buffer amplifier, powered by phantom power or a battery. They load high-impedance sources (like passive guitar pickups) very lightly.

For your synth on a stage, a DI is usually the right way into a PA, with the synth's output at line level into the DI's input (use its pad if needed).

## Key takeaways
- A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input.
- Select its input impedance and pad for the actual source.
- A compatible balanced line connection may remove the need for a DI.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: What does a DI box do when you plug your synth into a stage multicore?

options.explanation: DI stands for direct input (or inject), not digital interface.
DI boxes don't add effects.

options.text: Provides a balanced, low-impedance mic-level signal compatible with the console input
options.explanation: Correct. That suits long balanced cable runs to the desk.
Active DIs take phantom power for themselves; they don't power the instrument.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check the synth’s output level and whether it is balanced.
2. A suitable DI accepts its instrument/line signal and delivers balanced mic level for a mic input.
3. Use the appropriate pad and ground-lift facilities if needed. A compatible balanced line input may not require a DI.

lessons.title: Audience coverage and delay alignment
lessons.summary: main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs.
lessons.body:
## PA design

A typical live PA has several systems, each with its own job:

- **main speakers (front of house).** Left/right or mono speakers covering the audience, flown or on stands. Larger venues use **line arrays**: vertical columns of boxes that control vertical coverage and lose level more slowly with distance over part of their range.
- **Subwoofers.** Below about 80–120 Hz. Usually on the ground. Several subs can be arranged (end-fire, cardioid, arc) to steer low frequencies away from the stage.
- **Stage monitor loudspeakers.** What performers hear: **floor wedges** aimed up at each performer, side fills, or **in-ear monitors (IEMs)**. Fed from **pre-fader aux** mixes.
- **Front fills.** Small speakers along the stage lip for the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage.
- **Delay speakers.** Further back in large venues, where the main speakers have lost too much level.

### Delay speakers, worked

At a chosen listener position, compare the path from the main speaker with the path from the delay speaker. Sound from the main speakers has further to travel, so without an electronic delay the delay speaker's copy would arrive first and pull the sound image towards it. The delay to dial in is the extra travel time, plus any difference in processing latency between the two paths:

```formula
D = d_main − d_delay
t_align = D / c + t_lat
t_align = 40 m / (343 m/s) + 0
t_align ≈ 0.117 s = 117 ms
where
D: the path difference, in metres (m): how much further the listener is from the main speaker than from the delay speaker
d_main: the distance from the main speaker to the chosen listener position, in metres (m)
d_delay: the distance from the delay speaker to the same listener position, in metres (m)
t_align: the electronic delay to apply to the delay speaker so the two arrivals line up, in seconds (s)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
t_lat: main-path processing latency minus delay-speaker-path processing latency, in seconds (s); taken as 0 here. A negative total delay requires changing the other path or the design
m: metres
m/s: metres per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: delay the delay speaker by the time sound takes to cover the extra distance from the main speakers, so both arrive together at the listener.
```

If the main speakers path is **40 m longer**, about 117 ms aligns arrivals in this simplified example. It only holds exactly at the chosen position; listeners nearer or further away see a different path difference. A designer may choose an additional offset to favour the main speakers as the first arrival, but no universal 10–20 ms setting guarantees fusion or stage localisation. Those depend on signal, relative level, geometry and reflections; measure and listen throughout the overlap region. Exact universal precedence offsets are absent because reliable evidence for such a guarantee was not established.

## Studio vs live

| | Studio | Live |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Accurate monitoring | Coverage, level |
| Listeners | One position | Whole audience |
| Speakers | Near-field monitors | PA, subs, wedges |
| Feedback | Rarely an issue | Constant concern |
| Room | Treated (the room-acoustics units) | Take what you get |

In a studio the monitors must tell the truth, so you can make decisions that translate to other systems. In a live system the goal is even, intelligible, sufficiently loud coverage for everyone, with controlled exposure and compliance with applicable venue limits. WHO’s 100 dB LAeq,15 min ceiling is one part of its safe-listening venue standard, not a guarantee that a whole event is safe at that level (the hearing units).

## Key takeaways
- main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs.
- Align a fill using acoustic-path and processing-latency differences.
- Verify timing, localisation, overlap and exposure throughout the audience area.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: At the reference listener, the main-speaker path is 40 m longer than the delay-speaker path. Ignore electronic latency differences and take the speed of sound as 343 m/s. If the designer deliberately chooses an extra 10–20 ms after arrival alignment, what electronic delay follows?

options.explanation: About 117 ms aligns the arrivals under the stated assumptions; it excludes the offset expressly chosen in this question.
That's only the precedence offset, missing the travel time.
Correct: 116.6 + 10 to 20 gives 126.6–136.6 ms. The offset is a stated design choice, not a universal precedence rule.

options.text: No delay; just keep it quieter than the main speakers
options.explanation: With the specified path difference, zero electronic delay makes the delay speaker arrive much earlier. Perceived echo/localisation depends on signal and level.

questions.workedExample:
First find the time sound takes to cover the extra 40 m, then add the chosen offset.

```formula
t_path = D / c
t_path = 40 m / (343 m/s)
t_path ≈ 0.1166 s ≈ 116.6 ms
t = t_path + t_off
t_min ≈ 116.6 ms + 10 ms ≈ 127 ms
t_max ≈ 116.6 ms + 20 ms ≈ 137 ms
where
t_path: the extra travel time from the main speakers, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
D: the path difference, 40 metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, 343 metres per second (m/s)
t: the total electronic delay for the delay speaker, in milliseconds (ms)
t_off: the designer's chosen extra offset, somewhere between 10 and 20 milliseconds (ms)
t_min: the total delay with the smallest offset (10 ms), in milliseconds (ms)
t_max: the total delay with the largest offset (20 ms), in milliseconds (ms)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
m: metres
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: align the arrivals (about 117 ms), then add the chosen 10–20 ms, giving about 127–137 ms.
```

This arithmetic does not establish that the offset is suitable: verify fusion, localisation and interference across the listening area.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PA system components are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Subwoofer arrays can be arranged (for example cardioid or end-fire) to reduce low-frequency energy on stage
options.explanation: Correct. Several subs with suitable spacing and delay steer bass.

options.text: Monitor wedges are normally fed from the main L/R mix
options.explanation: Monitors get separate pre-fader aux mixes tailored to each performer.

options.text: Front fills cover the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage
options.explanation: Correct.

options.text: Line arrays control vertical coverage and lose level more slowly with distance over part of their range
options.explanation: Correct. Over part of their range they behave more like a line than a point source.

questions.workedExample:
Typical PA components:

- main speakers (point source or line array) for the audience.
- Subs for below ~80–120 Hz, sometimes in steerable arrays.
- Front fills for the front rows.
- Delays for the back of large venues.
- Monitors (wedges, side fills, IEMs) from aux mixes.

lessons.title: Improve gain before acoustic feedback
lessons.summary: Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain.
lessons.body:
## Acoustic feedback

**Acoustic feedback** happens when the sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone, is amplified, comes out of the speaker louder, and so on. Sustained feedback can develop where the **loop gain** magnitude reaches or exceeds one (0 dB) and the phase reinforces the circulating signal. The precise stability and onset depend on the whole loop. Feedback develops at a frequency where both loop magnitude and reinforcing phase conditions are met: often a peak in a speaker's or mic's response, or a room resonance.

How to get more **gain before feedback**:

1. **Get the mic close to the source.** Halving the source-to-mic distance gives about 6 dB more source level at the mic (inverse square law), so 6 dB less gain is needed.
2. **Keep speakers away from mics**, and put main speakers in front of the mic line.
3. **Use directional mics and their nulls.** Put wedges in the null of the mic's pattern (the microphone units).
4. **Fewer open mics.** In the usual approximate potential-acoustic-gain model, doubling similarly coupled **open microphones (NOM)** costs about 3 dB; actual loop paths can differ. Mute what isn't in use.
5. **EQ.** "Ringing out" the system: raise gain until it starts to ring, identify the frequency, and cut it with a narrow EQ band. Automatic notch-based feedback suppressors do this live, but they typically add only a few dB of margin.
6. **In-ear monitors** remove the wedge-to-mic path when wedges are actually removed from that mix.

The 6 dB figure in step 1 comes from the inverse square law. For a small source in open air, the level change when you move from one distance to another is:

```formula
L_d = 20 log_10(r_1 / r_2)
L_d = 20 log_10(0.10 / 0.05)
L_d ≈ 20 × 0.301 ≈ 6.0 dB
where
L_d: how much louder the source is at the new distance, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number
r_1: the old source-to-mic distance, in metres (m); here 10 cm = 0.10 m
r_2: the new, closer distance, in metres (m); here 5 cm = 0.05 m
dB: decibels, a logarithmic ratio of levels
In words: every halving of the distance gives about 6 dB more level at the mic, so the channel needs 6 dB less gain for the same output.
```

Very close to a directional mic, the proximity effect also boosts the bass, and a voice is not a point source, so treat 6 dB per halving as a guide.

The 3 dB figure in step 4 comes from the potential acoustic gain (PAG) model, where open mics that each pick up the PA about equally add up as uncorrelated signals:

```formula
G_NOM = 10 log_10(N_1 / N_2)
G_NOM = 10 log_10(4 / 2)
G_NOM ≈ 10 × 0.301 ≈ 3.0 dB
where
G_NOM: the gain before feedback you get back by reducing the number of open microphones, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
N_1: the number of open microphones (NOM) before muting
N_2: the number of open microphones after muting
dB: decibels
NOM: number of open microphones
In words: each halving of the number of open mics buys back about 3 dB of gain before feedback; each doubling costs about 3 dB.
```

It's 10 rather than 20 because the PAG approximation treats the similarly coupled microphone signals as uncorrelated on average. They are summed as voltages physically; their mean-square contributions add under that modelling assumption. Real stages differ: mics nearer a wedge contribute more than the model assumes.

## Key takeaways
- Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain.
- Improve source pickup while reducing loudspeaker pickup at microphones.
- The open-microphone count rule is an approximation; geometry and individual coupling matter.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

In the potential acoustic gain (PAG) model, open mics add their pickup of the PA as powers, so the change uses 10 × log₁₀ of the ratio of open-mic counts.

```formula
G_NOM = 10 log_10(N_1 / N_2)

G_NOM = 10 log_10(4)
```

lessons.title: Calculate rectangular-room mode frequencies
lessons.summary: Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families.
lessons.body:
Put the best monitors in the world in an untreated, square, bare-walled room and you'll hear the room as much as the speakers. Below a few hundred hertz, a small room's response at your listening position can swing by 20 dB or more between neighbouring frequencies. Mix there and you'll correct for problems that only exist in your room, and the mix will sound wrong everywhere else.

This lesson is about understanding what a room does, then placing monitors and treatment so you can trust what you hear.

## Room modes

Between two parallel walls, a sound wave reflects back and forth. At frequencies where a whole number of half-wavelengths fits exactly between the walls, the reflections reinforce each other into a **standing wave**: a **room mode** (or resonance).

To find those frequencies, start from the fact that one half-wavelength, two half-wavelengths, three and so on must fit the gap exactly, then use the link between wavelength, frequency and the speed of sound:

```formula
L = nλ / 2
λ = c / f_n
f_n = nc / (2L)
where
f_n: the frequency of the nth mode between this pair of walls, in hertz (Hz)
n: the mode number, a whole number 1, 2, 3 …; mode 1 is the lowest (fundamental), mode 2 is twice its frequency, and so on
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
L: the distance between the two parallel walls, in metres (m)
λ: lambda, the wavelength of the sound, in metres (m): the distance one cycle of the wave covers in air
In words: the lowest mode is the frequency whose half-wavelength exactly spans the gap between the walls, and every whole-number multiple of it is a mode too. The bigger the room, the lower the modes.
```

For two walls 5.0 m apart, the first mode is 343 ÷ (2 × 5.0) = 34.3 Hz, the second 68.6 Hz and the third 102.9 Hz. The formula assumes rigid, parallel, flat walls; real walls flex and absorb a little, which damps and slightly shifts the modes.

Those are **axial modes**: between one pair of surfaces. They usually carry the most energy and have the greatest influence on the low-frequency response. **Tangential modes** involve two pairs of surfaces and **oblique modes** all three. For a rectangular (shoebox) room, one formula covers all three kinds (exclude the all-zero mode-number combination, which is static pressure rather than an oscillating acoustic mode):

```formula
f = (c / 2) √((n_x / L_x)^2
    + (n_y / L_y)^2 + (n_z / L_z)^2)
where
f: the frequency of the mode, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
√: the square root of everything inside the brackets that follow it
n_x: the mode number along the length: 0, 1, 2 … (0 means the mode doesn't involve that pair of walls)
n_y: the mode number along the width: 0, 1, 2 …
n_z: the mode number along the height: 0, 1, 2 …
L_x: the room's length, in metres (m)
L_y: the room's width, in metres (m)
L_z: the room's height, in metres (m)
In words: each mode is labelled by three whole numbers saying how many half-wavelengths it has along each dimension. One non-zero number gives an axial mode, two a tangential mode, three an oblique mode.
```

When only one mode number is non-zero this reduces to the axial formula above. A tangential example, the (1, 1, 0) mode of a room with a 5.0 × 3.6 m floor plan:

```formula
f = (343 / 2) √((1 / 5.0)^2
    + (1 / 3.6)^2)
f ≈ 171.5 √(0.040 + 0.077)
f ≈ 171.5 × 0.342 ≈ 58.7 Hz
where
f: the frequency of the (1, 1, 0) tangential mode, in hertz (Hz)
√: the square root of the bracket that follows
≈: approximately equal to (values rounded)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: one half-wavelength along the length and one across the width combine into a mode at about 58.7 Hz, higher than either of the axial modes it combines (34.3 Hz and 47.6 Hz).
```

Like the axial formula, it assumes rigid walls and a perfectly rectangular room.

## Key takeaways
- Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families.
- Mode frequency depends on room dimensions and mode numbers.
- Wall flexibility and absorption modify the ideal result.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)
- [Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/rt60/rt60.html)
- [REW help — Room EQ Wizard](https://www.roomeqwizard.com/help/help_en-GB/html/index.html)

```formula
f_1 = c / (2L)
f_1 = 343 / (2 × 4.2) ≈ 40.8 Hz
where
f_1: the first axial mode, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, 343 metres per second (m/s)
L: the distance between the walls, 4.2 metres (m)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: the first mode is the frequency whose half-wavelength exactly spans the gap.
```
This divides 343 by 4.2 instead of by twice 4.2 (8.4). That gives 81.7 Hz, which is the second mode.
This divides 343 by four times the spacing (16.8) instead of twice it.
This multiplies 343 by 4.2 instead of dividing; the result isn't even a frequency.

```formula
f_n = nc / (2L)
f_1 = 1 × 343 / (2 × 4.2)
f_1 = 343 / 8.4 ≈ 40.8 Hz
f_2 = 2 × 40.8 ≈ 81.7 Hz
f_3 = 3 × 40.8 ≈ 122.5 Hz
where
f_n: the nth axial mode, in hertz (Hz)
n: the mode number, 1, 2, 3 …
f_1: the first mode, in hertz (Hz)
f_2: the second mode, in hertz (Hz)
f_3: the third mode, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, 343 metres per second (m/s)

Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: halve the wavelength to fit the gap: 343 ÷ 8.4 gives the first mode, and its multiples give the rest.
```

lessons.title: Relate modal frequencies to room position
lessons.summary: Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat.
lessons.body:
## Room dimensions and listener position

### Worked example

A small studio of 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m. Using the axial formula for each dimension:

```formula
f_1 = c / (2L)
f_1 = 1 × 343 / (2 × 5.0) = 34.3 Hz
f_1 = 1 × 343 / (2 × 3.6) ≈ 47.6 Hz
f_1 = 1 × 343 / (2 × 2.4) ≈ 71.5 Hz
where
f_1: the first (lowest) axial mode along one dimension, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound, 343 metres per second (m/s)
L: the dimension being tested: 5.0 m length, 3.6 m width, 2.4 m height
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: each dimension has its own lowest mode; the longest dimension gives the lowest one. Multiply each by 2, 3 … for the higher modes.
```

The same calculation in Python, for the first three modes of each dimension:

```python
c = 343
dims = {"length": 5.0, "width": 3.6,
        "height": 2.4}
for name, L in dims.items():
    # Each dimension has its own harmonics.
    modes = [round(n * c / (2 * L), 1)
             for n in (1, 2, 3)]
    print(f"{name:<6} {L} m: {modes}")
```

```output
length 5.0 m: [34.3, 68.6, 102.9]
width  3.6 m: [47.6, 95.3, 142.9]
height 2.4 m: [71.5, 142.9, 214.4]
```

Notice that 3.6 ÷ 2.4 = 1.5, so the width's third mode and the height's second land on the **same frequency, 142.9 Hz**. Coincident modal frequencies can produce strong response peaks, depending on how the sources excite them, the listener position and damping. Rooms whose dimensions are simple multiples of each other (a cube has particularly extensive degeneracy) bunch their modes; unrelated dimensions spread them out more evenly.

What a mode does at your seat depends on **where you sit**:

- For ideal rigid rectangular boundaries, each axial mode has pressure antinodes at its corresponding pair of walls. A general mode may still have nodes along other coordinates on a wall; corners are pressure antinodes of all these ideal modes.
- The first axial mode has a **pressure null** halfway between its walls. At the length midpoint, that ideal mode contributes no pressure; moving away can increase its contribution. The total response also contains direct sound and other modes, so it is not necessarily silent or boomy.
- So bass response varies dramatically with position. This is why many guides suggest avoiding the exact centre of the room for the listening position (Genelec suggests sitting in the front part of the room for music work, and at least 1 m from walls).

## Key takeaways
- Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat.
- Source excitation, damping and listener position all matter.
- Avoid treating a node of one mode as silence in the total sound field.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)
- [Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/rt60/rt60.html)
- [REW help — Room EQ Wizard](https://www.roomeqwizard.com/help/help_en-GB/html/index.html)

```formula
where
```

lessons.title: Estimate decay with Sabine’s equation
lessons.summary: Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay.
lessons.body:
## Reverberation and RT60

After a sound stops, its reflections take time to die away. **RT60** is the time for the sound level to fall by **60 dB**. Wallace Sabine's empirical equation (from experiments at Harvard around 1900) relates it to the room's volume and absorption. Use it to estimate how live a room will sound, and how much treatment you'd need to change that:

```formula
RT60 = 0.161V / A
A = Σ (S_i α_i)
where
RT60: the reverberation time, in seconds (s): how long the sound takes to fall by 60 decibels (dB) after the source stops
0.161: Sabine's constant for metric units, in seconds per metre (s/m); it comes from 24 × ln(10) ÷ 343 ≈ 0.161, where 343 m/s is the speed of sound
V: the room's volume, in cubic metres (m³)
A: the room's total absorption, in square metres (m²), also called metric sabins: the area of open window that would absorb the same amount
Σ: sigma, "add up the following for every surface"
i: a counter that runs over the room's surfaces (walls, floor, ceiling, panels)
S_i: the area of surface i, in square metres (m²)
α_i: alpha, the absorption coefficient of surface i: the effective fraction of incident energy not returned by that surface at the frequency considered, from 0 (perfect reflector) to 1 (perfect absorber)
In words: reverberation time grows with the room's volume and shrinks with how much absorbing surface it contains. Double the absorption and you halve RT60.
```

The total equivalent absorption area is each surface area multiplied by its frequency-dependent absorption coefficient, summed. Worked through for the 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m studio with bare surfaces averaging an absorption coefficient of 0.10, then with 10 m² of surface swapped for panels with an absorption coefficient of 0.90:

```formula
V = 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 = 43.2 m^3
S = 2 × (18 + 12 + 8.64) ≈ 77.3 m^2
A = 77.3 × 0.10 ≈ 7.73 m^2
RT60 = 0.161 × 43.2 / 7.73 ≈ 0.90 s
A_t = 7.73 − 10 × 0.10 + 10 × 0.90
A_t ≈ 15.73 m^2
RT60_t = 0.161 × 43.2 / 15.73 ≈ 0.44 s
where
V: the room's volume, in cubic metres (m³): length × width × height
S: the total surface area of the six faces, in square metres (m²): 2 × (5.0 × 3.6 + 5.0 × 2.4 + 3.6 × 2.4)
A: the bare room's total absorption, in square metres (m²): its area times the average absorption coefficient 0.10
RT60: the bare room's reverberation time, in seconds (s)
A_t: the treated room's absorption: remove 10 m² at 0.10, add 10 m² at 0.90
RT60_t: the treated room's reverberation time, in seconds (s)
0.161: Sabine's constant, in seconds per metre (s/m)
m: metres; m^2 is square metres, m^3 cubic metres
s: seconds
In words: ten square metres of good absorbers roughly doubles the room's absorption, so the reverberation time halves from about 0.9 s to about 0.44 s.
```

The same calculation as a Python script:

```python
import math

Lx, Ly, Lz = 5.0, 3.6, 2.4
V = Lx * Ly * Lz
S = 2 * (Lx*Ly + Lx*Lz + Ly*Lz)

A_bare = S * 0.10          # avg alpha 0.1
rt_bare = 0.161 * V / A_bare
# swap 10 m^2 of alpha 0.1 for 0.9 panels
A_tr = A_bare - 10 * 0.10 + 10 * 0.90
# The model is evaluated for one band.
rt_tr = 0.161 * V / A_tr

print(f"V={V:.1f} m3, S={S:.1f} m2")
print(f"bare:    RT60={rt_bare:.2f} s")
print(f"treated: RT60={rt_tr:.2f} s")
fs = 2000 * math.sqrt(rt_tr / V)
print(f"Schroeder ~{fs:.0f} Hz")
```

```output
V=43.2 m3, S=77.3 m2
bare:    RT60=0.90 s
treated: RT60=0.44 s
Schroeder ~202 Hz
```

Ten square metres of effective absorption halves the reverberation time. Two caveats:

- **Absorption coefficients depend on frequency.** A treatment that works at 2 kHz may do almost nothing at 100 Hz, so RT60 is quoted per octave band, and a room can be dead in the treble while still booming in the bass.
- **Sabine assumes a fairly live room with diffuse sound.** At higher broadly distributed absorption a diffuse-field Eyring model can improve the estimate; neither model is guaranteed for a strongly non-diffuse room, and in small rooms below the Schroeder frequency "reverberation time" is a rough description at best.

Control rooms are typically much drier than living rooms; recommended targets vary by standard and room size, so treat any single number as a guide.

## Key takeaways
- Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay.
- Sabine’s model uses room volume and equivalent absorption area.
- The diffuse-field and absorption assumptions limit its use, especially in small rooms.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)
- [Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/rt60/rt60.html)
- [REW help — Room EQ Wizard](https://www.roomeqwizard.com/help/help_en-GB/html/index.html)
